vr.5.11.30.line: I saw all the trusting wives of Ravana, yet my mind is not disturbed.
vr.5.11.30.claim: I saw them all, yet nothing in my mind has been stirred.

vr.5.11.31.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.11.31.line: The mind alone drives every sense, toward good or bad outcomes, and my mind is firmly settled on what is right.
vr.5.11.31.claim: The mind, not the eye, makes an act good or bad, and my mind is steady in what is right.

vr.5.11.32.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.11.32.line: I cannot look for Sita anywhere else, because when searching for a woman, one always searches among women.
vr.5.11.32.claim: There was nowhere else to look for her: a woman is searched for among women.

vr.5.11.34.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.11.34.line: I searched the entire inner palace with a pure mind, yet I do not see her.
vr.5.11.34.claim: I searched the whole inner palace with a clean mind, and still she is not here.

vr.5.13.3.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.3.line: I have searched all of Lanka for Rama, yet I cannot find Sita anywhere.
vr.5.13.3.claim: I have searched all of Lanka for Rama's sake, and still I cannot find her.

vr.5.13.17.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.17.line: If I report it, I am wrong, and if I stay silent, I am wrong. I do not see what I should do.
vr.5.13.17.claim: If I tell, it is wrong; if I keep silent, it is wrong. I cannot see what I should do.

vr.5.13.18.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.18.line: If I return to my lord without seeing Sita, my effort will be useless.
vr.5.13.18.claim: If I go back without finding her, what will all my effort have been worth?

vr.5.13.19.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.19.line: My leap across the sea and my entry into Lanka will have been for nothing, and I will have seen those demons for nothing.
vr.5.13.19.claim: My leap across the ocean, entering Lanka, facing the demons: all of it will have been for nothing.

vr.5.13.20.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.20.line: What will Sugriva and the other monkeys say when I get back to Kishkindha?
vr.5.13.20.claim: What will Sugriva say, and the others, and the two princes, when I come back?

vr.5.13.21.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.21.line: If I tell Rama I did not find Sita, he will give up his life.
vr.5.13.21.claim: If I tell Rama I did not find her, he will give up his life.

vr.5.13.35.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.35.line: I will not go back to Kishkindha because I cannot bear to see Sugriva without Sita.
vr.5.13.35.claim: So I will not go back to Kishkindha; I cannot face Sugriva without her.

vr.5.13.40.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.40.line: My good name, built from great deeds, is ruined forever because I did not find Sita.
vr.5.13.40.claim: The good name I built through fine deeds is broken, because I could not find her.

vr.5.13.41.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.41.line: I will live under a tree as a strict ascetic. I will not go back without seeing her.
vr.5.13.41.claim: I would rather live under the trees as an ascetic than go back without seeing her.

vr.5.13.44.speaker: Valmiki (narrator)
vr.5.13.44.line: He carried many kinds of sorrow in his mind, and he had not yet found the end of his grief.
vr.5.13.44.claim: Carrying many kinds of sorrow in his mind, he could not reach the far shore of his grief.

vr.5.13.47.speaker: Valmiki (narrator)
vr.5.13.47.line: He had not found Sita, and heavy with worry and grief, he began to think.
vr.5.13.47.claim: Not having found her, heavy with worry and grief, he began to think it through again.

vr.5.13.48.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.48.line: I will keep searching this city of Lanka again and again until I find the illustrious wife of Rama.
vr.5.13.48.claim: Until I find her, I will search this city again and again.

vr.5.13.50.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.50.line: I will stay right here, eating very little and keeping my senses in check, so that no one else dies because of me.
vr.5.13.50.claim: I will stay here, disciplined in food and senses, so that no one else is harmed by what I do.

vr.5.13.51.speaker: Hanuman
vr.5.13.51.line: This large Ashoka grove is full of massive trees. I will go there, since I have not searched it yet.
vr.5.13.51.claim: This great Ashoka grove I have not searched yet. I will go there.

vr.5.13.54.speaker: Valmiki (narrator)
vr.5.13.54.line: After a moment's thought he rose and bowed to Rama, Lakshmana, Sita and the gods.
vr.5.13.54.claim: After a moment's thought he rose, bowed to Rama, Lakshmana, Sita and the gods, and went on.

st.mbh.aruni_lies_in_breach.title: Aruni lies down in the broken dyke
st.mbh.aruni_lies_in_breach.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Paushya Parva (BORI 1.3, prose section)
st.mbh.aruni_lies_in_breach.teaching: Wholehearted commitment to a task given in trust opens learning that no amount of instruction can.
st.mbh.aruni_lies_in_breach.whole_arc_note: Do not turn this into a rule that one must suffer for a boss. The teacher notices he is missing, goes to find him and calls him out of the water. The story is about wholehearted ownership inside a relationship of trust, and it ends in blessing.

st.mbh.upamanyu_refuses_the_cake.title: Upamanyu, starved by every test, still will not eat before offering
st.mbh.upamanyu_refuses_the_cake.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Paushya Parva (BORI 1.3, prose with the Ashvin hymn)
st.mbh.upamanyu_refuses_the_cake.teaching: Integrity that holds when you are at your lowest and unobserved is what makes a person fit to receive.
st.mbh.upamanyu_refuses_the_cake.whole_arc_note: The text calls this a test and shows the teacher searching the forest for him at dusk. Do not present it as praise for a mentor who withholds food. Read it with the next scene, where the fellow student Veda, having lived this hardness, refuses to impose it on his own students.

st.mbh.veda_will_not_pass_it_on.title: Veda, who suffered as a student, decides his students will not
st.mbh.veda_will_not_pass_it_on.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Paushya Parva (BORI 1.3, prose section)
st.mbh.veda_will_not_pass_it_on.teaching: Hardship you lived through can be turned into care for those who come after you.
st.mbh.veda_will_not_pass_it_on.whole_arc_note: Veda does not condemn his own teacher and his training did bear fruit. The point is narrower and kinder: pain you have known can become the reason you spare others. Uttanka turning out upright shows gentleness did not ruin him.

st.mbh.agni_cursed_for_truth.title: Agni is cursed for telling the truth
st.mbh.agni_cursed_for_truth.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Pauloma Parva (BORI 1.5 to 1.7)
st.mbh.agni_cursed_for_truth.teaching: One who is questioned as a witness and conceals what he knows shares the wrong; honesty may be punished and still be what restores you.
st.mbh.agni_cursed_for_truth.whole_arc_note: The text does not say truth is always painless or that Agni was simply right. It shows a real bind, an unjust punishment, a dignified protest and a restoration. Do not clip it into "always tell the truth and all will be well".

st.mbh.ruru_gives_half_his_life.title: Ruru gives half his life for Pramadvara
st.mbh.ruru_gives_half_his_life.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Pauloma Parva (BORI 1.8 to 1.9)
st.mbh.ruru_gives_half_his_life.teaching: Love in this text is measured by what of your own life you are willing to share.
st.mbh.ruru_gives_half_his_life.whole_arc_note: This is a story of a boon, and the text is clear it was an exception arranged by the gods. Never offer it to a griever as if loss can be reversed. Its use is as an image of love that shares its own life. It also continues: Ruru's grief hardens into a vow to kill every snake, which the next episode corrects.

st.mbh.ruru_hatred_of_all_snakes.title: Ruru, hurt by one snake, vows to kill them all
st.mbh.ruru_hatred_of_all_snakes.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Pauloma Parva (BORI 1.9 to 1.12)
st.mbh.ruru_hatred_of_all_snakes.teaching: Pain caused by one must not become punishment of all who look like them.
st.mbh.ruru_hatred_of_all_snakes.whole_arc_note: The text does not mock his fear, which came from a real wound. It shows what the wound did next: it spread from the one who harmed him to everyone who resembled it.

st.mbh.jaratkaru_sees_his_ancestors.title: Jaratkaru sees his ancestors hanging by a thread
st.mbh.jaratkaru_sees_his_ancestors.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Astika Parva (BORI 1.13 and 1.41 to 1.42)
st.mbh.jaratkaru_sees_his_ancestors.teaching: A person stands in a line of givers; what you owe those who made you is part of your dharma, even on a path of renunciation.
st.mbh.jaratkaru_sees_his_ancestors.whole_arc_note: The text honours both things: his vow of austerity and his debt to his line. It does not say everyone must marry. He answers the call on terms he sets, and he remains an ascetic.

st.mbh.jaratkaru_wife_must_wake_him.title: Jaratkaru's wife must choose between his anger and his duty
st.mbh.jaratkaru_wife_must_wake_him.teaching: When both paths carry a cost, choose by which loss is heavier, and say plainly why you chose.
st.mbh.jaratkaru_wife_must_wake_him.whole_arc_note: Do not retell this as a wife who failed or as a model husband. The text gives her the careful reasoning and the right call, and gives him a rigid vow. What it shows is a person acting rightly inside a relationship with no margin for error, and the good that came from her choice.

st.mbh.vinata_impatience_and_wager.title: Vinata cannot wait, and then cannot refuse a bet
st.mbh.vinata_impatience_and_wager.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Astika Parva (BORI 1.14 and 1.18 to 1.20)
st.mbh.vinata_impatience_and_wager.teaching: What is still forming is harmed by being forced open, and comparison is what makes us force it.
st.mbh.vinata_impatience_and_wager.whole_arc_note: The curse comes with its own cure: patience with what is still forming. Kadru's cheating is not excused, and she in turn curses her own sons who refused to help her deceive. The story is not a scolding of Vinata. It shows comparison pushing a person into two bad decisions and patience undoing them.

st.mbh.garuda_frees_his_mother.title: Garuda is born into his mother's debt and pays it without tasting the prize
st.mbh.garuda_frees_his_mother.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Astika Parva (BORI 1.23 to 1.30)
st.mbh.garuda_frees_his_mother.teaching: Great strength shows its worth when it serves someone else's freedom and leaves the prize untouched.
st.mbh.garuda_frees_his_mother.whole_arc_note: Garuda does not accept the bondage as fate and he does not rage at the snakes either. He asks the terms, meets them exactly, and keeps faith with everyone, including Indra. The unfair bet is ended by strength used without greed.

st.mbh.shesha_leaves_his_brothers.title: Shesha walks away from a family that lives on envy
st.mbh.shesha_leaves_his_brothers.teaching: You may leave what is poisoned by envy; let the steadiness you save become something others can stand on.
st.mbh.shesha_leaves_his_brothers.whole_arc_note: The text does not call him a deserter. Brahma says "I know your brothers" and does not send him back. Leaving is honoured, and it is followed by responsibility, not by withdrawal for its own sake.

st.mbh.parikshit_tired_and_cruel_for_a_m.title: Parikshit, exhausted, insults a silent sage
st.mbh.parikshit_tired_and_cruel_for_a_m.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Astika Parva (BORI 1.36 to 1.40)
st.mbh.parikshit_tired_and_cruel_for_a_m.teaching: A single act done in tired anger can outrun a lifetime of good conduct; remorse is right, and it does not undo the act.
st.mbh.parikshit_tired_and_cruel_for_a_m.whole_arc_note: The text holds two things together. Parikshit was a just man and this was one moment of exhaustion, and one moment was enough. The sage himself had forgiven him at once. Do not clip the story at the insult or at the remorse; the consequence arrives anyway, and his son's revenge after it becomes the frame of the whole epic.

st.mbh.shamika_corrects_his_angry_son.title: Shamika tells his son the curse was wrong, though it was for him
st.mbh.shamika_corrects_his_angry_son.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Astika Parva (BORI 1.37 to 1.38)
st.mbh.shamika_corrects_his_angry_son.teaching: Anger steals the merit that hard practice has stored; a parent keeps correcting a child, however grown or gifted.
st.mbh.shamika_corrects_his_angry_son.whole_arc_note: Shamika's forbearance is his free choice as the injured party and as a man under a vow. It is not a rule that the wronged must stay silent: he speaks sharply to his own son and acts at once to limit the harm. Keep both the kshama and the correction.

st.mbh.astika_stops_the_snake_sacrifice.title: Astika, a boy, ends a king's war on a whole race
st.mbh.astika_stops_the_snake_sacrifice.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Astika Parva (BORI 1.46 to 1.53)
st.mbh.astika_stops_the_snake_sacrifice.teaching: Revenge that began with one wrong will consume the innocent unless someone asks, at the right moment, for it to stop.
st.mbh.astika_stops_the_snake_sacrifice.whole_arc_note: The king's grief for his father is real and the text does not belittle it. What it stops is vengeance spreading from one culprit to a whole people. Astika wins by honouring the king first and by perfect timing, not by defiance.

st.mbh.shakuntala_before_the_king.title: Shakuntala states the truth to a king who denies knowing her
st.mbh.shakuntala_before_the_king.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva, Shakuntalopakhyana (BORI 1.62 to 1.69; her speech 1.68 to 1.69)
st.mbh.shakuntala_before_the_king.teaching: The self within is the witness of every act; there is no dharma higher than truth, and a person denied may say so to anyone.
st.mbh.shakuntala_before_the_king.whole_arc_note: In the Mahabharata there is no ring and no curse of forgetfulness. The king knows and denies, and the text lets her rebuke stand in full. Do not soften it into a misunderstanding, and do not make her patient: she is truthful, angry and unafraid, and she is vindicated.

st.mbh.kacha_learns_among_enemies.title: Kacha studies for years in a house that wants him dead
st.mbh.kacha_learns_among_enemies.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva, Yayati upakhyana (BORI 1.71)
st.mbh.kacha_learns_among_enemies.teaching: The one who gives you knowledge is owed the loyalty you owe a parent, whatever camp he belongs to.
st.mbh.kacha_learns_among_enemies.whole_arc_note: Kacha came with a hidden purpose and the text does not hide that. What it honours is that he never betrays the teacher in conduct, even when betrayal was the easy exit. The story continues with Devayani's proposal and the two curses.

st.mbh.devayani_refused_by_kacha.title: Devayani is refused by the man she saved
st.mbh.devayani_refused_by_kacha.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva, Yayati upakhyana (BORI 1.72)
st.mbh.devayani_refused_by_kacha.teaching: Help freely given creates gratitude and does not create a claim on another person's heart.
st.mbh.devayani_refused_by_kacha.whole_arc_note: The text does not make either one a villain. Her love was real and her help was real. His no was honest. Do not clip this to "she was wrong to be angry" or "he was ungrateful". It shows that being owed gratitude is different from being owed love.

st.mbh.devayani_in_the_well_and_her_fath.title: Devayani, thrown in a well, is counselled to forbear and then backed completely
st.mbh.devayani_in_the_well_and_her_fath.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva, Yayati upakhyana (BORI 1.73 to 1.75)
st.mbh.devayani_in_the_well_and_her_fath.teaching: Mastering anger is strength, and a self-respecting person does not go on living among those who hold them in contempt.
st.mbh.devayani_in_the_well_and_her_fath.whole_arc_note: Shukra's verses on conquering anger are real teaching and sit in this chapter. But the father delivers them and then stands with his daughter completely. Never quote the akrodha verses to a wronged person without the second half, where the wrong is named and redressed.

st.mbh.sharmishtha_accepts_servitude_for.title: Sharmishtha gives up her rank so her people keep their teacher
st.mbh.sharmishtha_accepts_servitude_for.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva, Yayati upakhyana (BORI 1.75)
st.mbh.sharmishtha_accepts_servitude_for.teaching: Owning a wrong fully, at cost to your pride, can protect many people besides yourself.
st.mbh.sharmishtha_accepts_servitude_for.whole_arc_note: Do not present this as simple punishment or as a model of meekness. She owns a real fault and pays for it on behalf of others, and the text then gives her the lineage. Devayani's victory also turns bitter. Both women are left with something unresolved.

st.mbh.yayati_desire_never_ends_by_feedi.title: Yayati spends a thousand borrowed years on pleasure and finds it has no bottom
st.mbh.yayati_desire_never_ends_by_feedi.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva, Yayati upakhyana (BORI 1.78 to 1.80)
st.mbh.yayati_desire_never_ends_by_feedi.teaching: Desire is not exhausted by being fed; it grows with feeding, and peace comes from letting the thirst go.
st.mbh.yayati_desire_never_ends_by_feedi.whole_arc_note: Yayati is not painted as a sinner. He enjoys within dharma and still finds no end, and that is what gives his verse its weight. Do not use the verse to scold ordinary wanting. It is a man's own finding after the fullest possible trial, and the story continues with his pride and fall in heaven.

st.mbh.puru_gives_his_youth.title: Puru, the youngest, takes on his father's old age
st.mbh.puru_gives_his_youth.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva, Yayati upakhyana (BORI 1.79)
st.mbh.puru_gives_his_youth.teaching: What is given to a parent freely and without calculation returns as blessing.
st.mbh.puru_gives_his_youth.whole_arc_note: The text praises Puru and it also shows the father learning that what he asked for did not satisfy him. Do not turn this into a demand that children surrender their lives to parents' wants. It is a gift freely given, and it sits beside Yayati's own admission that the wanting was the problem. The elder brothers are not monsters for saying no.

st.mbh.yayati_falls_from_heaven.title: Yayati falls from heaven for one proud sentence
st.mbh.yayati_falls_from_heaven.teaching: Contempt for others burns up what a lifetime of effort has earned.
st.mbh.yayati_falls_from_heaven.whole_arc_note: The same man who saw through desire is caught by pride in his own renunciation. Keep both halves. He is restored by honesty about his fault and by refusing a shortcut, not by being excused.

st.mbh.shantanu_silent_until_the_eighth.title: Shantanu keeps his promise of silence while seven sons are drowned
st.mbh.shantanu_silent_until_the_eighth.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (BORI 1.92 to 1.93)
st.mbh.shantanu_silent_until_the_eighth.teaching: There are promises a person keeps at great cost, and there is a point where speaking is the truer act.
st.mbh.shantanu_silent_until_the_eighth.whole_arc_note: The text gives a hidden reason that makes Ganga's act a release and not a murder. Shantanu did not know that. His silence is shown as painful and his speaking as right for him. Do not teach from this that one should stay silent in a marriage about what is unbearable, and do not make Ganga a villain.

st.mbh.devavrata_becomes_bhishma.title: Devavrata gives up throne and marriage so his father can marry
st.mbh.devavrata_becomes_bhishma.teaching: A vow made out of love for a parent can be magnificent and binding beyond anything its maker foresaw.
st.mbh.devavrata_becomes_bhishma.whole_arc_note: The Mahabharata honours the vow and then spends seventeen books showing its cost: no heir of his own, two short-lived half-brothers, a throne he must guard and cannot fill, and silence in the dice hall. Never present it as a simple model. It is greatness with a price that others also pay. Shantanu, for his part, never asked.

st.mbh.bhishma_refuses_satyavati.title: Bhishma will not break his vow even when the vow's own beneficiary begs him
st.mbh.bhishma_refuses_satyavati.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (BORI 1.97 to 1.99)
st.mbh.bhishma_refuses_satyavati.teaching: A person's word, once given as a vow, is not altered because circumstances have made it inconvenient.
st.mbh.bhishma_refuses_satyavati.whole_arc_note: The text admires his steadiness and shows what it cost. He solves the problem without breaking his word, yet the solution is flawed. Do not flatten this into "always keep your word" or "he was rigid". Both readings are held. Satyavati is not wrong to ask.

st.mbh.mandavya_punished_out_of_proporti.title: Mandavya, impaled for a crime he did not commit, asks Dharma why
st.mbh.mandavya_punished_out_of_proporti.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva, Animandavya upakhyana (BORI 1.101)
st.mbh.mandavya_punished_out_of_proporti.teaching: Punishment must fit the act and the understanding of the one who acted; even Dharma answers for excess.
st.mbh.mandavya_punished_out_of_proporti.whole_arc_note: The text lets a wronged man hold the cosmic order itself to account and win. It does not tell him his suffering was fair. Do not use this to say "everything is your past karma": the sage hears that answer and rejects its proportion.

st.mbh.gandhari_binds_her_eyes.title: Gandhari learns her husband is blind and covers her own eyes
st.mbh.gandhari_binds_her_eyes.teaching: A vow taken freely to share another's condition becomes a source of inner power.
st.mbh.gandhari_binds_her_eyes.whole_arc_note: The tradition reads this as a vow of fidelity and shared fate freely taken, and as the source of her tapas and moral authority. It must not be offered as a rule that a wife should shrink to her husband's limits. In the Udyoga and Stri Parvas she speaks harder truths to the men than anyone, so the vow did not silence her.

st.mbh.dhritarashtra_cannot_give_up_the_.title: Dhritarashtra is warned about his newborn son and keeps him
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_cannot_give_up_the_.teaching: Affection that cannot refuse its child anything becomes the child's ruin and the family's.
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_cannot_give_up_the_.whole_arc_note: This is not a call to abandon a child because of omens, and no modern reader should hear it that way. What the text is tracing is a parent's pattern that begins here: seeing, being told, and not acting because love will not let him. The cost arrives in the dice hall and at Kurukshetra, and he names his own failure in the Stri Parva.

st.mbh.pandu_one_arrow.title: Pandu's one careless arrow changes the rest of his life
st.mbh.pandu_one_arrow.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (BORI 1.109 to 1.110)
st.mbh.pandu_one_arrow.teaching: A moment's heedlessness can set the terms of a whole life; what remains is how one lives inside those terms.
st.mbh.pandu_one_arrow.whole_arc_note: The sage himself says the fault was the cruelty of the timing, not hunting as such. Pandu's remorse is real and so is his over-correction. His wives will not accept being discarded for his penance. And the curse is not escaped: carry the story to Adi 116.

st.mbh.madri_entrusts_her_sons.title: Madri admits she could not love Kunti's sons as her own and asks Kunti to love hers
st.mbh.madri_entrusts_her_sons.teaching: Knowing the limits of your own impartiality, and entrusting children to the one who has none, is itself an act of love.
st.mbh.madri_entrusts_her_sons.whole_arc_note: Madri's death on the pyre is part of the text and must not be praised or offered as a model; this story is never for anyone at risk. What is usable is her honesty about her limits and Kunti's lifelong answer to that trust, which the Yaksha Prashna completes.

st.mbh.bhima_poisoned_duryodhana_resentm.title: Duryodhana, beaten at every game, decides to remove his cousin
st.mbh.bhima_poisoned_duryodhana_resentm.teaching: Envy that cannot bear another's strength stops trying to grow and starts trying to remove.
st.mbh.bhima_poisoned_duryodhana_resentm.whole_arc_note: Two sides are true. Bhima's roughness was thoughtless and it humiliated others. Duryodhana's answer was attempted murder. The Pandavas respond with watchfulness, not accusation, because they have no power at court. The pattern set here, envy answered by scheming, runs to the lac house and the dice.

st.mbh.drona_son_cries_for_milk.title: Drona watches his son dance for joy over flour stirred in water
st.mbh.drona_son_cries_for_milk.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva; Drona's own account to Bhishma (vulgate/Gita Press Adi 130; partly in BORI 1.122)
st.mbh.drona_son_cries_for_milk.teaching: A parent can bear his own want; seeing his child go without, and be mocked for it, is what moves him.
st.mbh.drona_son_cries_for_milk.whole_arc_note: The poverty was honourable and the love is plain. The wound it left drives everything Drona does afterwards, including what he asks of his students and of Ekalavya. Tell the tenderness and do not hide where it leads.

st.mbh.drupada_friendship_is_between_equ.title: Drupada tells his boyhood friend that kings have no poor friends
st.mbh.drupada_friendship_is_between_equ.teaching: Contempt shown to an old friend in need is remembered longer than any kindness, by both sides.
st.mbh.drupada_friendship_is_between_equ.whole_arc_note: Drupada's words are quoted in the text as the insult, not as wisdom, and they cost him half his realm. But Drona's answer does not end it. Drupada performs a rite for a son to kill Drona, and that son does. The story is honest about the hurt and about what nursing it for decades produced.

st.mbh.ekalavya_shut_out_and_self_taught.title: Ekalavya, refused as a student, teaches himself and pays for it
st.mbh.ekalavya_shut_out_and_self_taught.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (BORI 1.123.10 to 39)
st.mbh.ekalavya_shut_out_and_self_taught.teaching: Faith and practice can make a master without anyone's permission, and a person's truthfulness remains theirs even when what is asked of them is harsh.
st.mbh.ekalavya_shut_out_and_self_taught.whole_arc_note: Follow the tradition here: it holds Ekalavya up for guru-bhakti and truthfulness, and it does not call Drona's act gentle. Drona was bound by a public promise to Arjuna and by his service to the Kuru house, and the text lets the cost stand without explaining it away. Never use this to tell someone shut out that they should accept it. What belongs to Ekalavya is that no one's refusal stopped him from becoming excellent, and that his integrity was his own.

st.mbh.arjuna_sees_only_the_eye.title: Arjuna sees only the eye of the bird
st.mbh.arjuna_sees_only_the_eye.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (BORI 1.123.45 to 66)
st.mbh.arjuna_sees_only_the_eye.teaching: Skill is completed by attention that has narrowed to one point and holds nothing else.
st.mbh.arjuna_sees_only_the_eye.whole_arc_note: The others are not mocked. They saw what was really there. The test shows what attention is when it stops taking in everything available. It also sits a few verses after Ekalavya, and the text lets both stand together.

st.mbh.arjuna_practises_in_the_dark.title: Arjuna notices his hand finds his mouth in the dark, and starts practising at night
st.mbh.arjuna_practises_in_the_dark.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (BORI 1.123.1 to 9)
st.mbh.arjuna_practises_in_the_dark.teaching: Mastery belongs to the one who turns an accident into a method and practises when no one requires it.
st.mbh.arjuna_practises_in_the_dark.whole_arc_note: The excellence is Arjuna's own doing, drawn from an ordinary moment. The promise Drona makes here is the same promise that later weighs on Ekalavya; keep that link in view when the two stories are used together.

st.mbh.karna_at_the_tournament.title: Karna is asked for his lineage and has no answer
st.mbh.karna_at_the_tournament.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha-daha Parva, the display of arms (BORI 1.126 to 1.127)
st.mbh.karna_at_the_tournament.teaching: A person shut out for his birth will give everything to the one who first treats him as an equal.
st.mbh.karna_at_the_tournament.whole_arc_note: The insult is real and the text makes us feel it. Duryodhana's gesture is real too, and it is also useful to him. That one act of recognition purchases a loyalty that carries Karna through the dice hall and to his death, and he says so himself to Krishna in the Udyoga Parva. Kunti, watching, recognises her son and faints, and says nothing.

st.mbh.karna_bows_to_adhiratha.title: Karna, minutes after being crowned, bows to the charioteer who raised him
st.mbh.karna_bows_to_adhiratha.teaching: Honouring the parents who raised you, at the moment the world is judging you by them, is its own nobility.
st.mbh.karna_bows_to_adhiratha.whole_arc_note: This is the root of Karna's later answer to Krishna and to Kunti: Radha and Adhiratha are his parents because they did what parents do. Keep the taunt in the telling; the dignity of the bow is measured against it.

st.mbh.vidura_warns_in_code.title: Vidura warns Yudhishthira in words only he will understand
st.mbh.vidura_warns_in_code.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha-daha Parva (BORI 1.130 to 1.133)
st.mbh.vidura_warns_in_code.teaching: When open opposition is impossible, the wise still find the act that protects, and say what must be said in the way it can be heard.
st.mbh.vidura_warns_in_code.whole_arc_note: Vidura is the epic's picture of the honest insider with no authority. He never deserts the king he serves and never joins the wrong. He finds the narrow act that is still possible. Dhritarashtra's part must be kept: he knew enough to refuse and did not.

st.mbh.a_year_in_the_house_of_lac.title: The Pandavas live a year in a house they know is built to burn
st.mbh.a_year_in_the_house_of_lac.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha-daha Parva (BORI 1.134 to 1.137)
st.mbh.a_year_in_the_house_of_lac.teaching: When you cannot yet leave a danger, live in it awake: show nothing, learn every exit and prepare your own.
st.mbh.a_year_in_the_house_of_lac.whole_arc_note: Do not clip the cost. Purochana burns, and so do a Nishada woman and her five sons who had come to the feast and slept there, and whose bodies let the Kauravas believe the plot worked. The text records it and calls them driven by time. It is not offered as clean.

st.mbh.bhima_keeps_watch_over_his_sleepi.title: Bhima watches his mother sleep on the bare ground
st.mbh.bhima_keeps_watch_over_his_sleepi.teaching: The one who carries everyone is allowed his grief, and keeps watch all the same.
st.mbh.bhima_keeps_watch_over_his_sleepi.whole_arc_note: The grief and the anger are both given full voice. He does not act on the anger because the time and the elder's word are not with him. Do not read this as suppression: the text lets the strongest man in the story cry over his sleeping family.

st.mbh.hidimba_asks_kunti.title: Hidimba, an outsider, asks the mother for her son
st.mbh.hidimba_asks_kunti.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Hidimba-vadha Parva (BORI 1.139 to 1.143)
st.mbh.hidimba_asks_kunti.teaching: One who has given up everything to come to you in good faith is to be received, not judged by where she came from.
st.mbh.hidimba_asks_kunti.whole_arc_note: The family's first response is suspicion, and the text records it. What changes it is her direct appeal to the mother and the elder's insistence on dharma over fear. The terms have a limit, and she keeps them. Her son gives his life for them at Kurukshetra.

st.mbh.brahmin_family_decides_who_will_g.title: A family argues over which of them will go to the demon
st.mbh.brahmin_family_decides_who_will_g.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Baka-vadha Parva (BORI 1.145 to 1.147)
st.mbh.brahmin_family_decides_who_will_g.teaching: In a family's worst hour each one's love shows as readiness to take the blow, and rescue often comes from someone who simply overheard.
st.mbh.brahmin_family_decides_who_will_g.whole_arc_note: The scene is one of the most ordinary and tender in the epic: no heroes, only a family doing arithmetic that cannot be done. The father's despair speech is honest and is not corrected by argument. Help comes from a neighbour who was listening. Keep the brahmin's refusal; he would rather die than be saved by a wrong.

st.mbh.kunti_offers_her_son_for_her_host.title: Kunti repays her hosts with the one thing she has
st.mbh.kunti_offers_her_son_for_her_host.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Baka-vadha Parva (BORI 1.148 to 1.150)
st.mbh.kunti_offers_her_son_for_her_host.teaching: A favour received is repaid in greater measure, and gratitude is shown in what you are willing to risk.
st.mbh.kunti_offers_her_son_for_her_host.whole_arc_note: Kunti's offer rests on real knowledge of her son, not recklessness, and she gives her reasoning to the son who questions her. It is gratitude acted on, and it is also a mother trusting what she raised.

st.mbh.vishvamitra_shame_on_this_power.title: Vishvamitra, a king with an army, is beaten by a sage and changes his life
st.mbh.vishvamitra_shame_on_this_power.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Chaitraratha Parva, Vasishtha upakhyana (BORI 1.165)
st.mbh.vishvamitra_shame_on_this_power.teaching: Outer force meets its limit before inner power; seeing that clearly can turn a person toward a different kind of strength.
st.mbh.vishvamitra_shame_on_this_power.whole_arc_note: The change begins in wounded pride and greed, and the text does not pretend otherwise. His road is long and includes the killing of Vasishtha's sons through Kalmashapada. A humiliating defeat can redirect a life; it does not purify it at once.

st.mbh.vasishtha_cannot_die_of_grief.title: Vasishtha, grieving a hundred sons, hears a voice behind him
st.mbh.vasishtha_cannot_die_of_grief.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Chaitraratha Parva, Vasishtha upakhyana (BORI 1.166 to 1.168)
st.mbh.vasishtha_cannot_die_of_grief.teaching: Even the wisest can be flattened by loss; what calls a person back is often a life that still depends on theirs.
st.mbh.vasishtha_cannot_die_of_grief.whole_arc_note: This is a self_harm_theme story and must never reach anyone at risk. The text does not praise the attempts; the elements themselves refuse him. What turns him is not an argument. It is the sound of something still alive that needs him. He does not take vengeance at any point.

st.mbh.aurva_puts_his_anger_in_the_ocean.title: Aurva is told to let go of a justified rage and asks where it should go
st.mbh.aurva_puts_his_anger_in_the_ocean.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Chaitraratha Parva, Aurva upakhyana (BORI 1.169 to 1.171)
st.mbh.aurva_puts_his_anger_in_the_ocean.teaching: Anger born of real injustice is not to be suppressed into oneself or loosed on the world; it must be given a place where it does not destroy.
st.mbh.aurva_puts_his_anger_in_the_ocean.whole_arc_note: The text takes Aurva's argument seriously and quotes it at length. The elders do not say "forgive and forget". They ask him not to destroy the innocent with the guilty, and they help him find where the fire can live. Anger is contained, never denied.

st.mbh.arjuna_unknown_at_the_svayamvara.title: Arjuna, in a beggar's deerskin, stands up where kings have failed
st.mbh.arjuna_unknown_at_the_svayamvara.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Draupadi-svayamvara Parva (BORI 1.176 to 1.181)
st.mbh.arjuna_unknown_at_the_svayamvara.teaching: What a person can do is not announced by their present circumstances.
st.mbh.arjuna_unknown_at_the_svayamvara.whole_arc_note: He does not announce who he is, before or after. The worth is shown by the act alone. The fury of the kings at being bested by a nobody is part of the scene. The CE does not contain the rejection of Karna that popular tellings include; do not add it.

st.mbh.drupada_who_took_my_daughter.title: Drupada does not know who has taken his daughter home
st.mbh.drupada_who_took_my_daughter.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Draupadi-svayamvara and Vaivahika Parvas (BORI 1.184 to 1.187)
st.mbh.drupada_who_took_my_daughter.teaching: A parent's fear for a child's choice is best met by finding out who the person is, from how they live.
st.mbh.drupada_who_took_my_daughter.whole_arc_note: Drupada's fear is a parent's fear and the text gives it without mockery. He does not storm in. He observes, tests gently and asks. The marriage question that follows is a separate matter the text settles by Vyasa.

st.mbh.given_the_wasteland.title: The Pandavas are given the barren half and build a city on it
st.mbh.given_the_wasteland.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Viduragamana and Rajyalambha Parvas (BORI 1.195 to 1.199)
st.mbh.given_the_wasteland.teaching: What is given grudgingly can be made great by those who put their effort into building it.
st.mbh.given_the_wasteland.whole_arc_note: The division was unequal and the text knows it. Yudhishthira's acceptance is a choice made from strength, with allies and options, not advice to the powerless to take scraps. And it does not buy peace: their success is what provokes the dice game.

st.mbh.sunda_upasunda_and_the_rule.title: Two inseparable brothers destroy each other, and five brothers make a rule
st.mbh.sunda_upasunda_and_the_rule.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Arjuna-vanavasa Parva, Sundopasundopakhyana (BORI 1.200 to 1.205)
st.mbh.sunda_upasunda_and_the_rule.teaching: Those who are closest should set their boundaries before a conflict of desire tests them.
st.mbh.sunda_upasunda_and_the_rule.whole_arc_note: The lesson Narada draws is practical and falls on the brothers, not on the woman. Tilottama is an instrument of the gods and is honoured by Brahma. The usable point is the Pandavas' response: agree on boundaries while you are still on good terms.

st.mbh.arjuna_will_not_take_the_loophole.title: Arjuna breaks a rule for a good reason and refuses to be excused
st.mbh.arjuna_will_not_take_the_loophole.teaching: Dharma is not to be kept through a technicality; whoever breaks an agreement for a good reason still honours its price.
st.mbh.arjuna_will_not_take_the_loophole.whole_arc_note: Both decisions are his: to break the rule for someone else's need, and to refuse an exemption made for his sake. Yudhishthira's offer is generous and reasonable, and Arjuna still declines. This is integrity about one's own word, not a standard to impose on others.

st.mbh.jarita_and_her_fledglings_in_the_.title: Jarita and her four chicks in the burning forest
st.mbh.jarita_and_her_fledglings_in_the_.source_ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Khandava-daha Parva, Sharngakopakhyana (BORI 1.220 to 1.225)
st.mbh.jarita_and_her_fledglings_in_the_.teaching: Sometimes love means letting the other go to safety, and trusting what cannot be controlled.
st.mbh.jarita_and_her_fledglings_in_the_.whole_arc_note: Do not make Jarita a mother who abandoned her children. The text has her agonise, has the children insist, and has her return at the first moment. The absent father's anxiety and her anger at him are both kept, and she is not asked to pretend otherwise.

st.mbh.narada_asks_do_you.title: Narada asks the new king a hundred questions beginning "do you"
st.mbh.narada_asks_do_you.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Sabha-kriya / Lokapala-sabhakhyana Parva, the Kaccid adhyaya (BORI 2.5). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.narada_asks_do_you.teaching: The time to examine how you are running your life is when everything is going well.
st.mbh.narada_asks_do_you.whole_arc_note: The questions come at the height of success, which is when they are least asked. They are about care for dependents and one's own discipline, not about strategy for winning.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_asks_krishna_for_the.title: Yudhishthira distrusts the yes of everyone around him and sends for Krishna
st.mbh.yudhishthira_asks_krishna_for_the.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Mantra Parva (BORI 2.12 to 2.15). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_asks_krishna_for_the.teaching: Before a great undertaking, seek the one counsellor who has no reason to flatter you, and hear the obstacle named.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_asks_krishna_for_the.whole_arc_note: Yudhishthira's caution is treated as wisdom, not weakness, and it is what draws out honest counsel. He does not overcome fear by bravado. He finds one adviser with nothing to gain, hears the real obstacle, feels the fear, and then proceeds with a specific plan.

st.mbh.krishna_and_the_hundred_offences.title: Krishna bears a hundred insults because he promised, and then stops
st.mbh.krishna_and_the_hundred_offences.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Arghabhiharana and Shishupala-vadha Parvas (BORI 2.33 to 2.42). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.krishna_and_the_hundred_offences.teaching: Forbearance is a strength when it is chosen and has a limit; the limit, once reached, is to be stated and held.
st.mbh.krishna_and_the_hundred_offences.whole_arc_note: This is forbearance with a boundary, and both parts are essential. The patience was a promise freely made to someone he loved, kept to the letter. It was never unlimited, and when it ended he said why, publicly, before acting. Do not use it to tell anyone to absorb abuse, and do not strip out the hundred to make it a tale of quick retaliation.

st.mbh.duryodhana_falls_in_the_pool.title: Duryodhana walks into a wall and falls into a pool while his cousins' household laughs
st.mbh.duryodhana_falls_in_the_pool.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva opening (BORI 2.43; retold by him at 2.46). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.duryodhana_falls_in_the_pool.teaching: A small humiliation, replayed and fed, grows into a grievance large enough to justify anything.
st.mbh.duryodhana_falls_in_the_pool.whole_arc_note: The embarrassment is real and anyone would feel it. The text shows what he does with it: he replays it, enlarges it, and makes it a reason. Yudhishthira had clothes sent to him, which he does not mention. The line "the blind man's son is blind" from popular tellings is not in the critical text and should not be attributed to Draupadi.

st.mbh.duryodhana_names_his_envy.title: Duryodhana, who has everything, tells his father he cannot bear what his cousins have
st.mbh.duryodhana_names_his_envy.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (BORI 2.43 to 2.50). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.duryodhana_names_his_envy.teaching: Envy makes a person poor in the middle of plenty, and it will dress itself as ambition if you let it.
st.mbh.duryodhana_names_his_envy.whole_arc_note: The text lets envy speak in its own voice at length and gives the father's sound answer beside it, so the reader sees both the pain and the choice. His threats of self-harm are spoken as leverage and also show how consuming the state is. The remedy named by Dhritarashtra is right and is not followed; the cost is the whole war.

st.mbh.dhritarashtra_knows_and_gives_in.title: Dhritarashtra sees the dice game is wrong, is warned, and orders it anyway
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_knows_and_gives_in.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (BORI 2.45 to 2.52). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_knows_and_gives_in.teaching: Calling a choice fate, because refusing a loved one is painful, is how the clear-sighted go wrong.
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_knows_and_gives_in.whole_arc_note: The text is exact about this pattern and repeats it for thirteen years: he sees, he is advised, he sighs about fate, he yields. It never excuses him, and in the end he says himself that he did not listen. Do not let "it was destiny" stand as the teaching. It is the evasion the story is exposing.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_goes_to_the_game.title: Yudhishthira knows the game is a trap and goes because he was called
st.mbh.yudhishthira_goes_to_the_game.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (BORI 2.52 to 2.53). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_goes_to_the_game.teaching: A rule kept without discernment can deliver you to those who know your rule.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_goes_to_the_game.whole_arc_note: The tradition does not make Yudhishthira blameless here; Bhima, Draupadi and Balarama all hold him to account later, and he accepts it. It also does not make him a simple addict: he walks in bound by vow and by deference. The usable truth is how a virtue held without discernment becomes the opening.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_cannot_stop.title: Yudhishthira loses, stakes more, and loses his brothers, himself and his wife
st.mbh.yudhishthira_cannot_stop.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (BORI 2.53 to 2.58). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_cannot_stop.teaching: In the grip of a game, each loss argues for one more throw, and a person will stake what was never theirs to stake.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_cannot_stop.whole_arc_note: Tell it without softening. The Mahabharata blames Shakuni's cheating and Duryodhana's malice, and it also lets Draupadi, Bhima and Yudhishthira himself name his part. The later books show him living with it: the Nala story is told to him as a mirror, and he learns the dice so it cannot happen again.

st.mbh.vidura_told_to_leave_for_speaking.title: Vidura speaks up mid-game and is called a snake in the house
st.mbh.vidura_told_to_leave_for_speaking.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (BORI 2.55 to 2.57). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.vidura_told_to_leave_for_speaking.teaching: The adviser who says what is true and unwelcome is rare, and so is the one who can hear him.
st.mbh.vidura_told_to_leave_for_speaking.whole_arc_note: Vidura is wronged for honesty and the text's answer is not that he should have been more tactful or kept quiet. He holds his ground and his dignity and goes on serving. Later the king does banish him, repents within a day, and sends for him.

st.mbh.draupadi_asks_her_question.title: Draupadi, dragged into the hall, asks a question no elder will answer
st.mbh.draupadi_asks_her_question.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (BORI 2.59 to 2.62). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.draupadi_asks_her_question.teaching: Where a person is wronged in public and those with authority stay silent, the silence is itself the adharma.
st.mbh.draupadi_asks_her_question.whole_arc_note: This is the epic's central wrong and must never be told as her lesson. She is right, the hall is wrong, and the text says so through Vidura, Vikarna and the omens. Her question is never formally answered, and the tradition holds that the war is the answer. In the critical text the garment is replenished without a spoken prayer; the popular prayer to Krishna belongs to the vulgate and may be noted as such. The hall's silence is the thing to keep.

st.mbh.vikarna_stands_up.title: Vikarna, the youngest in the room, says what the elders will not
st.mbh.vikarna_stands_up.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (BORI 2.61). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.vikarna_stands_up.teaching: When those with rank stay silent, the one who sees clearly must speak, whatever his place.
st.mbh.vikarna_stands_up.whole_arc_note: He fails to stop it, and the story is honest about that. He still fights for his brothers in the war and dies at Bhima's hand, and Bhima grieves. Speaking up did not make him safe or successful. It made him right, and the text records it by name.

st.mbh.bhishma_cannot_answer.title: Bhishma, who knows the law better than anyone, says he cannot decide
st.mbh.bhishma_cannot_answer.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (BORI 2.60 and 2.62). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.bhishma_cannot_answer.teaching: Learning and good character do not by themselves produce the courage to rule against those you serve.
st.mbh.bhishma_cannot_answer.whole_arc_note: The tradition does not treat this as Bhishma's finest hour, and he does not either. Do not defend his silence with the subtlety argument alone, and do not flatten him into a coward. A good man bound to a throne by his own vow could not find his voice when it counted. His later admission belongs with this scene.

st.mbh.vidura_on_the_silent_witness.title: Vidura tells the hall that those who watch and say nothing share the wrong
st.mbh.vidura_on_the_silent_witness.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (BORI 2.61); the Prahlada, Virochana and Sudhanvan account. Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.vidura_on_the_silent_witness.teaching: A witness who knows what is right and stays silent takes a share of the wrong.
st.mbh.vidura_on_the_silent_witness.whole_arc_note: The teaching is aimed at bystanders with standing, not at the victim. It should never be turned around to ask why the wronged person did not speak sooner. The Prahlada story is retold by Vidura in the Udyoga Parva as well.

st.mbh.draupadi_takes_only_two_boons.title: Draupadi is offered anything and asks only for her husbands' freedom
st.mbh.draupadi_takes_only_two_boons.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (BORI 2.63). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.draupadi_takes_only_two_boons.teaching: Dignity takes what is right and no more, and trusts its own strength for the rest.
st.mbh.draupadi_takes_only_two_boons.whole_arc_note: Her restraint is strength and trust in her own, not meekness, and it does not mean the wrong is settled. She keeps her hair unbound and her claim open for thirteen years. Do not present the refusal of the third boon as letting the offenders off.

st.mbh.bhima_rages_at_his_own_brother.title: Bhima wants to burn the hands of the brother who gambled them away
st.mbh.bhima_rages_at_his_own_brother.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (BORI 2.61). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.bhima_rages_at_his_own_brother.teaching: Anger at one's own who caused the harm is real; do not let it serve the purpose of those who set the trap.
st.mbh.bhima_rages_at_his_own_brother.whole_arc_note: The text lets Bhima say the unsayable to the family member who harmed them, and does not rebuke him for feeling it. Arjuna's point is strategic and loyal, not "calm down". The anger is redirected to where it belongs. Bhima raises it again in the forest, and Yudhishthira accepts the reproach.

st.mbh.called_back_for_one_more_throw.title: Freed and on the road home, Yudhishthira is called back for one last throw
st.mbh.called_back_for_one_more_throw.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Anudyuta Parva (BORI 2.66 to 2.67). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.called_back_for_one_more_throw.teaching: Having escaped once is no protection against going back; the pull returns wearing the face of obligation.
st.mbh.called_back_for_one_more_throw.whole_arc_note: The second game is the one that sticks, and it follows a rescue. The text shows a man returning to the table hours after being saved from it, with a reason that sounds like duty. Gandhari's plea, a mother asking that her own son be given up, is the wiser voice and is overruled.

st.mbh.kunti_watches_them_leave.title: Kunti watches her sons and daughter-in-law walk into exile
st.mbh.kunti_watches_them_leave.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Anudyuta Parva (BORI 2.68 to 2.70). Adhyaya numbers are BORI and given from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva.
st.mbh.kunti_watches_them_leave.teaching: A parent's part, when the children must go, is to bless them truthfully and bear the waiting.
st.mbh.kunti_watches_them_leave.whole_arc_note: Kunti does not counsel acceptance. Her grief, her anger and her confidence in Draupadi are all in the scene. The parent left behind is not a passive figure in this epic, and her next word to her sons is a call to act.

st.mbh.dhritarashtra_drives_vidura_away.title: Dhritarashtra drives his brother away in anger and cannot breathe until he is back
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_drives_vidura_away.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Aranyaka sub-parva (corpus 3.4 to 3.6; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_drives_vidura_away.teaching: A man may drive away in anger the person he most relies on; remorse can bring the person back, but only listening changes the course.
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_drives_vidura_away.whole_arc_note: Do not end on the warm reunion. Dhritarashtra wanted his brother back, and the text shows he still would not take his brother's counsel; the remorse is real and it is partial. Vidura's side is told in st.mbh.vidura_told_to_leave_for_speaking; he does not soften his advice to win his place back.

st.mbh.draupadi_why_no_anger.title: Draupadi asks Yudhishthira why his anger does not rise
st.mbh.draupadi_why_no_anger.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Arjunabhigamana sub-parva, Draupadi's lament and the Prahlada and Bali dialogue (corpus 3.27 to 3.29; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.draupadi_why_no_anger.teaching: Neither force at all times nor forgiveness at all times is right; one must know the time for each, and the one who never shows his fire is trampled.
st.mbh.draupadi_why_no_anger.whole_arc_note: Never read this as Draupadi learning to forgive. Her anger is named manyu, the hurt of the wronged, and the Prahlada passage she cites gives her ground. The arc lands in Udyoga Parva, where she brings her loosened hair to Krishna before his peace mission (st.mbh.draupadi_shows_her_hair), and in the war. Yudhishthira's patience is tied to a time-bound pledge, not a rule that wronged people must absorb wrong.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_dharma_not_a_trade.title: Draupadi asks why be good if goodness pays nothing, and Yudhishthira answers
st.mbh.yudhishthira_dharma_not_a_trade.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Arjunabhigamana sub-parva (corpus 3.30 to 3.32; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.yudhishthira_dharma_not_a_trade.teaching: Dharma is done because it is due, not traded for reward; and action is still required of everyone, for fate alone and chance alone are both poor guides.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_dharma_not_a_trade.whole_arc_note: Draupadi's case for effort is not a mistake corrected by her husband. The text keeps her argument whole, and the later books act on it. Do not use this to tell a wronged person that their complaint about injustice is spiritual immaturity.

st.mbh.bhima_count_the_months_as_years.title: Bhima cannot bear to wait thirteen years
st.mbh.bhima_count_the_months_as_years.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Arjunabhigamana sub-parva (corpus 3.33 to 3.36; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.bhima_count_the_months_as_years.teaching: A pledge is not broken by a clever reading of it; time that must be waited out can be spent getting ready.
st.mbh.bhima_count_the_months_as_years.whole_arc_note: The answer to Bhima is not that his anger is wrong. It is that the means matter and the waiting can be used. The arc lands in Arjuna's return with the weapons (Vana) and in the war, where Bhima fulfils every vow he made in the dice hall.

st.mbh.arjuna_beaten_by_the_hunter.title: Arjuna, the best archer alive, is beaten by a mountain hunter
st.mbh.arjuna_beaten_by_the_hunter.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Kairata sub-parva (corpus 3.39 to 3.41; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.arjuna_beaten_by_the_hunter.teaching: When every skill one has fails, the one we face may be the very one we came to meet; surrender to him is not defeat.
st.mbh.arjuna_beaten_by_the_hunter.whole_arc_note: Arjuna fought with everything he had before he turned to worship; the turning is not giving up early. The defeat was the test that came before the gift, and the weapon he received is the one he needs years later, in the war.

st.mbh.arjuna_refuses_urvashi.title: Arjuna refuses Urvashi in Indra's heaven and is cursed for it
st.mbh.arjuna_refuses_urvashi.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Indralokabhigamana sub-parva (corpus 3.44; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.arjuna_refuses_urvashi.teaching: A boundary rooted in one's own dharma may be kept courteously and completely, even against a powerful person, even at a cost.
st.mbh.arjuna_refuses_urvashi.whole_arc_note: Urvashi is not cast as wicked; she acts within the customs of her world and is hurt by rejection. Arjuna is not praised for coldness but for keeping his own boundary with courtesy. The arc lands in Virata Parva, where the curse is the cover that keeps the Pandavas hidden.

st.mbh.is_anyone_unluckier_than_me.title: Yudhishthira asks if any king has ever been less fortunate than he is
st.mbh.is_anyone_unluckier_than_me.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana sub-parva, the frame (corpus 3.49; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.is_anyone_unluckier_than_me.teaching: One who believes no one has suffered as he has is told the story of one who suffered more and recovered, and is given a skill against the cause.
st.mbh.is_anyone_unluckier_than_me.whole_arc_note: Brihadashva does not tell him his grief is exaggerated or that he brought it on himself. He gives him company in it and then a skill. The story he is told ends in recovery through a learned skill, which is what he is given.

st.mbh.nala_leaves_her_sleeping.title: Nala, ruined, leaves his wife sleeping in the forest
st.mbh.nala_leaves_her_sleeping.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana sub-parva (corpus 3.58 to 3.60; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.nala_leaves_her_sleeping.teaching: Shame can tell a person that the ones who love him are better off without him; the text calls that thought delusion.
st.mbh.nala_leaves_her_sleeping.whole_arc_note: Never present the leaving as a noble sacrifice. The text attributes it to a clouded mind and gives Damayanti the last word on it. The arc lands at their reunion (Vana, Nalopakhyana end), which needs his full acknowledgment.

st.mbh.damayanti_alone_sets_her_terms.title: Damayanti, abandoned in the forest, keeps going and sets her own terms
st.mbh.damayanti_alone_sets_her_terms.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana sub-parva (corpus 3.60 to 3.62; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.damayanti_alone_sets_her_terms.teaching: Even in total loss a person can grieve fully and still decide what she will and will not accept.
st.mbh.damayanti_alone_sets_her_terms.whole_arc_note: She is the active one in the recovery of the marriage; do not shrink her to a patient waiting wife. Her lament is not corrected and her conditions are not treated as pride.

st.mbh.nala_as_bahuka.title: Nala lives in disguise as a cook and driver, and every night recites one verse
st.mbh.nala_as_bahuka.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana sub-parva (corpus 3.63 to 3.70; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.nala_as_bahuka.teaching: A fallen man may live through his shame by working honestly in obscurity, and the skill he learns there can undo the cause of his fall.
st.mbh.nala_as_bahuka.whole_arc_note: The recovery comes through humble work done well and a new skill learned from someone else, and it ends in restraint: he does not curse Kali, and he does not punish his brother. Keep the long hidden years; the turn is not quick.

st.mbh.ashtavakra_cursed_for_correcting_.title: A father curses his unborn son for correcting him in front of his students
st.mbh.ashtavakra_cursed_for_correcting_.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Tirthayatra sub-parva, Ashtavakriya (corpus 3.134; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.ashtavakra_cursed_for_correcting_.teaching: A parent's anger at being corrected can wound a child for years; the child who does not take it as his worth may yet restore the parent.
st.mbh.ashtavakra_cursed_for_correcting_.whole_arc_note: The curse is the father's anger at being corrected, not a judgment on the child, and the arc ends with the son restoring the father who cursed him and being made whole by him. Keep both halves: the wrong done to the child and the reconciliation that the child brings about.

st.mbh.ashtavakra_too_young_at_the_door.title: Ashtavakra is stopped at the king's door for being a child
st.mbh.ashtavakra_too_young_at_the_door.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Tirthayatra sub-parva, Ashtavakriya (corpus 3.134 to 3.136; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.ashtavakra_too_young_at_the_door.teaching: Wisdom, not age or appearance, makes an elder; one who knows may speak at any age.
st.mbh.ashtavakra_too_young_at_the_door.whole_arc_note: He is turned away for age and body, and he does not prove himself by becoming acceptable to them; he proves himself by what he knows. The story affirms the young and the differently-bodied without saying the elders were all wrong; Janaka listens once the boy speaks.

st.mbh.yavakrita_and_the_sand_dam.title: Yavakrita wants the Vedas without a teacher, and finds Indra building a dam of sand
st.mbh.yavakrita_and_the_sand_dam.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Tirthayatra sub-parva, Yavakritopakhyana (corpus 3.137 to 3.139; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.yavakrita_and_the_sand_dam.teaching: Learning taken by force, without a teacher and the time it needs, breeds pride instead of wisdom.
st.mbh.yavakrita_and_the_sand_dam.whole_arc_note: The story begins in envy on his father's behalf and ends in disaster because the shortcut skipped the formation that a teacher gives. Do not clip it at the sand dam as a cute lesson about patience; the warning is about what a gain without discipline does to the one who gets it. The assault is part of the arc and is told as his crime.

st.mbh.shibi_and_the_dove.title: King Shibi will not hand over the dove that came to him for refuge
st.mbh.shibi_and_the_dove.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Tirthayatra sub-parva, Shyena-kapotiya (corpus 3.132 to 3.133; a second telling by Markandeya at 3.200; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.shibi_and_the_dove.teaching: Abandoning one who has come to you for protection is condemned; a protector pays the price himself rather than hand him over.
st.mbh.shibi_and_the_dove.whole_arc_note: The hawk's claim is taken seriously, which is why the answer is costly. The test is whether a person will pay from his own body to protect someone who trusted him. Do not reduce it to self-sacrifice for its own sake; the point is protection of the one who sought refuge.

st.mbh.bhima_cannot_lift_the_tail.title: Bhima, strongest of men, cannot move an old monkey's tail
st.mbh.bhima_cannot_lift_the_tail.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Tirthayatra sub-parva, Bhima's search for the saugandhika flower (corpus 3.146 to 3.151; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.bhima_cannot_lift_the_tail.teaching: Strength used without regard for the weak and the old is a kind of ignorance; the one in your path may be the elder you most need.
st.mbh.bhima_cannot_lift_the_tail.whole_arc_note: Hanuman does not humiliate him for its own sake; he rebukes the heedless strength that terrifies the forest and then gives him a brother's love and strength for what lies ahead. Bhima keeps his errand: he goes on and brings Draupadi the flowers.

st.mbh.bhima_in_the_pythons_grip.title: Bhima is held helpless by a python, and only answers can free him
st.mbh.bhima_in_the_pythons_grip.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Ajagara sub-parva (corpus 3.178 to 3.183; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.bhima_in_the_pythons_grip.teaching: Even great strength can be held still; prosperity deludes even the wise, and a person is known by conduct, not birth.
st.mbh.bhima_in_the_pythons_grip.whole_arc_note: Two falls sit together: Nahusha's pride that made him a serpent, and Bhima's strength that suddenly counts for nothing. Bhima is saved by his brother's understanding, not his own effort; the text does not mock his helplessness.

st.mbh.markandeya_finds_the_child.title: Markandeya, exhausted and alone in the flood, hears a child say: I know you are tired
st.mbh.markandeya_finds_the_child.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-samasya sub-parva (corpus 3.191.86 to 3.192; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.markandeya_finds_the_child.teaching: When there is no shelter left anywhere, the one who holds the world knows we are tired and offers rest.
st.mbh.markandeya_finds_the_child.whole_arc_note: This is a vision of grace given to the exhausted, not a reward earned by effort; Markandeya is told he was shown it because of his devotion and his long discipline. Keep the long lonely swim before the tree.

st.mbh.kaushika_and_the_housewife.title: A proud ascetic is made to wait, and a housewife says: I am not a crane
st.mbh.kaushika_and_the_housewife.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-samasya sub-parva, Pativratopakhyana (corpus 3.209; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.kaushika_and_the_housewife.teaching: Anger is an enemy living in one's own body; power to harm proves nothing, and dharma may be better known by an ordinary householder than an ascetic.
st.mbh.kaushika_and_the_housewife.whole_arc_note: The frame praises a wife's devotion to her household, and her authority comes from that discipline; she is the teacher here and the proud man is corrected. Use the story for Kaushika's anger and self-importance and for her calm, not as a prescription for women. Continues in st.mbh.dharmavyadha_sends_him_home.

st.mbh.dharmavyadha_sends_him_home.title: A meat-seller teaches the scholar, and sends him home to his blind parents
st.mbh.dharmavyadha_sends_him_home.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-samasya sub-parva, Vyadha Gita (corpus 3.210 to 3.219; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.dharmavyadha_sends_him_home.teaching: Honest work in one's own place, and care for one's parents, are dharma no learning surpasses.
st.mbh.dharmavyadha_sends_him_home.whole_arc_note: The teacher is a man who does a trade others despise and does it honestly, as his inherited work; the text does not ask him to leave it. The point lands on Kaushika: knowledge sought by walking out on aged parents is incomplete. Do not use this to shame a person who left a harmful home; Kaushika's parents had done him no wrong.

st.mbh.mudgala_declines_heaven.title: Mudgala, who lives on gleaned grain, is offered heaven and asks what is wrong with it
st.mbh.mudgala_declines_heaven.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Vrihidraunika sub-parva (corpus 3.260 to 3.262; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.mudgala_declines_heaven.teaching: A peace that does not change when everything is taken is worth more than any reward that can run out.
st.mbh.mudgala_declines_heaven.whole_arc_note: Mudgala is content from the start; the story does not cure him of anything. It is a light, affirming story about a person whose peace does not depend on circumstances. Do not use it to tell the poor to be grateful for poverty.

st.mbh.draupadi_and_the_empty_pot.title: Ten thousand hungry guests arrive after the last grain is eaten
st.mbh.draupadi_and_the_empty_pot.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Draupadi-harana sub-parva, Durvasa's visit (corpus 3.263 to 3.264; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.draupadi_and_the_empty_pot.teaching: When there is nothing left to give and the need is at the door, call on the Lord; what little is left is enough in his hands.
st.mbh.draupadi_and_the_empty_pot.whole_arc_note: The trap was set deliberately by Duryodhana; Draupadi is not careless. The rescue is grace, and the story is devotional. Keep Krishna's insistence that she bring the pot: the little left over is what is used.

st.mbh.draupadi_no_one_is_mine.title: Draupadi tells Krishna: I have no husbands, no sons, no kin, not even you
st.mbh.draupadi_no_one_is_mine.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Kirmiravadha / Arjunabhigamana sub-parva, Krishna's first visit to the forest (corpus 3.12.120 to 3.12.137; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.draupadi_no_one_is_mine.teaching: One who has been wronged while others watched may say so to everyone, even to God, and be answered with a promise rather than a lesson.
st.mbh.draupadi_no_one_is_mine.whole_arc_note: Draupadi is not asked to calm down, forgive or wait. She accuses even Krishna and he accepts the accusation and answers with a vow. Do not move her to kshama; her healing state is the dignity of being heard and the promise of justice. The arc lands in Udyoga (st.mbh.draupadi_shows_her_hair) and in the war.

st.mbh.duryodhana_goes_to_gloat.title: Duryodhana goes to the forest to show off, and is taken prisoner
st.mbh.duryodhana_goes_to_gloat.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Ghosha-yatra sub-parva (corpus 3.237 to 3.243; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.duryodhana_goes_to_gloat.teaching: Prosperity paraded to wound others carries its owner into disgrace.
st.mbh.duryodhana_goes_to_gloat.whole_arc_note: The text says plainly why he went: to burn the exiles with the sight of his wealth. The humiliation comes from his own errand. The arc continues in st.mbh.duryodhana_cannot_bear_being_saved and does not end in insight.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_rescues_his_enemy.title: Yudhishthira sends his brothers to rescue the cousin who exiled them
st.mbh.yudhishthira_rescues_his_enemy.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Ghosha-yatra sub-parva (corpus 3.244 to 3.247; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.yudhishthira_rescues_his_enemy.teaching: Between ourselves we may be divided; against outsiders the family stands together, and helping a fallen enemy is a greater deed than winning a kingdom.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_rescues_his_enemy.whole_arc_note: This is not forgiveness that erases the wrong; the quarrel is unchanged and the Pandavas still go to war. It is the refusal to stand by while one's family is shamed by strangers. Do not use it to tell a person to rescue an abuser; Yudhishthira acts from strength, with his brothers, and expects nothing.

st.mbh.duryodhana_cannot_bear_being_save.title: Rescued by the people he hates, Duryodhana decides he would rather die
st.mbh.duryodhana_cannot_bear_being_save.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Ghosha-yatra sub-parva (corpus 3.247 to 3.252; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.duryodhana_cannot_bear_being_save.teaching: Envy can make being helped by a rival feel worse than death; such shame, unexamined, feeds the very feud that caused it.
st.mbh.duryodhana_cannot_bear_being_save.whole_arc_note: This is shame born of envy: being helped by those one hates feels worse than death. The text does not resolve it into humility; Duryodhana chooses to live for the feud. It is a portrait for recognition, not imitation. Mark self-harm honestly; do not serve where risk is present.

st.mbh.draupadi_pushes_jayadratha.title: Alone at the hermitage, Draupadi refuses a king and knocks him down
st.mbh.draupadi_pushes_jayadratha.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Draupadi-harana and Jayadratha-vimokshana sub-parvas (corpus 3.265 to 3.272; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.draupadi_pushes_jayadratha.teaching: A woman alone may meet a powerful man's entitlement with plain rebuke and force, and the truth of her own conduct is her strength.
st.mbh.draupadi_pushes_jayadratha.whole_arc_note: Draupadi is not rescued as a passive prize; she resists, rebukes and frightens him. The release is Yudhishthira's mercy for the sake of his cousin-sister, not a lesson to her. The arc does not end there: Jayadratha does austerities for a boon to hold back the Pandavas for one day, and that day is the day Abhimanyu dies (Drona Parva).

st.mbh.savitri_chooses_with_open_eyes.title: Savitri is told the man she chose has one year to live, and does not change her mind
st.mbh.savitri_chooses_with_open_eyes.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya sub-parva, Savitri upakhyana (corpus 3.294 to 3.296; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.savitri_chooses_with_open_eyes.teaching: A choice made by the mind, spoken and then acted on, with full knowledge of its cost, is to be kept and carried with resolve.
st.mbh.savitri_chooses_with_open_eyes.whole_arc_note: She is not passive or merely obedient: she chooses, against her father's wish, with open eyes, and then prepares. The arc lands at the year's end, when she walks after Death himself (st.mbh.savitri_follows_yama). Do not use this to tell anyone to stay in a harmful marriage; the story is about a free and informed choice, owned.

st.mbh.savitri_follows_yama.title: Savitri walks behind Death and keeps talking
st.mbh.savitri_follows_yama.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya sub-parva, Savitri upakhyana (corpus 3.297 to 3.299; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.savitri_follows_yama.teaching: The good do not sink or tremble; steadiness, truthful speech and goodness move even Death.
st.mbh.savitri_follows_yama.whole_arc_note: Savitri does not plead or bargain in desperation. She speaks well, steadily, and asks first for others. Her composure and intelligence win, not mere persistence. This story speaks to a person facing a loved one's death; it must not suggest that their loved one died because they were not devoted or clever enough.

st.mbh.karna_gives_his_armour.title: Karna is warned in a dream and gives away his armour anyway
st.mbh.karna_gives_his_armour.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Kundala-harana sub-parva (corpus 3.300 to 3.311; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.karna_gives_his_armour.teaching: For a person whose word is his self, keeping it is worth more than the protection breaking it would bring.
st.mbh.karna_gives_his_armour.whole_arc_note: Karna knew the cost and gave anyway; the text honours his generosity and also shows the fame he chose over life. Do not turn it into a lesson that one must always say yes; it is the story of a man whose giving was his identity, and the arc lands in Drona Parva where the weapon is spent and in Karna Parva where he dies without the armour.

st.mbh.kunti_sets_the_basket_adrift.title: Kunti, an unmarried girl, sets her newborn son adrift on the river
st.mbh.kunti_sets_the_basket_adrift.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Kundala-harana sub-parva (corpus 3.307 to 3.309; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ); also Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (corpus Adi 1.104)
st.mbh.kunti_sets_the_basket_adrift.teaching: A mother may let a child go out of fear and still bless him with her whole heart; the secret, kept, does not stop costing.
st.mbh.kunti_sets_the_basket_adrift.whole_arc_note: Kunti is both pressed and frightened; the text gives her grief in full and does not condemn her, and it does not excuse the cost to Karna either. The arc runs through Udyoga (she meets Karna before the war, st.mbh.kunti_meets_karna) and Stri Parva (she tells the truth too late, st.mbh.kunti_tells_too_late in mbh_2). Handle with care: this speaks to people who gave up a child or were given up.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_at_the_lake.title: Yudhishthira finds all four brothers dead at the lake, and answers the questions
st.mbh.yudhishthira_at_the_lake.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Araneya sub-parva, Yaksha Prashna (corpus 3.312 to 3.315; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.yudhishthira_at_the_lake.teaching: In the worst moment, stopping to understand the cause before acting is what saves; grief is named as not-knowing.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_at_the_lake.whole_arc_note: Yudhishthira weeps first; the text does not make him impassive. His steadiness is that he does not drink in panic as each brother did. Do not use the wonder-of-death answer to hurry anyone's grief.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_chooses_nakula.title: Allowed one brother back, Yudhishthira chooses his stepmother's son
st.mbh.yudhishthira_chooses_nakula.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Araneya sub-parva, Yaksha Prashna (corpus 3.314.125 to 3.314.135; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate (Nilakantha) numbering of 315 Vana adhyayas; BORI numbers differ)
st.mbh.yudhishthira_chooses_nakula.teaching: Non-cruelty is the highest dharma; fairness to those who have the least claim is what dharma protects.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_chooses_nakula.whole_arc_note: The choice costs him his strongest allies, and it is made in grief; it is not a trick that he knew would be rewarded. It lands as the clearest picture of fairness in a blended family in the epic.

st.mbh.arjuna_chooses_krishna_unarmed.title: Offered an army or one unarmed friend, Arjuna chooses the friend
