st.mbh.arjuna_chooses_krishna_unarmed.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Senodyoga sub-parva (corpus 5.7; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.arjuna_chooses_krishna_unarmed.teaching: One trusted guide who will stand beside you is worth more than numbers that will only fight for you.
st.mbh.arjuna_chooses_krishna_unarmed.whole_arc_note: The choice is not a sentimental one against practical power; it is a judgment about what actually decides outcomes. The arc lands in Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva, where the unarmed charioteer is the one who turns Arjuna back to his task.

st.mbh.shalya_bound_by_hospitality.title: Shalya comes to help one side and is bound to the other by its hospitality
st.mbh.shalya_bound_by_hospitality.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Senodyoga sub-parva (corpus 5.8; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.shalya_bound_by_hospitality.teaching: Favours received unawares can bind a person to a side he did not choose; once bound, he serves divided.
st.mbh.shalya_bound_by_hospitality.whole_arc_note: Shalya's story shows how gifts create obligations and how a person caught that way divides himself. The text does not praise the arrangement; it is a compromise, and its working-out in Karna Parva is ugly (see st.mbh.shalya_asked_to_drive in mbh_2).

st.mbh.shachi_and_nahusha.title: Shachi is pursued by the new king of heaven, and the gods tell her to go to him
st.mbh.shachi_and_nahusha.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Indra-vijaya upakhyana within Senodyoga (corpus 5.11 to 5.17; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.shachi_and_nahusha.teaching: One who comes for refuge must not be given up to keep peace with the powerful; a harasser drunk on power can be undone by his own arrogance.
st.mbh.shachi_and_nahusha.whole_arc_note: The institution that should protect her asks her to go to her harasser; one person refuses, and she and her protector use time and strategy. She is never told to accept. Nahusha's fall comes from his own arrogance toward the sages, set in motion by her. The python he becomes is the one who later seizes Bhima (st.mbh.bhima_in_the_pythons_grip).

st.mbh.five_villages.title: Yudhishthira asks for only five villages
st.mbh.five_villages.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Sanjaya-yana sub-parva (corpus 5.31; repeated to Krishna at 5.71 and 5.81; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.five_villages.teaching: Ask for the least that justice allows, say plainly what follows if it is refused, and be ready for either.
st.mbh.five_villages.whole_arc_note: The five villages are offered from a position of strength and with war named as the alternative; it is not appeasement. When it is refused, the Pandavas fight. Do not use this to tell a wronged person to keep lowering their ask.

st.mbh.dhritarashtra_cannot_sleep.title: Dhritarashtra cannot sleep and sends for Vidura in the night
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_cannot_sleep.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Prajagara sub-parva, the opening of Vidura Niti (corpus 5.33; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_cannot_sleep.teaching: Sleeplessness comes to the one who is overpowered, who has lost, who craves, and to the one who has taken what is not his.
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_cannot_sleep.whole_arc_note: The teaching is complete and the king is moved; the text is honest that hearing wisdom is not the same as following it. The night's counsel continues in the Sanatsujatiya (st.mbh.sanatsujata_heedlessness_is_death).

st.mbh.sanatsujata_heedlessness_is_death.title: Dhritarashtra asks a sage whether death is real
st.mbh.sanatsujata_heedlessness_is_death.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Sanatsujata sub-parva (corpus 5.42 to 5.46; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.sanatsujata_heedlessness_is_death.teaching: Heedlessness is death and heedfulness is immortality; anger, carelessness and greed are death's real forms.
st.mbh.sanatsujata_heedlessness_is_death.whole_arc_note: This is the epic's own answer to fear of death, given to a man who has let his attachments decide everything. Do not use it to dismiss a grieving person's loss; it speaks to fear and to the way one lives.

st.mbh.krishna_goes_knowing_it_will_fail.title: Krishna goes on a peace mission he expects to fail
st.mbh.krishna_goes_knowing_it_will_fail.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Bhagavad-yana sub-parva (corpus 5.72 and 5.92 to 5.93; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.krishna_goes_knowing_it_will_fail.teaching: One who tries his utmost to turn a friend from ruin is blameless whatever the outcome; one who does not try is called cruel.
st.mbh.krishna_goes_knowing_it_will_fail.whole_arc_note: The effort is not naive; Krishna expects the refusal and goes to make the attempt complete. The arc lands in the war; the failure of the embassy is what makes the war just in the eyes of the text.

st.mbh.draupadi_shows_her_hair.title: Before the peace mission, Draupadi holds up her hair: remember this
st.mbh.draupadi_shows_her_hair.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Bhagavad-yana sub-parva (corpus 5.81.29 to 5.81.49; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.draupadi_shows_her_hair.teaching: When others speak of making peace, the one who was wronged has the right to be remembered first.
st.mbh.draupadi_shows_her_hair.whole_arc_note: Her anger has been held for thirteen years, and it is not rebuked here, by Krishna or by the text. Peace is still attempted, but her claim is kept in front of it. Never present this as a woman who could not let go; she is the conscience of the wronged in the assembly of those who want things settled.

st.mbh.not_a_needles_point.title: Duryodhana will not give up as much land as a needle's point
st.mbh.not_a_needles_point.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Bhagavad-yana sub-parva (corpus 5.127; the same line at 5.58; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.not_a_needles_point.teaching: One who would rather break than bend, and will not yield even a needle's point, brings ruin on himself and all who follow him.
st.mbh.not_a_needles_point.whole_arc_note: He sincerely believes he is in the right, and the text lets him say so. The arc lands in Shalya Parva, in the lake and on the field with his thigh broken (see st.mbh.duryodhana_in_the_lake and st.mbh.duryodhana_last_words in mbh_2). Use for recognition of one's own refusal to give an inch, not to label an opponent.

st.mbh.gandhari_speaks_to_her_son.title: Gandhari has her son brought back into the hall and tells him the truth
st.mbh.gandhari_speaks_to_her_son.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Bhagavad-yana sub-parva (corpus 5.129; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.gandhari_speaks_to_her_son.teaching: Desire and anger are the enemies that pull a person away from his own good; mastering them is the only conquest that lasts.
st.mbh.gandhari_speaks_to_her_son.whole_arc_note: Gandhari does not excuse her son or her husband, and the text gives her full authority in the hall. The refusal is his. Her arc lands in Stri Parva (st.mbh.gandhari_holds_back_her_curse in mbh_2), where the mother who spoke the truth before the war must grieve all her sons after it.

st.mbh.vidula_rouses_her_son.title: Vidula finds her defeated son lying in bed and will not let him stay there
st.mbh.vidula_rouses_her_son.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Bhagavad-yana sub-parva, Vidulaputranushasana, told by Kunti to Krishna (corpus 5.133 to 5.136; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.vidula_rouses_her_son.teaching: Do not lie down under defeat; better to blaze for a moment than to smoulder for years, and the friends who remain will rise with you.
st.mbh.vidula_rouses_her_son.whole_arc_note: Vidula speaks to a capable man who has collapsed after a defeat and has resources and friends to call on; her harshness is a mother's fire, and the son does rise. This is a rebuke that only works inside its scene. Do not serve it to someone in clinical depression, grief or risk; it is for the defeated who are able, and for those who need permission to fight back.

st.mbh.krishna_offers_karna_the_throne.title: Krishna tells Karna who he is and offers him the throne
st.mbh.krishna_offers_karna_the_throne.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Bhagavad-yana sub-parva (corpus 5.140 to 5.143; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.krishna_offers_karna_the_throne.teaching: Loyalty to those who raised and stood by you outweighs a birthright offered too late.
st.mbh.krishna_offers_karna_the_throne.whole_arc_note: Karna is wronged by his birth and by every hall that mocked his lineage; the text does not make his refusal a mistake to be corrected but a loyalty to be honoured, and it also lets him see the cost. The arc lands in Karna Parva, where he dies, and Stri Parva, where Kunti reveals him (mbh_2).

st.mbh.kunti_meets_karna.title: Kunti comes to Karna at the river, and he tells her what she did
st.mbh.kunti_meets_karna.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Bhagavad-yana sub-parva, Karna-Kunti samvada (corpus 5.144 to 5.146; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.kunti_meets_karna.teaching: One who was abandoned may name the wrong in full and still be generous; loyalty to those who stood by him is not betrayal of the one who did not.
st.mbh.kunti_meets_karna.whole_arc_note: Karna's accusation stands; the text does not have him forgive her or make her the villain. Both are wronged and both are honoured. Do not reframe Karna's anger as bitterness to be healed; he speaks the truth and then gives her more than she asked. The arc lands in Drona Parva (st.mbh.karna_spares_bhima in mbh_2), Karna Parva and Stri Parva (st.mbh.kunti_tells_too_late).

st.mbh.amba_turned_away_by_everyone.title: Amba is taken by force, released, and then refused by everyone
st.mbh.amba_turned_away_by_everyone.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Ambopakhyana sub-parva (corpus 5.173 to 5.177; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly); the abduction itself in Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva
st.mbh.amba_turned_away_by_everyone.teaching: When each person's rule adds up to another's ruin, she may name every one of them and seek redress.
st.mbh.amba_turned_away_by_everyone.whole_arc_note: Never frame Amba's story as a woman who should have accepted her fate. Every man in it acts within his own rules and the sum of their rules is her ruin; the text lets her say so and backs her resolve with a god's boon. Her self-blame is a stage she passes through, not the text's verdict. The arc lands in Bhishma Parva, where Shikhandi stands before Bhishma.

st.mbh.amba_will_not_turn_back.title: Amba refuses to be talked out of her resolve
st.mbh.amba_will_not_turn_back.source_ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Ambopakhyana sub-parva (corpus 5.186 to 5.187; adhyaya numbers as in the corpus, which follows the vulgate numbering of 196 Udyoga adhyayas; BORI numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.amba_will_not_turn_back.teaching: A wronged person's resolve, held through every refusal and failure, may be granted by the gods themselves.
st.mbh.amba_will_not_turn_back.whole_arc_note: The text vindicates her: her resolve is granted by Shiva and fulfilled. Do not soften it into a lesson about letting go of anger, and do not glamorise the self-immolation; mark it honestly and keep it from readings with risk. The arc lands in Bhishma Parva (Shikhandi on the tenth day).

st.mbh.pandavas_choose_their_disguises.title: Five princes and a queen choose the humble jobs they will live in for a year
st.mbh.pandavas_choose_their_disguises.source_ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Pandava-pravesha sub-parva, opening adhyayas. The corpus has no Virata Parva; sub-parva given from memory, adhyaya numbers deliberately not given
st.mbh.pandavas_choose_their_disguises.teaching: When circumstances force one into a humbler role, choose the one your real skills can serve, and live it fully until the time is complete.
st.mbh.pandavas_choose_their_disguises.whole_arc_note: The humility is chosen for a purpose and with a time limit; it is not a lesson that the wronged should accept degradation. Yudhishthira's grief for each of them is kept. The arc lands at the end of Virata Parva, when they reveal themselves.

st.mbh.dhaumya_how_to_live_in_a_kings_ho.title: Dhaumya teaches the Pandavas how to work in another man's court
st.mbh.dhaumya_how_to_live_in_a_kings_ho.source_ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Pandava-pravesha sub-parva, Dhaumya's counsel on living in royal service. The corpus has no Virata Parva; sub-parva given from memory, adhyaya numbers deliberately not given
st.mbh.dhaumya_how_to_live_in_a_kings_ho.teaching: In another's house be discreet, speak when asked, never presume, and keep what you learn to yourself.
st.mbh.dhaumya_how_to_live_in_a_kings_ho.whole_arc_note: This is counsel for a dangerous situation with a time limit, not a rule that one should always make oneself small. It sits beside the Kichaka episode, which shows that discretion does not protect against everything and that some wrongs must be answered.

st.mbh.sairandhri_kicked_before_the_cour.title: Draupadi, harassed by the commander, is kicked in front of the king, and no one moves
st.mbh.sairandhri_kicked_before_the_cour.source_ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Kichaka-vadha sub-parva. The corpus has no Virata Parva; sub-parva given from memory, adhyaya numbers deliberately not given
st.mbh.sairandhri_kicked_before_the_cour.teaching: A court whose king will not protect the weak is no court; one who is wronged in public may say so to everyone present.
st.mbh.sairandhri_kicked_before_the_cour.whole_arc_note: This is the clearest picture in the epic of harassment by a powerful man while the institution, the employer and even family stand by. The text gives her the right and the words. Yudhishthira's restraint has a reason (discovery would cost them another twelve years), but it is not presented as kindness to her, and she does not accept it. Never frame it as a lesson in patience.

st.mbh.draupadi_wakes_bhima_in_the_kitch.title: Draupadi goes to the kitchen at night and wakes the one who will act
st.mbh.draupadi_wakes_bhima_in_the_kitch.source_ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Kichaka-vadha sub-parva. The corpus has no Virata Parva; sub-parva given from memory, adhyaya numbers deliberately not given
st.mbh.draupadi_wakes_bhima_in_the_kitch.teaching: When those responsible will not act, the wronged may go to the one who will, and act with a plan.
st.mbh.draupadi_wakes_bhima_in_the_kitch.whole_arc_note: The text endorses her action and Bhima's. It does not ask her to forgive or endure. Keep both nights together: the public failure and the private ally. The violence is the text's; for content, the point is that she found the person who would stand with her and acted with a plan.

st.mbh.uttara_boasts_and_runs.title: Prince Uttara boasts in front of the women, then sees the army and runs
st.mbh.uttara_boasts_and_runs.source_ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Go-grahana sub-parva. The corpus has no Virata Parva; sub-parva given from memory, adhyaya numbers deliberately not given
st.mbh.uttara_boasts_and_runs.teaching: Fear can undo the boaster; the right companion turns panic into a task one can do.
st.mbh.uttara_boasts_and_runs.whole_arc_note: The story is gentle with the frightened boy. His boast is mocked by the narrative, but Arjuna's response is to give him a smaller role he can fill, and Uttara grows. Do not make it a story about a coward; it is about fear meeting a steady companion.

st.mbh.kanka_struck_with_the_dice.title: The king throws the dice in Yudhishthira's face, and he catches the blood
st.mbh.kanka_struck_with_the_dice.source_ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Go-grahana sub-parva end and Vaivahika sub-parva. The corpus has no Virata Parva; sub-parva given from memory, adhyaya numbers deliberately not given
st.mbh.kanka_struck_with_the_dice.teaching: Holding back in the moment of injury can protect others from a greater harm; truth comes out, and the one who struck apologises.
st.mbh.kanka_struck_with_the_dice.whole_arc_note: Yudhishthira's forbearance here is chosen, with a purpose and with the end of the hiding days in view; he is vindicated and the king apologises. It is not a rule for anyone being hit by a boss or partner. Use for the hard moment when a person holds back so that a worse harm does not follow.

st.mbh.arjuna_will_not_marry_his_student.title: Arjuna refuses to marry the princess he taught, and protects her name
st.mbh.arjuna_will_not_marry_his_student.source_ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Vaivahika sub-parva. The corpus has no Virata Parva; sub-parva given from memory, adhyaya numbers deliberately not given
st.mbh.arjuna_will_not_marry_his_student.teaching: One who has been trusted as a teacher must protect that trust, even by refusing what is offered.
st.mbh.arjuna_will_not_marry_his_student.whole_arc_note: This is a boundary kept by the person with power over a student. The arc lands in the line of Parikshit, born after Abhimanyu's death (Drona and Ashvamedhika Parvas).

st.mbh.krishna_left_mathura.title: Krishna tells Yudhishthira how his people abandoned their city to a stronger enemy
st.mbh.krishna_left_mathura.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Mantra sub-parva (around BORI 2.13; adhyaya from memory; the corpus has no Sabha Parva)
st.mbh.krishna_left_mathura.teaching: When an enemy cannot be beaten now, it is wise to withdraw, rebuild, and return when the time and means are right.
st.mbh.krishna_left_mathura.whole_arc_note: Withdrawal here is strategy with a later return, not defeat accepted forever. The arc lands in the Jarasandha-vadha sub-parva of Sabha Parva.

st.bg.dhritarashtra_mine_and_pandus.title: The blind king asks what 'my sons' and 'Pandu's sons' did
st.bg.dhritarashtra_mine_and_pandus.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 1.1
st.bg.dhritarashtra_mine_and_pandus.teaching: The sense of 'mine' divides what belongs together, and a parent's partiality is paid for by the children.
st.bg.dhritarashtra_mine_and_pandus.whole_arc_note: Do not make him a villain or a victim. The tradition reads 'mamakah' as the root of the whole war: partiality that was never examined. He also hears the teaching in full and stays as he is; hearing alone was not enough.

st.bg.duryodhana_counts_the_enemy.title: Duryodhana counts the other side's strengths before his own
st.bg.duryodhana_counts_the_enemy.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 1.2-12
st.bg.duryodhana_counts_the_enemy.teaching: The one who keeps measuring the rival is uneasy even when he holds the larger force.
st.bg.duryodhana_counts_the_enemy.whole_arc_note: This is a portrait, with no teaching spoken. Do not turn it into mockery of him: the text simply shows that having more does not quiet a mind that is measuring.

st.bg.arjuna_collapse_between_armies.title: Arjuna asks to see who he must fight, and his body gives way
st.bg.arjuna_collapse_between_armies.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 1.20-47
st.bg.arjuna_collapse_between_armies.teaching: Even the strongest person can be undone when duty and love pull in opposite directions; that collapse is where the Gita begins.
st.bg.arjuna_collapse_between_armies.whole_arc_note: Do not skip to the answer. The traditional commentators call this chapter Arjuna Vishada Yoga: the despair itself is counted as a yoga because it brings him to ask. Also do not read him as a pacifist hero; the text calls his state delusion and pity born of attachment, and Krishna will not accept his reasoning.

st.bg.arjuna_i_will_not_fight.title: The pep talk that did not work: 'I will not fight'
st.bg.arjuna_i_will_not_fight.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 2.1-9
st.bg.arjuna_i_will_not_fight.teaching: Being told to snap out of it does not lift grief; understanding does, and it begins when the person is ready to hear.
st.bg.arjuna_i_will_not_fight.whole_arc_note: Krishna's opening lines (klaibyam ma sma gamah) are a teacher's rebuke inside a scene and must not be served alone to a person in despair. Show that they did not move Arjuna, and that Krishna then changed his approach and taught for seventeen chapters.

st.bg.arjuna_i_am_your_student.title: 'I am your student. Tell me what is right.'
st.bg.arjuna_i_am_your_student.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 2.7-10
st.bg.arjuna_i_am_your_student.teaching: Clarity begins when a person admits he cannot see and asks one who can.
st.bg.arjuna_i_am_your_student.whole_arc_note: He asks for what is 'shreyas', the lasting good, and for a definite answer. He does not ask to be made comfortable. Keep both halves: the honest admission of confusion and the act of asking someone who knows.

st.bg.arjuna_mixed_messages.title: 'You are confusing me. Tell me one thing.'
st.bg.arjuna_mixed_messages.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 3.1-8, and again at 5.1
st.bg.arjuna_mixed_messages.teaching: No one reaches freedom by merely stopping; do the work that is yours, without attachment.
st.bg.arjuna_mixed_messages.whole_arc_note: The Gita does not rank action above knowledge in general; Shankara and the others read it as fitting the path to the person. Do not flatten it into 'just act'. What the story gives is permission to say 'I do not follow' to a teacher, twice.

st.bg.arjuna_what_drives_wrong.title: 'What makes a person do wrong against his own will?'
st.bg.arjuna_what_drives_wrong.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 3.36-43
st.bg.arjuna_what_drives_wrong.teaching: The force that pushes a person against his own judgement is desire and its child, anger; it is mastered from above, by what is higher in him.
st.bg.arjuna_what_drives_wrong.whole_arc_note: The three images are three depths of covering: smoke clears with a breath, a mirror needs wiping, a child needs time. Keep the ladder of 3.42-43; without it the passage is only a diagnosis.

st.bg.arjuna_mind_like_wind.title: 'The mind is harder to hold than the wind'
st.bg.arjuna_mind_like_wind.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 6.33-36
st.bg.arjuna_mind_like_wind.teaching: The mind is truly hard to master, and it is mastered by repeated practice and by loosening its attachments.
st.bg.arjuna_mind_like_wind.whole_arc_note: The concession and the method belong together. Without 'asamshayam' it sounds like a demand; without 'abhyasena tu' it sounds like permission to give up.

st.bg.arjuna_what_if_i_fail.title: 'What happens to the one who tries and does not make it?'
st.bg.arjuna_what_if_i_fail.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 6.37-45
st.bg.arjuna_what_if_i_fail.teaching: Sincere effort toward the good is never wasted, and the one who makes it does not come to ruin.
st.bg.arjuna_what_if_i_fail.whole_arc_note: The reassurance is about sincere effort on the path, across lives, in the text's own frame of rebirth. Do not turn it into a promise that every project succeeds. Do not strip rebirth out either; say it as the text says it.

st.bg.arjuna_sees_and_is_afraid.title: Arjuna asks to see everything, and cannot bear it
st.bg.arjuna_sees_and_is_afraid.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 11.1-31 and 11.45-51
st.bg.arjuna_sees_and_is_afraid.teaching: The whole truth can overwhelm even the one who asked for it; the Lord consoles and comes in the form a person can hold.
st.bg.arjuna_sees_and_is_afraid.whole_arc_note: Both halves are needed: reality on that scale is terrifying even to the one who asked, and the Lord meets the devotee in the form the devotee can bear. Do not present the fear as a failure of Arjuna's.

st.bg.arjuna_apology_to_friend.title: Arjuna apologises for every time he said 'hey, Krishna'
st.bg.arjuna_apology_to_friend.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 11.41-44
st.bg.arjuna_apology_to_friend.teaching: Seeing the greatness of the one who has been beside you brings humility, and love keeps its place.
st.bg.arjuna_apology_to_friend.whole_arc_note: The apology is not accepted as proof that friendship was wrong. The tradition treasures the sakhya between them. The story is about waking up to how much one has been given, and the intimacy survives it.

st.bg.i_am_time_be_the_instrument.title: 'Be only the instrument'
st.bg.i_am_time_be_the_instrument.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 11.31-34
st.bg.i_am_time_be_the_instrument.teaching: The outcome is in the Lord's hands; a person is the instrument, and must still stand up and act.
st.bg.i_am_time_be_the_instrument.whole_arc_note: This is spoken to a warrior in a just war about the limits of his agency. It is never a comfort to give the bereaved, and it gives no licence for harm or for passivity: the same verse says 'rise'. Read with Shankara and Sridhara: the Lord is the doer, the person the means.

st.bg.if_you_cannot_then.title: 'If you cannot do that, then do this'
st.bg.if_you_cannot_then.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 12.1-12
st.bg.if_you_cannot_then.teaching: The Lord meets a person at the step he can actually take.
st.bg.if_you_cannot_then.whole_arc_note: The steps are a descent in difficulty offered out of care. The commentators differ on how to rank 12.12; do not claim the last rung is 'the best practice of all' without that note. The point for a reader is that the Gita itself offers a fallback.

st.bg.reflect_and_do_as_you_wish.title: 'Think it over fully, then do as you wish'
st.bg.reflect_and_do_as_you_wish.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 18.63-66
st.bg.reflect_and_do_as_you_wish.teaching: The teacher gives everything and leaves the decision to the student; the Lord's last word is refuge and 'do not grieve'.
st.bg.reflect_and_do_as_you_wish.whole_arc_note: Freedom and refuge are given together and in that order. Do not quote 18.66 as a command to drop one's duties; Shankara, Ramanuja and the Gita Press all read it as taking refuge in the Lord while acting, and the same chapter insists on doing one's own work. 'Ma shuchah', do not grieve, answers the grief of 2.11.

st.bg.my_delusion_is_gone.title: 'My confusion is gone. I will do as you say.'
st.bg.my_delusion_is_gone.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 18.72-73
st.bg.my_delusion_is_gone.teaching: When delusion goes, a person remembers who he is and can act without doubt in the very situation that broke him.
st.bg.my_delusion_is_gone.whole_arc_note: He credits grace, 'tvat prasadat', and the clarity comes after a long, honest dialogue with every doubt voiced. Do not present it as a sudden mood. And keep that the hard thing remained hard; he acted with clarity inside it.

st.bg.sanjaya_remembering.title: Sanjaya tells a hard truth to the king, still thrilled by what he heard
st.bg.sanjaya_remembering.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva (Gita Press Bhishma adhyayas 25 to 42; BORI 6.23 to 6.40); Bhagavad Gita 18.74-78
st.bg.sanjaya_remembering.teaching: Joy in what is true grows each time it is remembered, and where the Lord and right effort stand together, the good follows.
st.bg.sanjaya_remembering.whole_arc_note: Sanjaya is a model of two things together: gratitude that keeps renewing, and plain speech to power. Do not use him to gloat over Dhritarashtra.

st.mbh.dhritarashtra_refuses_sight.title: Offered eyes to watch the war, Dhritarashtra says no
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_refuses_sight.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Jambukhanda Vinirmana Parva, adhyaya 2 (Gita Press; BORI 6.2), adhyaya number from memory
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_refuses_sight.teaching: What a person refuses to look at does not go away; it is only heard about later, when nothing can be done.
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_refuses_sight.whole_arc_note: The text does not mock him. It shows a man who looked away for years and at the end still chooses to look away, and a father telling a son the truth without cruelty. He is also warned once more that he could restrain Duryodhana, and does not.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_walks_unarmed.title: Yudhishthira takes off his armour and walks to the enemy's elders
st.mbh.yudhishthira_walks_unarmed.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhishmavadha Parva, adhyaya 43 (Gita Press; BORI 6.41), immediately after the Gita
st.mbh.yudhishthira_walks_unarmed.teaching: Respect for elders and firm opposition to them can be held in the same hour.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_walks_unarmed.whole_arc_note: Two things together: opposing someone does not cancel what you owe them, and the elders, who know which side is right, admit they are tied by their salary. Do not make the elders simply noble; the text lets their confession stand as a sad one.

st.mbh.yuyutsu_crosses_over.title: Yuyutsu leaves his brothers' side when the drum sounds
st.mbh.yuyutsu_crosses_over.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhishmavadha Parva, adhyaya 43 (Gita Press), end of the adhyaya
st.mbh.yuyutsu_crosses_over.teaching: When one's own side is in the wrong, leaving it openly is also a dharma.
st.mbh.yuyutsu_crosses_over.whole_arc_note: The epic also honours those who stayed with a wrong side out of loyalty, such as Karna and Bhishma. Yuyutsu is not offered as the only right answer. He is the one who chose conscience and paid for it in belonging.

st.mbh.krishna_breaks_his_vow.title: Krishna breaks his own vow and runs at Bhishma
st.mbh.krishna_breaks_his_vow.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhishmavadha Parva: third day, adhyaya 59, and ninth day, adhyaya 106 (Gita Press; BORI 6.55 and 6.102), numbers from memory
st.mbh.krishna_breaks_his_vow.teaching: The Lord holds his devotee dearer than his own vow.
st.mbh.krishna_breaks_his_vow.whole_arc_note: The tradition reads this as the Lord letting his own word fall so that his devotee's word stands. It also shows Arjuna what his hesitation is costing. It gives no general permission to break promises.

st.mbh.bhishma_accused_of_partiality.title: Bhishma, giving everything, is told at night that he is not really trying
st.mbh.bhishma_accused_of_partiality.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhishmavadha Parva, night after the eighth day, adhyayas 97 to 98 (Gita Press), numbers from memory
st.mbh.bhishma_accused_of_partiality.teaching: The one who serves faithfully is often suspected by the one he serves; his conduct answers for him.
st.mbh.bhishma_accused_of_partiality.whole_arc_note: The text shows the hurt as real: 'pierced by word-arrows'. It does not say he should have absorbed it. It also shows that he kept his own judgement of the war while keeping his word.

st.mbh.bhishma_tells_how_to_fell_him.title: The Pandavas ask their grandfather how to defeat him, and he tells them
st.mbh.bhishma_tells_how_to_fell_him.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhishmavadha Parva, night after the ninth day, adhyaya 107 (Gita Press; BORI 6.103), number from memory
st.mbh.bhishma_tells_how_to_fell_him.teaching: The elder who knows his time has come can help the young do what they must, and free them of the guilt of it.
st.mbh.bhishma_tells_how_to_fell_him.whole_arc_note: Three things must stay: the old man's weariness and consent, Arjuna's anguish, and Krishna's firmness that the duty remains. It is no simple trick and no simple heroism.

st.mbh.bhishma_pillow_of_arrows.title: On the bed of arrows, Bhishma asks for a pillow and only Arjuna understands
st.mbh.bhishma_pillow_of_arrows.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhishmavadha Parva, tenth day and after, adhyayas 119 to 121 (Gita Press; BORI 6.114 to 6.116), numbers from memory; the bed of arrows and its length (fifty-eight nights) are corroborated in Anushasana Parva 13.273.27 (Kumbakonam numbering, local corpus). The Bhishma Parva text itself is not in the local corpus.
st.mbh.bhishma_pillow_of_arrows.teaching: To serve someone at the end is to understand what he needs, and a warrior meets his end as he lived.
st.mbh.bhishma_pillow_of_arrows.whole_arc_note: The scene is about dignity at the end and about what care looks like: giving the person what fits their reality, which may differ from what comforts the giver. Keep his last plea for peace; he does not die satisfied with the war.

st.mbh.karna_visits_bhishma.title: Karna comes alone to the man who insulted him
st.mbh.karna_visits_bhishma.source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhishmavadha Parva, adhyaya 122 (Gita Press; BORI 6.117), the last adhyaya of the parva, number from memory
st.mbh.karna_visits_bhishma.teaching: A harsh word can come from concern, and an old quarrel can be ended at a deathbed without either side giving up what he stands for.
st.mbh.karna_visits_bhishma.whole_arc_note: Neither man changes his position on the war. The reconciliation is personal and complete anyway. Do not edit Karna's refusal into a mistake or into pure nobility; the text gives him his reasons and gives Bhishma his sorrow.

st.mbh.abhimanyu_way_in_not_out.title: Abhimanyu knows the way in and not the way out
st.mbh.abhimanyu_way_in_not_out.source_ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Abhimanyuvadha Parva, adhyayas 33 to 49 (Gita Press; BORI 7.32 onward), numbers approximate
st.mbh.abhimanyu_way_in_not_out.teaching: When elders send the young into what they themselves cannot handle, the young pay; courage does not make up for a rule broken by the powerful.
st.mbh.abhimanyu_way_in_not_out.whole_arc_note: The text is hard on the elders, on both sides: those who sent a boy in, and those who broke the code to kill him. It does not blame Abhimanyu for going. Do not turn this into a lesson about a young person's overconfidence.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_guilt_abhimanyu.title: 'I sent the child in': Yudhishthira after Abhimanyu
st.mbh.yudhishthira_guilt_abhimanyu.source_ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Abhimanyuvadha Parva, adhyayas 51 to 54 (Gita Press), with Vyasa's account of the origin of Death; numbers approximate; the origin-of-Death tale that Vyasa tells here is told again in Shanti Parva 12.262 to 12.264 (Kumbakonam numbering, local corpus), see st.mbh.death_weeps. The Drona Parva text itself is not in the local corpus.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_guilt_abhimanyu.teaching: Death comes to every creature and no one is its author; grief has to be carried, and the work in front of one still done.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_guilt_abhimanyu.whole_arc_note: Vyasa's consolation is for a man about to collapse in the middle of a war. It widens the frame and does not say he was right to send the boy. Never offer the 'death comes to all' teaching to someone as a reason they should not feel responsible.

st.mbh.arjuna_returns_to_silence.title: Arjuna comes back to a silent camp
st.mbh.arjuna_returns_to_silence.source_ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Pratijna Parva, adhyayas 72 to 73 (Gita Press), numbers approximate
st.mbh.arjuna_returns_to_silence.teaching: The heart knows before it is told; and grief, unattended, reaches for an oath.
st.mbh.arjuna_returns_to_silence.whole_arc_note: Include the dread before the news; it is what readers recognise. The vow is shown as grief's first move and Krishna's unease is in the text: he says Arjuna spoke without consulting him. Do not present the vow as a model.

st.mbh.krishna_sleepless_before_the_vow_.title: Krishna cannot sleep and quietly prepares his own chariot
st.mbh.krishna_sleepless_before_the_vow_.source_ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Pratijna Parva, adhyaya 79 (Gita Press), number approximate
st.mbh.krishna_sleepless_before_the_vow_.teaching: A friend's care shows in what he readies quietly, before he is asked.
st.mbh.krishna_sleepless_before_the_vow_.whole_arc_note: A portrait of friendship: worry that turns into preparation and stays out of the friend's sight. Also: even Krishna, in his human role, is shown sleepless with concern. Do not use it to tell an anxious person that worry is good.

st.mbh.arjuna_rests_the_horses.title: In the middle of the hardest day, they stop to water the horses
st.mbh.arjuna_rests_the_horses.source_ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Jayadrathavadha Parva, adhyayas 99 to 100 (Gita Press), numbers approximate
st.mbh.arjuna_rests_the_horses.teaching: Those who carry you must be cared for, most of all when there is no time.
st.mbh.arjuna_rests_the_horses.whole_arc_note: The pause is not a break from the vow; it is how the vow gets kept. Arjuna keeps working while the horses rest.

st.mbh.bhurishravas_and_two_wrongs.title: Bhurishravas: a rule broken to save a friend, and a worse act after
st.mbh.bhurishravas_and_two_wrongs.source_ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Jayadrathavadha Parva, adhyayas 142 to 143 (Gita Press), numbers approximate
st.mbh.bhurishravas_and_two_wrongs.teaching: Dharma in a crisis is subtle; a wrong done in revenge on the helpless does not fade with time.
st.mbh.bhurishravas_and_two_wrongs.whole_arc_note: Keep both acts and the difference between them: one a reluctant breach to protect, one revenge on a man who had laid down his arms. And keep the long tail in the Mausala Parva.

st.mbh.ghatotkacha_and_the_spent_weapon.title: Ghatotkacha dies, the camp weeps, and Krishna dances
st.mbh.ghatotkacha_and_the_spent_weapon.source_ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Ghatotkachavadha Parva, adhyayas 179 to 183 (Gita Press), numbers approximate
st.mbh.ghatotkacha_and_the_spent_weapon.teaching: What saves the whole can cost a beloved one; the one who sees further is not thereby excused from honouring the loss.
st.mbh.ghatotkacha_and_the_spent_weapon.whole_arc_note: Do not resolve it too neatly. Krishna's joy is explained and is still hard, and the epic lets Yudhishthira say so. The child of the less-honoured mother was the one spent. Tell it with his worth named, as Yudhishthira names it.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_half_truth.title: 'Ashvatthama is dead', and under his breath, 'the elephant'
st.mbh.yudhishthira_half_truth.source_ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Dronavadha Parva, adhyayas 190 to 192 (Gita Press; BORI 7.164 to 7.165), numbers approximate
st.mbh.yudhishthira_half_truth.teaching: A half-truth told for a good end still lowers the one who tells it, and is accounted for.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_half_truth.whole_arc_note: Hold all of it: Krishna's argument that a lie to save lives is no sin, Arjuna's refusal, the technical truth, the chariot dropping, and the bill arriving in the Svargarohana Parva. The text neither excuses nor simply condemns him.

st.mbh.after_drona_the_allies_turn_on_ea.title: After the shameful win, the allies turn on each other
st.mbh.after_drona_the_allies_turn_on_ea.source_ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Narayanastramoksha Parva, adhyayas 196 to 198 (Gita Press), numbers approximate
st.mbh.after_drona_the_allies_turn_on_ea.teaching: Shame after a wrongful success turns companions against each other; it is quieted by a gentle word and by forgiving, with the wrong still named.
st.mbh.after_drona_the_allies_turn_on_ea.whole_arc_note: The value here is the honest picture: a win by a wrong means does not feel like a win, and guilt comes out as blame. Do not tidy it into a moral about unity.

st.mbh.narayanastra_lay_down_arms.title: The weapon that grows stronger the more you resist it
st.mbh.narayanastra_lay_down_arms.source_ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Narayanastramoksha Parva, adhyayas 199 to 200 (Gita Press), numbers approximate
st.mbh.narayanastra_lay_down_arms.teaching: Some forces are met by setting down one's weapons and bowing; knowing which is discernment, and no shame.
st.mbh.narayanastra_lay_down_arms.whole_arc_note: The teaching is specific: this force feeds on opposition. The same Krishna urges fierce resistance elsewhere. Do not generalise it into 'never resist' and never apply it to a person being wronged by another.

st.mbh.karna_spares_bhima.title: Karna has Bhima at his mercy and remembers a promise
st.mbh.karna_spares_bhima.source_ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Jayadrathavadha Parva, Bhima and Karna's duels, around adhyaya 139 (Gita Press), number approximate; the promise is given to Kunti in Udyoga Parva
st.mbh.karna_spares_bhima.teaching: A word given is kept even when breaking it would be easy, profitable and unseen.
st.mbh.karna_spares_bhima.whole_arc_note: He is not gentle about it: he insults Bhima, and the text keeps that. His integrity and his bitterness sit side by side. Do not make him a saint and do not hide that he fought for a wrong cause.

st.mbh.shalya_asked_to_drive.title: A king is asked to be the driver, and a driver who undermines
st.mbh.shalya_asked_to_drive.source_ref: Mahabharata, Karna Parva, adhyayas 32 to 45 (Gita Press), including the fable of the crow and the swans at adhyaya 41; numbers approximate
st.mbh.shalya_asked_to_drive.teaching: A person who knows his own measure can do his work even beside one who keeps telling him he will fail.
st.mbh.shalya_asked_to_drive.whole_arc_note: Keep that Shalya's fable has a true point about Karna's past boasting, and that Karna's answer is honest self-knowledge, not denial. Keep also that Karna loses his temper first.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_and_arjuna_quarrel.title: Two exhausted brothers nearly destroy each other in a tent
st.mbh.yudhishthira_and_arjuna_quarrel.source_ref: Mahabharata, Karna Parva, adhyayas 66 to 71 (Gita Press; BORI 8.46 to 8.50), numbers approximate
st.mbh.yudhishthira_and_arjuna_quarrel.teaching: Dharma is subtle, and a vow is not kept by an act that destroys what the vow was for.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_and_arjuna_quarrel.whole_arc_note: All four beats are needed: the unjust outburst from a broken man, the rigid vow, the harsh words actually spoken, the remorse on both sides. Krishna does not say the vow was foolish and the anger nothing; he finds how to honour the word without the harm. Self-harm is contemplated and turned aside in the scene.

st.mbh.kaushika_the_truth_teller.title: The ascetic whose truthful answer got people killed
st.mbh.kaushika_the_truth_teller.source_ref: Mahabharata, Karna Parva, adhyaya 69 (Gita Press; BORI 8.49), told by Krishna to Arjuna with the story of the hunter Balaka; number approximate
st.mbh.kaushika_the_truth_teller.teaching: A rule followed without understanding its purpose can do the very harm it exists to prevent.
st.mbh.kaushika_the_truth_teller.whole_arc_note: This is told inside a scene to stop a killing. It ranks protecting the innocent above literal speech in that kind of extremity; Krishna lists narrow cases. It is not a general permission to lie for convenience, and the tradition still holds truth the highest duty.

st.mbh.karna_wheel_in_the_mud.title: The wheel sinks and the mantra will not come
st.mbh.karna_wheel_in_the_mud.source_ref: Mahabharata, Karna Parva, adhyayas 90 to 91 (Gita Press; BORI 8.66 to 8.67), numbers approximate; the two curses behind the scene (the earth will swallow his wheel, the brahmastra will not come to him at need) and Narada's account of how they were fulfilled are verified in Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyayas 2 to 5 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering, local corpus). The Karna Parva battlefield text itself is not in the local corpus.
st.mbh.karna_wheel_in_the_mud.teaching: Old acts ripen at their own hour; a person's dignity is in how he stands when they do.
st.mbh.karna_wheel_in_the_mud.whole_arc_note: Both truths stand: he was wronged from birth and brave to the end, and he took part in real wrongs that Krishna names. His silence at Krishna's words is the text's own detail. Do not use this to tell a struggling person that their bad luck is deserved.

st.mbh.duryodhana_refuses_kripa.title: 'It is too late for peace': Duryodhana answers Kripa
st.mbh.duryodhana_refuses_kripa.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shalya Parva, adhyayas 4 to 5 (Gita Press; BORI 9.3 to 9.4), numbers approximate
st.mbh.duryodhana_refuses_kripa.teaching: Pride that will not take the offered way out goes on to finish what it began.
st.mbh.duryodhana_refuses_kripa.whole_arc_note: The text gives him real dignity and a real argument, and has already shown through seventeen days what this pride cost everyone else. Present it as a portrait of sunk cost and honour, not as a model and not as a cartoon.

st.mbh.duryodhana_in_the_lake.title: Duryodhana in the lake: 'I do not want the kingdom any more'
st.mbh.duryodhana_in_the_lake.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shalya Parva, Hradapravesha and Gadayuddha Parvas, adhyayas 29 to 32 (Gita Press), numbers approximate
st.mbh.duryodhana_in_the_lake.teaching: Emptiness after loss is no renunciation; and pride can still choose the honourable way to end.
st.mbh.duryodhana_in_the_lake.whole_arc_note: Three people are in this scene: a beaten man whose emptiness is real, a victor whose generosity is reckless, and Krishna, who sees the risk. Duryodhana's world-weariness is not repentance; the text never says he regretted the wrongs.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_weeps_for_duryodhana.title: Bhima kicks the fallen Duryodhana, and Yudhishthira stops him
st.mbh.yudhishthira_weeps_for_duryodhana.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shalya Parva, Gadayuddha Parva, adhyayas 58 to 60 (Gita Press), numbers approximate
st.mbh.yudhishthira_weeps_for_duryodhana.teaching: Even a defeated enemy is not to be humiliated; a win over one's own kin is half a grief.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_weeps_for_duryodhana.whole_arc_note: Do not make Bhima a monster; his rage has thirteen years of cause and Krishna defends him. The point is the limit Yudhishthira draws: the wrongdoer is defeated, and is still not to be degraded.

st.mbh.duryodhana_last_words.title: Duryodhana's last speech: 'Who has had a better end than I?'
st.mbh.duryodhana_last_words.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shalya Parva, Gadayuddha Parva, adhyayas 61 and 64 to 65 (Gita Press), numbers approximate
st.mbh.duryodhana_last_words.teaching: A man can meet death without flinching and still never have seen his own fault.
st.mbh.duryodhana_last_words.whole_arc_note: The epic refuses a simple verdict. His courage and consistency are honoured with flowers; his envy caused the ruin of the clan; he repents nothing. Use this as a portrait of unbroken pride and of what such pride cannot feel. Never as an example to follow.

st.mbh.balarama_stays_out.title: Balarama loves both sides and goes on pilgrimage
st.mbh.balarama_stays_out.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shalya Parva, Gadayuddha Parva, Balarama's pilgrimage, adhyayas 35 to 54 (Gita Press); his departure is told in the Udyoga Parva
st.mbh.balarama_stays_out.teaching: Standing apart from a family war keeps one's affection for both sides, and gives up any part in its outcome.
st.mbh.balarama_stays_out.whole_arc_note: The text does not condemn his withdrawal; his pilgrimage fills many chapters with sacred lore. It also shows the cost: he keeps his hands clean and loses his voice. Present both.

st.mbh.trita_in_the_well.title: Trita, left in a well by his brothers
st.mbh.trita_in_the_well.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shalya Parva, Gadayuddha Parva, Balarama's pilgrimage, the story of Udapana tirtha, adhyaya 36 (Gita Press), number approximate
st.mbh.trita_in_the_well.teaching: The one who is abandoned can still act from where he has fallen, and what is done with a whole mind reaches its mark.
st.mbh.trita_in_the_well.whole_arc_note: He is not told to forgive, and he does not. The text is entirely on his side. The strength of the story is that he does his work with what is at hand while still in the pit; rescue follows.

st.mbh.mankanaka_dances.title: Mankanaka dances at his own achievement
st.mbh.mankanaka_dances.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shalya Parva, Gadayuddha Parva, Balarama's pilgrimage, Saptasarasvata tirtha, adhyaya 38 (Gita Press); also told in Vana Parva; number approximate
st.mbh.mankanaka_dances.teaching: However far one has come, someone has gone further; delight in one's own attainment is the point where it stalls.
st.mbh.mankanaka_dances.whole_arc_note: Gentle story, gentle correction. His attainment was real; the mistake was being carried away by it. Keep Shiva's kindness.

st.mbh.sarasvata_keeps_the_learning.title: The boy who kept studying through the twelve-year drought
st.mbh.sarasvata_keeps_the_learning.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shalya Parva, Gadayuddha Parva, Balarama's pilgrimage, the story of Sarasvata, adhyaya 51 (Gita Press), number approximate
st.mbh.sarasvata_keeps_the_learning.teaching: What is practised daily through the lean years is what survives them; knowledge, not age, makes the teacher.
st.mbh.sarasvata_keeps_the_learning.whole_arc_note: He is supported, by his mother, and the story says so; staying is not pure willpower. The line about age is traditional and should be kept as his reply, without contempt for the elders.

st.mbh.ashvatthama_cannot_sleep.title: Ashvatthama cannot sleep, and Kripa says 'wait until morning'
st.mbh.ashvatthama_cannot_sleep.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sauptika Parva, adhyayas 1 to 5 (Gita Press and BORI 10.1 to 10.5)
st.mbh.ashvatthama_cannot_sleep.teaching: Anger at night passes for clear thinking; no decision made in it should be carried out before morning and before asking the wise.
st.mbh.ashvatthama_cannot_sleep.whole_arc_note: Kripa's counsel is the teaching and it fails; show both. The rage has a true cause and the text grants it. It also shows the elders' complicity, and the full consequence. Never present the act with any sympathy that reads as justification.

st.mbh.victors_defeated_by_carelessness.title: 'We who won have lost': the night after victory
st.mbh.victors_defeated_by_carelessness.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sauptika Parva, adhyaya 10 (Gita Press and BORI 10.10)
st.mbh.victors_defeated_by_carelessness.teaching: Heedlessness after success undoes what effort won.
st.mbh.victors_defeated_by_carelessness.whole_arc_note: The teaching about heedlessness is Yudhishthira's own, spoken about himself in fresh grief. It can be used for relapse and complacency after success. Never direct it at a bereaved person as blame.

st.mbh.draupadi_lets_ashvatthama_live.title: Draupadi and the man who killed her sons
st.mbh.draupadi_lets_ashvatthama_live.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sauptika Parva, Aishika Parva, adhyayas 11 and 16 (Gita Press; BORI 10.11 and 10.16)
st.mbh.draupadi_lets_ashvatthama_live.teaching: The wronged may rightly demand an answer; having received it, the great stop short of the last cruelty.
st.mbh.draupadi_lets_ashvatthama_live.whole_arc_note: She is wronged and the text never asks her to forgive first. She demands and receives justice, and only then draws her own line short of killing. Do not tell this as 'Draupadi forgave'; tell it as a mother who made her loss count and then stopped.

st.mbh.weapon_that_cannot_be_recalled.title: Arjuna can call his weapon back; Ashvatthama cannot
st.mbh.weapon_that_cannot_be_recalled.source_ref: Mahabharata, Sauptika Parva, Aishika Parva, adhyayas 13 to 16 (Gita Press; BORI 10.13 to 10.16); Krishna's promise at the Aishika to revive Uttara's child is corroborated in the local corpus at Ashvamedhika Parva 14.66.17 (Kumbakonam numbering). The Sauptika text itself is not in the local corpus.
st.mbh.weapon_that_cannot_be_recalled.teaching: What is released in fear and anger cannot be called back; only the self-controlled can withdraw what they send out.
st.mbh.weapon_that_cannot_be_recalled.whole_arc_note: This is about power acquired without the self-mastery to hold it, and about acts done in panic that cannot be undone. Parikshit's revival belongs to the whole arc.

st.mbh.vidura_man_in_the_well.title: Vidura's parable: the man in the well, licking honey
st.mbh.vidura_man_in_the_well.source_ref: Mahabharata, Stri Parva, Jalapradanika Parva, adhyayas 5 to 6 (Gita Press; BORI 11.5 to 11.6), numbers approximate
st.mbh.vidura_man_in_the_well.teaching: Life hangs by a thread that time is gnawing, and people forget it for a drop of honey; seeing this clearly is where freedom begins.
st.mbh.vidura_man_in_the_well.whole_arc_note: Vidura speaks as a brother to a bereaved brother who asked. The parable describes the human condition; it does not scold grief. Keep that the consolation only half holds; the text is honest about that.

st.mbh.dhritarashtra_crushes_iron_bhima.title: Dhritarashtra crushes the iron Bhima
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_crushes_iron_bhima.source_ref: Mahabharata, Stri Parva, Jalapradanika Parva, adhyaya 12 (Gita Press; BORI 11.11), number approximate
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_crushes_iron_bhima.teaching: Grief carries a rage that wants someone to break; let it spend itself where it harms no one, and then look at one's own part.
st.mbh.dhritarashtra_crushes_iron_bhima.whole_arc_note: Three parts: the anger is real and physical; someone who loved both sides foresaw it and gave it a harmless object; and only afterwards did the truth get said and heard. Krishna does not shame him for the rage, and he does not excuse him either.

st.mbh.gandhari_holds_back_her_curse.title: Gandhari holds back her curse, and asks one question
st.mbh.gandhari_holds_back_her_curse.source_ref: Mahabharata, Stri Parva, Jalapradanika Parva, adhyayas 14 to 15 (Gita Press; BORI 11.13 to 11.15), numbers approximate
st.mbh.gandhari_holds_back_her_curse.teaching: Even righteous anger can be held by remembering what one has always stood for; and a grief may ask a question that has no answer.
st.mbh.gandhari_holds_back_her_curse.whole_arc_note: She is a wronged and bereaved mother and the text gives her question full weight; Bhima does not have a good answer to it. Her restraint is her own act, helped by a reminder of her own words. Do not present it as an instruction to the bereaved to forgive.

st.mbh.gandhari_comforts_draupadi.title: Two mothers who have lost all their sons
st.mbh.gandhari_comforts_draupadi.source_ref: Mahabharata, Stri Parva, Jalapradanika Parva, adhyaya 15 (Gita Press), end of the adhyaya; number approximate
st.mbh.gandhari_comforts_draupadi.teaching: The one who is equally wounded can console where no teaching can.
st.mbh.gandhari_comforts_draupadi.whole_arc_note: No doctrine is offered here, only company in the same loss across the line of the war. Keep it small and quiet.

st.mbh.gandhari_curses_krishna.title: Gandhari's curse, and Krishna's answer
st.mbh.gandhari_curses_krishna.source_ref: Mahabharata, Stri Parva, Strivilapa Parva, adhyayas 16 to 25 (Gita Press; BORI 11.16 to 11.25), the curse at the end
st.mbh.gandhari_curses_krishna.teaching: Grief may accuse even the Lord, and he bears it; what is to come to each, comes, and he does not exempt himself.
st.mbh.gandhari_curses_krishna.whole_arc_note: The text lets a grieving woman accuse God to his face and lets the accusation land: he takes the curse on himself. It also has him answer her frankly. Both must be kept. Do not use his reply to silence anger at God, and do not cut it to make him only meek.

st.mbh.kunti_tells_too_late.title: Kunti tells the truth about Karna, too late
st.mbh.kunti_tells_too_late.source_ref: Mahabharata, Stri Parva, Shraddha Parva, adhyaya 27 (Gita Press), and Shanti Parva adhyayas 1 and 6 (Kumbakonam numbering in the local corpus)
st.mbh.kunti_tells_too_late.teaching: A truth kept back to protect a family returns when it can no longer help anyone.
st.mbh.kunti_tells_too_late.whole_arc_note: The curse on women is spoken in anguish and is in the text; mention it only as his outburst, never as a teaching, and it is flagged here. Keep Kunti's side too: her fear as a young girl, and her attempt to tell Karna. The story is about what a family secret does when it finally comes out.

st.mbh.narada_many_causes_of_karnas_deat.title: 'Do not grieve as if you alone killed him'
st.mbh.narada_many_causes_of_karnas_deat.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyayas 2 to 5 (Kumbakonam numbering, local corpus; Gita Press 12.2 to 12.5)
st.mbh.narada_many_causes_of_karnas_deat.teaching: An outcome ripens from many causes over a long time; no one person is its single author.
st.mbh.narada_many_causes_of_karnas_deat.whole_arc_note: Narada does not say 'it was not your fault' as a kindness; he lays out the actual chain. And the text admits it only half works. Use for people carrying total responsibility for an outcome that had many authors.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_victory_like_defeat.title: 'This victory looks to me like defeat'
st.mbh.yudhishthira_victory_like_defeat.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyayas 1 and 7 (Kumbakonam numbering, local corpus; Gita Press 12.1 and 12.7)
st.mbh.yudhishthira_victory_like_defeat.teaching: Success bought at the cost of one's own people tastes like defeat; the answer the epic gives is to make the gain serve others.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_victory_like_defeat.whole_arc_note: Do not treat his grief as weakness to be fixed; the tradition treats it as the conscience of the epic. And do not stop at the wish to renounce; the whole arc is that he is talked back into responsibility, and the kingdom is ruled well for thirty-six years by a man who never enjoyed having won it.

st.mbh.family_argues_yudhishthira_back.title: Four brothers and Draupadi argue him out of walking away
st.mbh.family_argues_yudhishthira_back.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyayas 8 to 19 (Kumbakonam numbering, local corpus; Draupadi's speech is adhyaya 14)
st.mbh.family_argues_yudhishthira_back.teaching: The wish to walk away from everything after a great loss is to be answered by those who love the person, with reasons, and more than once.
st.mbh.family_argues_yudhishthira_back.whole_arc_note: Some of their arguments are sharp to the point of insult, and Yudhishthira's replies on contentment are among the finest verses in the book. Neither side is simply right. What decides it is responsibility to others, and it takes many voices and much patience.

st.mbh.janaka_and_his_queen.title: Janaka's queen catches him renouncing a kingdom and clutching a handful of barley
st.mbh.janaka_and_his_queen.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyaya 18 (Kumbakonam numbering, local corpus; Gita Press 12.18), told by Arjuna
st.mbh.janaka_and_his_queen.teaching: Leaving one's duties and clinging to a begging bowl is still clinging; real renunciation is of the inner claim, not the outer role.
st.mbh.janaka_and_his_queen.whole_arc_note: The story is told by Arjuna to make a case, and Yudhishthira replies that Arjuna knows weapons, not the subtle path. Keep the queen's reasoning as the strong part: a wife who argues, and wins on the merits. It does not disparage genuine renunciation.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_ashamed_before_bhish.title: Yudhishthira is too ashamed to go near Bhishma
st.mbh.yudhishthira_ashamed_before_bhish.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyayas 54 to 55 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.yudhishthira_ashamed_before_bhish.teaching: The one who fears to face the elder he hurt may find the elder waiting to receive him.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_ashamed_before_bhish.whole_arc_note: The elder he wronged is the one who lifts the shame, and he does it by giving the young man work: ask. Someone else had to speak first for him.

st.mbh.krishna_asks_bhishma_to_teach.title: Krishna gives a dying man his last work
st.mbh.krishna_asks_bhishma_to_teach.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyayas 46 to 54 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.krishna_asks_bhishma_to_teach.teaching: An elder's last and best gift is what he knows; the kindest thing is to ask him for it.
st.mbh.krishna_asks_bhishma_to_teach.whole_arc_note: The grace is specific: relief of pain and a task that only he can do. Krishna deliberately steps back so the elder is the one who gives.

st.mbh.krishna_family_troubles.title: Krishna confides that his own family is impossible
st.mbh.krishna_family_troubles.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyaya 81 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly); Gita Press 12.81, the Vasudeva-Narada dialogue
st.mbh.krishna_family_troubles.teaching: Family strife is met with the weapon that is not iron: giving, patience, honesty, gentleness and due respect.
st.mbh.krishna_family_troubles.whole_arc_note: A rare passage where Krishna is the one hurting and asking. The counsel is for the strong member of a family on whom all lean; it is not advice to someone being abused to keep absorbing it.

st.mbh.sage_and_the_crow.title: The sage, the crow and the corrupt officers
st.mbh.sage_and_the_crow.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyaya 82 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.sage_and_the_crow.teaching: The one who guards what is common will be attacked by those who steal it; speak for the friend's good, and secure your own safety as you do.
st.mbh.sage_and_the_crow.whole_arc_note: The whistleblower pays first: his crow is killed. He then protects himself before saying more, and advises gradual action. It is not a tale of reckless truth-telling.

st.mbh.kshemadarshi_fallen_prince.title: The prince who lost everything asks how to live
st.mbh.kshemadarshi_fallen_prince.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyaya 104 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.kshemadarshi_fallen_prince.teaching: What is lost is not restored by grieving; settle the mind in what is at hand, and clarity returns.
st.mbh.kshemadarshi_fallen_prince.whole_arc_note: Acceptance comes first and a plan second; the sage gives both. Do not present it as 'stop wanting things'.

st.mbh.honest_jackal_framed.title: The honest minister who was framed, cleared, and left anyway
st.mbh.honest_jackal_framed.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyaya 111 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly); the tiger and the jackal
st.mbh.honest_jackal_framed.teaching: Trust once broken by a hasty accusation does not return to what it was; the honourable may decline to stay.
st.mbh.honest_jackal_framed.whole_arc_note: The text sides with the jackal's decision to leave; he is not asked to forgive and resume. The final fast is a renunciant's death in the story's own idiom and should not be dwelt on.

st.mbh.lazy_camel.title: The camel who got a long neck and stopped walking
st.mbh.lazy_camel.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyaya 112 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.lazy_camel.teaching: A convenience used as a reason to stop exerting oneself becomes the cause of ruin.
st.mbh.lazy_camel.whole_arc_note: A fable told to a king about staying active. Light in tone. The fault was in using the gift to stop moving; the wish for ease by itself was harmless.

st.mbh.river_and_the_reeds.title: The ocean asks the rivers why they never bring down the cane
st.mbh.river_and_the_reeds.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyaya 113 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.river_and_the_reeds.teaching: Before a force one cannot match, bend and keep one's roots; rise when it has passed.
st.mbh.river_and_the_reeds.whole_arc_note: This is counsel about strategy before overwhelming force, and the cane rises again. It is not a teaching that the wronged should submit, and the same Bhishma elsewhere says the too-soft are trampled (12.103.34).

st.mbh.dog_who_became_a_sharabha.title: The dog who was raised up and turned on the one who raised him
st.mbh.dog_who_became_a_sharabha.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyayas 116 to 117 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.dog_who_became_a_sharabha.teaching: One raised by another's kindness who turns on that kindness loses what he was given.
st.mbh.dog_who_became_a_sharabha.whole_arc_note: The teaching is addressed to the one who promotes, about judging character and not only loyalty or need. It is not about birth; the dog's fault is what he did with what he was given.

st.mbh.three_fish.title: Three fish and the draining pond
st.mbh.three_fish.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Apaddharma Parva, adhyaya 137 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.three_fish.teaching: Act before the danger arrives, or act fast when it does; the one who keeps saying 'later' is lost.
st.mbh.three_fish.whole_arc_note: Keep the second fish. The story does not say only planners survive; it says the one who neither plans nor responds is lost.

st.mbh.cat_and_mouse_truce.title: The mouse who freed the cat, and then declined the friendship
st.mbh.cat_and_mouse_truce.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Apaddharma Parva, adhyaya 138 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.cat_and_mouse_truce.teaching: In danger even an enemy may be an ally; when the danger has passed, do not mistake that alliance for safety.
st.mbh.cat_and_mouse_truce.whole_arc_note: This is apad-dharma, counsel for emergencies with someone who can harm you. It does not teach general distrust of friends; Bhishma teaches the worth of true friends elsewhere. It suits working relationships with rivals.

st.mbh.pujani_leaves.title: Pujani the bird leaves the palace
st.mbh.pujani_leaves.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Apaddharma Parva, adhyaya 139 (Kumbakonam numbering, as in the local corpus and library ids; Gita Press numbers differ slightly)
st.mbh.pujani_leaves.teaching: After real mutual injury, kind words do not restore trust; it is wise to part.
st.mbh.pujani_leaves.whole_arc_note: Her retaliation is in the text and is not praised; the teaching Bhishma draws is about trust after mutual injury. Her leaving is presented as wisdom. Never use this to urge someone to stay and reconcile.

st.mbh.yudhishthira_will_starve_himself.title: The king who won announces he will sit down and starve
st.mbh.yudhishthira_will_starve_himself.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyayas 26 to 27 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ); Vyasa answers with the Ashma Gita
st.mbh.yudhishthira_will_starve_himself.teaching: Everything that is gathered is scattered; grief that refuses this truth turns on the one who grieves.
st.mbh.yudhishthira_will_starve_himself.whole_arc_note: Keep both halves: the vow to die is real and stated in his own words, and so is the slow return through many voices. Do not shorten it to 'he was consoled'. This is a story about self-destructive guilt after an outcome you caused; mark it as such.

st.mbh.senajit_and_the_logs_in_the_sea.title: A king who has lost his son, and the friend who asks him a hard question
st.mbh.senajit_and_the_logs_in_the_sea.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyaya 173, verses 8 to 57 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
st.mbh.senajit_and_the_logs_in_the_sea.teaching: Beings meet and part like logs on the sea; seeing this clearly is what loosens grief.
st.mbh.senajit_and_the_logs_in_the_sea.whole_arc_note: The friend's opening is blunt, and it lands because he is a friend who came, and because the king himself asks for the knowledge. Do not serve the blunt line cold to someone newly bereaved; serve the whole scene, including the question the king asks.

st.mbh.pingala_stops_waiting.title: Pingala waits all night for someone who does not come, and then stops
st.mbh.pingala_stops_waiting.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyaya 173, verses 58 to 64 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ), told to Senajit
st.mbh.pingala_stops_waiting.teaching: Expectation that hangs on someone else keeps you awake; letting it go is what lets you sleep.
st.mbh.pingala_stops_waiting.whole_arc_note: Her 'nairashya' is giving up the hope that hangs on another person's coming, not giving up on life. Read it as freedom from waiting, never as despair. Her trade is not the point; she is the teacher here.

st.mbh.janaka_mithila_burns.title: Mithila is on fire, and the king says nothing of his is burning
st.mbh.janaka_mithila_burns.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyaya 223, verses 1 to 18 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ); the verse also quoted at 12.17.19 and 12.176.56
st.mbh.janaka_mithila_burns.teaching: One who holds nothing as 'mine' loses nothing when it burns, and so can act without fear.
st.mbh.janaka_mithila_burns.whole_arc_note: Janaka did not abandon Mithila; he went on ruling it well. The verse describes a ruler who acts fully and owns nothing inside. Do not use it to tell someone their house or savings should not matter to them; use it for the fear of losing what you hold.

st.mbh.manki_and_the_two_young_bulls.title: Manki puts his last money into two young bulls, and a camel runs off with them
st.mbh.manki_and_the_two_young_bulls.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyaya 176, verses 4 to 54 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
st.mbh.manki_and_the_two_young_bulls.teaching: Craving is born of one's own imagining; stop feeding it and it dies at the root.
st.mbh.manki_and_the_two_young_bulls.whole_arc_note: The arc moves from 'it is all fate' to 'it is my craving'. Do not stop at the fatalist lines in the middle. Also, this is not advice to stop working; Bhishma tells it to a king asking how a man who fails to gain wealth can still be happy.

st.mbh.medhavin_wakes_his_father.title: A son tells his father not to wait for later
st.mbh.medhavin_wakes_his_father.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyaya 174 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
st.mbh.medhavin_wakes_his_father.teaching: Death does not wait for the work to be done; do the work that matters now, not after.
st.mbh.medhavin_wakes_his_father.whole_arc_note: The child is the teacher and the parent listens; keep that. The urgency is about the inner work, not about cramming more tasks into a day.

st.mbh.kashyapa_and_the_jackal.title: Knocked down by a rich man's chariot, Kashyapa decides to die, and a jackal talks to him about hands
st.mbh.kashyapa_and_the_jackal.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyaya 178 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
st.mbh.kashyapa_and_the_jackal.teaching: Before counting what you lack, count what you have; a human life with hands is already the great gain.
st.mbh.kashyapa_and_the_jackal.whole_arc_note: This is a story about wanting to die after humiliation and money envy. It must be served only where there is no risk, and the jackal's turn is gratitude for what one has, never 'others have it worse, so stop'. Keep the merchant's arrogance in view; Kashyapa was wronged.

st.mbh.bali_after_the_fall.title: The king who lost everything, asked by the winner how it feels
st.mbh.bali_after_the_fall.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyayas 230 to 231 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
st.mbh.bali_after_the_fall.teaching: Fortune moves on by time's turn; the one who knows this neither crumbles in a fall nor gloats in a rise.
st.mbh.bali_after_the_fall.whole_arc_note: Bali's calm is not resignation; he keeps his dignity and corrects the winner to his face. Use for loss of status, never to tell a wronged person their loss does not matter.

st.mbh.vishvamitra_and_the_dogs_meat.title: Starving in a famine, the great sage steals dog's meat from an outcaste's hut
st.mbh.vishvamitra_and_the_dogs_meat.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Apaddharma Parva, adhyaya 141 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
st.mbh.vishvamitra_and_the_dogs_meat.teaching: In real extremity, staying alive is itself a duty; the code bends for the crisis and returns after it.
st.mbh.vishvamitra_and_the_dogs_meat.whole_arc_note: Do not reduce this to 'rules do not matter'. The text frames it strictly as apaddharma: true emergency, no other way, argued in the open, and with the inner rule kept where possible. The chandala is shown as articulate and right on many points; do not make him a prop. Caste language is in the text; tell it without endorsing hierarchy.

st.mbh.jajali_and_tuladhara.title: The ascetic proud of birds nesting in his hair is sent to learn from a shopkeeper
st.mbh.jajali_and_tuladhara.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyayas 267 to 270 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
st.mbh.jajali_and_tuladhara.teaching: One who is a friend to all beings in deed, thought and word knows dharma, whatever his work.
st.mbh.jajali_and_tuladhara.whole_arc_note: The story does not mock austerity; it targets the pride that grows out of it. Do not turn it into 'ordinary work beats spiritual practice'. The point is that goodwill toward all, practised in ordinary dealing, is the measure.

st.mbh.vyasa_runs_after_shuka.title: Vyasa runs after his grown son calling 'Son!', and only the echo answers
st.mbh.vyasa_runs_after_shuka.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, the Shuka narrative, adhyayas 333 to 341, the departure at 341 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
st.mbh.vyasa_runs_after_shuka.teaching: A parent can be proud of a child's freedom and still ache at being left; both are true, and grace meets the ache.
st.mbh.vyasa_runs_after_shuka.whole_arc_note: Do not cut it at the echo; the father's mixed joy and shame, and Shiva's gentleness with him, are the heart. The son is not dead; he has gone on to his own life. Do not use as consolation after a child's death.

st.mbh.death_weeps.title: Death is created, and the first thing she does is weep
st.mbh.death_weeps.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharma section, adhyayas 262 to 264 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ); the same story is told by Vyasa to Yudhishthira in Drona Parva after Abhimanyu's death
st.mbh.death_weeps.teaching: Death comes at its time to every being and is no one's cruelty; seeing this, grief can loosen.
st.mbh.death_weeps.whole_arc_note: The image is Death weeping and not wanting to do it. Keep that. Do not frame death as punishment. Told after Abhimanyu's death to a guilty, grieving Yudhishthira; it consoles by removing the idea that someone malicious took the person away.

st.mbh.srinjaya_and_the_sixteen_kings.title: A father whose son was killed, and the list of the great who also died
st.mbh.srinjaya_and_the_sixteen_kings.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyayas 28 to 30 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ); Krishna retells Narada's words to Yudhishthira
st.mbh.srinjaya_and_the_sixteen_kings.teaching: Even the greatest and most righteous die; no one is singled out, and seeing this lightens the weight.
st.mbh.srinjaya_and_the_sixteen_kings.whole_arc_note: Do not present the revival as something a grieving parent can expect; lead with the sixteen kings, and say plainly that the boy's return is a miracle of this story. Not for a parent recently bereaved of a child as a plan-day story unless the plan is explicitly about reading the text, because the happy ending can wound.

st.mbh.fowler_and_the_pigeons.title: The hunter who sheltered under a tree, and the bird who fed him
st.mbh.fowler_and_the_pigeons.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Apaddharma Parva, adhyayas 143 to 148 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
st.mbh.fowler_and_the_pigeons.teaching: Kindness shown even to one's enemy can break a hard heart where nothing else could.
st.mbh.fowler_and_the_pigeons.whole_arc_note: This story contains two self-sacrifices by fire, and the female's words idealise a wife following her husband in death. Do not present either as a model. The usable arc is the hunter's: a hard man undone by a kindness he did not deserve. Serve only where risk is none.

st.mbh.gautama_kills_his_benefactor.title: The man who was rescued, fed and made rich, and killed his friend for the journey home
st.mbh.gautama_kills_his_benefactor.source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Apaddharma Parva, Kritaghnopakhyana, adhyayas 166 to 172 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
st.mbh.gautama_kills_his_benefactor.teaching: Ingratitude to the one who helped you is the wrong for which the text sees no atonement.
st.mbh.gautama_kills_his_benefactor.whole_arc_note: The crane's last act, asking life for the man who killed him, is part of the story; do not stop at the punishment. The tale contains caste insults against Gautama for his way of life; leave those out when retelling.
