st.rcm.angad_asks_to_stay.source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand, dohas 19 to 21 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
st.rcm.angad_asks_to_stay.teaching: Love can mean being sent to your own life; carry the one you love in your heart and go.
st.rcm.angad_asks_to_stay.whole_arc_note: The request is not granted. The text does not make Angad's wish come true; it gives him an embrace, the garland from Ram's own chest, and a duty elsewhere. Keep the ending as it is: he goes.

st.rcm.ram_asks_to_be_corrected.title: Ram, now king, tells his people to stop him if he says anything wrong
st.rcm.ram_asks_to_be_corrected.source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand, dohas 45 to 46 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
st.rcm.ram_asks_to_be_corrected.teaching: A leader who asks to be stopped when wrong, and leaves people free to choose, is trusted.
st.rcm.ram_asks_to_be_corrected.whole_arc_note: The invitation to correct him is not a rhetorical flourish; the tradition reads it as the mark of Ram Rajya. The rest of the address is a strong call to use human life well, given with permission to accept or decline.

st.rcm.garuda_doubts_after_rescue.title: Garuda frees Ram from a snake-noose and starts to doubt him
st.rcm.garuda_doubts_after_rescue.source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand, dohas 58 to 62 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
st.rcm.garuda_doubts_after_rescue.teaching: Doubt born of seeing the great appear small is cured by humble listening in good company, not by argument.
st.rcm.garuda_doubts_after_rescue.whole_arc_note: The doubt is not punished; it is taken seriously by three great teachers, each of whom admits they are under maya too. The cure is humility (learning from a crow) and patient listening, not argument.

st.rcm.kakbhushundi_doubts_the_toddler.title: Kakbhushundi watches the child Ram chase him and cannot believe this is God
st.rcm.kakbhushundi_doubts_the_toddler.source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand, dohas 76 to 84 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
st.rcm.kakbhushundi_doubts_the_toddler.teaching: When the ordinary hides the infinite, doubt is natural; the answer is not proof but humble love for the form that confused you.
st.rcm.kakbhushundi_doubts_the_toddler.whole_arc_note: The doubt comes from love, from close watching, not from distance. The vision overwhelms rather than refutes it. And the boon he chooses is devotion to the very form he doubted.

st.rcm.student_who_would_not_rise.title: A proud student refuses to rise for his teacher, and the teacher prays for him
st.rcm.student_who_would_not_rise.source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand, dohas 101 to 104 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
st.rcm.student_who_would_not_rise.teaching: A true teacher answers the student's insult with prayer for him; pride before one's teacher costs more than the teacher will ever ask.
st.rcm.student_who_would_not_rise.whole_arc_note: The guru never asked for justice; the curse came from Shiva. The teacher's response to insult was compassion, and that compassion changed the student's fate. Keep the student's arrogance plain, and keep the teacher's prayer central. The passage has caste language in the narrator's self-description (7.101 to 7.102); it is not the point and is kept out.

st.rcm.kakbhushundi_cursed_and_glad.title: Kakbhushundi argues with a great sage, is cursed into a crow, and flies off happy
st.rcm.kakbhushundi_cursed_and_glad.source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand, dohas 106 to 110 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
st.rcm.kakbhushundi_cursed_and_glad.teaching: Meet a harsh outcome without resentment, and it may become the very form of your blessing.
st.rcm.kakbhushundi_cursed_and_glad.whole_arc_note: He was arguing with a revered teacher, and the text does not call that wrong; it calls his steadiness devotion. What turns it is his response to an unjust outcome: no resentment, no fear, and a reading of it that made it grace. Do not use this to tell a wronged person to welcome mistreatment.

st.rcm.manas_rog.title: Garuda asks what the diseases of the mind are, and is given a diagnosis and a cure
st.rcm.manas_rog.source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand, dohas 117 to 118 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
st.rcm.manas_rog.teaching: Delusion is the root of the mind's diseases; grace, a true teacher, restraint and devotion are the cure.
st.rcm.manas_rog.whole_arc_note: The diagnosis is sobering (everyone is ill, knowing is not curing), and the remedy is specific and devotional. Do not present it as self-help; the text says grace, a teacher, restraint and devotion together.

st.rcm.lamp_and_the_gem.title: Kakbhushundi explains why the lamp of knowledge goes out and the gem of devotion does not
st.rcm.lamp_and_the_gem.source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand, dohas 114 to 116 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
st.rcm.lamp_and_the_gem.teaching: Knowledge is a lamp the winds can put out; devotion is a gem that shines by itself.
st.rcm.lamp_and_the_gem.whole_arc_note: Kakbhushundi does not dismiss knowledge; he calls it true and describes it with respect. The contrast is about fragility and labour, not worth. Present it as the Manas's own position, a devotional one.

st.rcm.tara_consoled.title: Tara weeps over her husband, and the one who killed him consoles her
st.rcm.tara_consoled.source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand, dohas 11 to 12 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
st.rcm.tara_consoled.teaching: The body is made of elements and lies before us; the one we love is not only that.
st.rcm.tara_consoled.whole_arc_note: Note who speaks and how: it is grace given in person, at the right moment, and the text says it removed maya rather than merely argued. Using this verse to tell a fresh griever 'why are you crying' would invert it. Her earlier warning to Bali, which he dismissed, is part of the arc.

st.bhakti.tulsi_turned_by_ratnavali.title: Tulsidas follows his wife across a flooded river and is turned by her words
st.bhakti.tulsi_turned_by_ratnavali.source_ref: Hagiography: Priyadas, Bhaktirasabodhini commentary on Nabhadas's Bhaktamal (1712), and the later Mool Gosain Charit attributed to Benimadhav Das (authenticity disputed). Not told in Tulsidas's own works.
st.bhakti.tulsi_turned_by_ratnavali.teaching: Intense love, redirected, can become devotion; a sharp word at the right moment can turn a life.
st.bhakti.tulsi_turned_by_ratnavali.whole_arc_note: This is hagiography, told for centuries but not attested by Tulsidas himself; his own poems speak instead of an abandoned childhood and begging for scraps (see st.bhakti.tulsi_abandoned_as_a_child). The tale is usually told to praise the wife's words; it can also be read as a husband leaving a wife. Tell it as a tradition, with that ambiguity, and do not present the verse as Tulsi's.

st.bhakti.tulsi_abandoned_as_a_child.title: Tulsidas tells his own story: left at birth, begging for scraps
st.bhakti.tulsi_abandoned_as_a_child.source_ref: Tulsidas, Kavitavali, Uttar Kand 57 and 72 (corpus ids tulsi_kv.7.57, tulsi_kv.7.72); Vinay Patrika 227
st.bhakti.tulsi_abandoned_as_a_child.teaching: Even the one whom parents and fate abandoned is taken in by the Name; asking once, honestly, is enough.
st.bhakti.tulsi_abandoned_as_a_child.whole_arc_note: Do not turn this into a rags-to-riches story. Tulsi keeps calling himself low and faulty even after the honour; the gratitude is to the Name, not to his own effort. These are his own poems, the most reliable source for his life.

st.bhakti.tulsi_no_more_wasting.title: Tulsidas resolves: till now I wasted my life; I will not waste it any more
st.bhakti.tulsi_no_more_wasting.teaching: What was wasted is past; by grace one wakes, and can refuse to sleep again.
st.bhakti.tulsi_no_more_wasting.whole_arc_note: The resolve rests on grace (rama kripa), not willpower alone. Do not turn it into a productivity slogan; it is a devotee's waking.

st.bhakti.tulsi_bahuk_pain_in_the_arm.title: Old Tulsidas, in unbearable pain, argues with Hanuman
st.bhakti.tulsi_bahuk_pain_in_the_arm.source_ref: Tulsidas, Hanuman Bahuk (corpus ids tulsi_hb.21, tulsi_hb.36, tulsi_hb.38 [verse 37 in the text], tulsi_hb.42)
st.bhakti.tulsi_bahuk_pain_in_the_arm.teaching: In pain one may complain openly to the one we trust; complaint and trust can live in the same breath.
st.bhakti.tulsi_bahuk_pain_in_the_arm.whole_arc_note: Keep the ambiguity of cause and the absence of a reported cure in the text itself. The value is in how he prays in pain: frank, intimate, unresolved. The cure is tradition.

st.bhakti.tulsi_call_me_what_you_like.title: People call Tulsidas a rogue, a weaver, a Rajput; he does not argue
st.bhakti.tulsi_call_me_what_you_like.source_ref: Tulsidas, Kavitavali, Uttar Kand (corpus id tulsi_kv.7.106; the corpus text gives only the first half of the verse)
st.bhakti.tulsi_call_me_what_you_like.teaching: When you need nothing from your critics, their labels have nothing to hold on to.
st.bhakti.tulsi_call_me_what_you_like.whole_arc_note: The verse is his own. The hostility of the Kashi pandits is tradition. The tone is wry, not wounded; keep it that way, and do not inflate it into defiance.

st.bhakti.meera_leaves_the_family_way.title: Meera refuses the life her royal family expects of her
st.bhakti.meera_leaves_the_family_way.source_ref: Meera's padas (traditionally attributed; Meera texts vary widely). Corpus: meera.kk.8 (verified). 'Mere to Giridhar Gopal' and 'Pag ghunghroo bandh' are from memory, not in corpus. Hagiography: Nabhadas, Bhaktamal; Priyadas's commentary.
st.bhakti.meera_leaves_the_family_way.teaching: When devotion is real, the world's labels and threats lose their grip; there is no second.
st.bhakti.meera_leaves_the_family_way.whole_arc_note: This is a devotee's story. It is not a lesson in individualism; what she chooses is Krishna, not herself. The poison and snake are hagiography; what her padas say directly is the social cost: called mad, called a destroyer of the family. Mark confidence honestly. Wronged stance: she is not told to adjust.

st.bhakti.meera_no_one_knows_my_pain.title: Meera: only the wounded know the wounded
st.bhakti.meera_no_one_knows_my_pain.source_ref: Meera pada 'He ri main to prem diwani' (corpus id meera.kk.3, Kavitakosh popular reading)
st.bhakti.meera_no_one_knows_my_pain.teaching: Only one who has been wounded understands the wound; the pain of longing for God is healed only by God.
st.bhakti.meera_no_one_knows_my_pain.whole_arc_note: This is devotional viraha; the 'beloved' is Krishna. It speaks to anyone who is not understood in their pain, but do not flatten it into a romance or a diagnosis.

st.bhakti.meera_found_the_jewel.title: Meera has found the jewel of Ram's name and wants nothing more
st.bhakti.meera_found_the_jewel.source_ref: Meera pada 'Payo ji maine ram ratan dhan payo' (corpus id meera.kk.13, Kavitakosh popular reading)
st.bhakti.meera_found_the_jewel.teaching: The wealth that grows when spent and cannot be stolen is the Name, received by grace.
st.bhakti.meera_found_the_jewel.whole_arc_note: Use this for people who are grateful or content; it should never be framed as a fix for a problem. It is the voice of someone who already has what she wants.

st.bhakti.sur_danced_enough.title: Surdas: I have danced enough, Gopal
st.bhakti.sur_danced_enough.source_ref: Surdas, Vinay pada 'Ab main nachyo bahut Gopal' (corpus id sur.vp.200, Sursagar vinay padas, Gita Press OCR)
st.bhakti.sur_danced_enough.teaching: Seen clearly, the life driven by craving is a costume dance; one can ask to stop.
st.bhakti.sur_danced_enough.whole_arc_note: The weariness is real and honest; it is not depression and should not be served as such. It is the devotee's turning from performing to asking.

st.bhakti.sur_stop_wailing.title: Surdas sings only of his own sins until his guru tells him to sing of Krishna
st.bhakti.sur_stop_wailing.source_ref: Surdas's vinay padas (corpus sur.vp.195, sur.vp.271, verified). The meeting with Vallabhacharya is from the Chaurasi Vaishnavan ki Varta (hagiography; from memory).
st.bhakti.sur_stop_wailing.teaching: Confession has its place; then stop wailing and sing of the One who turns iron to gold.
st.bhakti.sur_stop_wailing.whole_arc_note: The self-reproach padas are his own and are not wrong; the tradition does not throw them away. The Vallabha turn is hagiography and should be told as such. The pairing is the point: honest confession, then the instruction to stop dwelling and sing of what is good.

st.bhakti.sur_krishna_misses_his_mother.title: Krishna, now a prince in Mathura, sends word home: no one here calls me Kanhaiya
st.bhakti.sur_krishna_misses_his_mother.source_ref: Surdas, Bhramargeet padas 'Pathik sandeso kahiyo jaay' and 'Nike rahiyo Jasumati maiya' (corpus ids sur.bgs.9, sur.bgs.10, ed. Ramchandra Shukla)
st.bhakti.sur_krishna_misses_his_mother.teaching: Splendour abroad cannot replace being known by your childhood name at home.
st.bhakti.sur_krishna_misses_his_mother.whole_arc_note: Do not tidy the ending: 'four or five days' becomes a long absence. The tenderness of the message and the pain of the delay both belong to the scene.

st.bhakti.sur_gajendra_calls_last.title: The elephant king fights the crocodile with all his strength, and calls only when it is gone
st.bhakti.sur_gajendra_calls_last.source_ref: Surdas, Vinay pada 'Bharoso nam ko bhari' (corpus id sur.vp.241); story from Bhagavata Purana 8.2 to 8.4
st.bhakti.sur_gajendra_calls_last.teaching: When your own strength is spent, call; help comes to the one who calls with nothing left.
st.bhakti.sur_gajendra_calls_last.whole_arc_note: Do not moralise this as 'should have called sooner'. The text honours the struggle and the call; Surdas adds his own impatience to it. For a secular reader, it is about asking for help when your own strength is finished.

st.bhakti.kabir_looking_for_the_bad_one.title: Kabir goes looking for a bad person and finds himself
st.bhakti.kabir_looking_for_the_bad_one.source_ref: Kabir dohas (corpus kabir.kk.146 from Kavita-Kaumudi; kabir.kkdv.421 from a popular compilation)
st.bhakti.kabir_looking_for_the_bad_one.teaching: Look for fault in your own heart first; keep the one who criticises you close.
st.bhakti.kabir_looking_for_the_bad_one.whole_arc_note: This is not self-hatred: Kabir's voice is wry and clear-eyed. And it is not advice to keep abusers close; nindak here is the one who points out your faults. Kabir's life is mostly legend; these dohas are popular readings, attributed with medium confidence.

st.bhakti.kabir_the_weavers_sheet.title: Kabir the weaver: the body is a fine sheet, to be returned unstained
st.bhakti.kabir_the_weavers_sheet.source_ref: Kabir pada 'Jhini jhini bini chadariya' (traditional, not in corpus). Supporting dohas in corpus: kabir.kk.23 (the clay and the potter), kabir.kk.19 (do tomorrow's work today).
st.bhakti.kabir_the_weavers_sheet.teaching: The body is lent cloth: wear it carefully, do your work now, and give it back clean.
st.bhakti.kabir_the_weavers_sheet.whole_arc_note: The chadariya pada is quoted from memory and not verified here; the dohas are verified. Kabir's biography (weaver, Kashi, Niru and Nima, Ramanand) is tradition with low historical confidence.

st.bhakti.kabir_slowly_mind.title: Kabir to his own restless mind: slowly, slowly
st.bhakti.kabir_slowly_mind.source_ref: Kabir doha 'Dhire dhire re mana' (corpus id kabir.kkdv.12, popular compilation)
st.bhakti.kabir_slowly_mind.teaching: Water faithfully; the fruit comes in its season, not because you poured more.
st.bhakti.kabir_slowly_mind.whole_arc_note: Keep the hundred pots: the teaching is effort without forcing the season, not passivity.

st.bhakti.rahim_when_the_days_turn.title: Rahim, once the empire's great general, writes about the turning of days
st.bhakti.rahim_when_the_days_turn.source_ref: Rahim's dohe (corpus rahim.169, rahim.26, rahim.58, rahim.37). Biography of Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan (Akbar's commander; fall from favour under Jahangir) from memory.
st.bhakti.rahim_when_the_days_turn.teaching: Fortune turns; in the bad days stay quiet, learn who your friends are, and go where the exiled go.
st.bhakti.rahim_when_the_days_turn.whole_arc_note: The biography is history from memory and should be told lightly. The dohas are his own (Wikisource text). 'Sit quiet' here is about not panicking or begging during a downturn; it is not advice to a wronged person to accept injustice.

st.bhakti.rahim_lowered_eyes.title: Rahim gives with his eyes lowered, and explains why
st.bhakti.rahim_lowered_eyes.source_ref: Rahim doha 'Denhar kou aur hai' (corpus id rahim.95, verified). The question attributed to Tulsidas is tradition, from memory.
st.bhakti.rahim_lowered_eyes.teaching: When you give, remember who the Giver is; that is why the eyes go down.
st.bhakti.rahim_lowered_eyes.whole_arc_note: Rahim's reply is verified in the corpus; the question and its attribution to Tulsidas are tradition with low confidence. Keep it light.

st.up.nachiketa_questions_father.title: Nachiketa watches his father give away worn-out cows
st.up.nachiketa_questions_father.teaching: A gift that costs the giver nothing leads to joyless worlds; faith shows as the courage to say so.
st.up.nachiketa_questions_father.whole_arc_note: Do not clip this to 'a child shames his father'. Shankara reads Nachiketa as wanting to save his father from the fruit of a false gift. And the first thing he later asks of Death is that his father's anger be calmed.

st.up.nachiketa_three_nights_first_boon.title: Three nights at Death's door, and the first wish is for his father's peace
st.up.nachiketa_three_nights_first_boon.teaching: Before the largest questions, he sets right the relationship at home.
st.up.nachiketa_three_nights_first_boon.whole_arc_note: The reconciliation is asked for by the one who was wronged, freely, from a position of strength, after the father's wrong has been named. It is not advice to a hurt child to forgive first.

st.up.nachiketa_refuses_bribes.title: Nachiketa refuses everything Death offers in place of an answer
st.up.nachiketa_refuses_bribes.teaching: The good and the pleasant both come to a person; the wise sort them and choose the good.
st.up.nachiketa_refuses_bribes.whole_arc_note: Yama's offers are a teacher's test of readiness, and the text does not condemn wealth for those who want it. Nachiketa's refusal belongs to someone with one burning question; it is not a rule for everyone.

st.up.ushasti_famine.title: Ushasti eats a stranger's leftovers in a famine and refuses the water
st.up.ushasti_famine.teaching: In real need, taking what keeps you alive is no fall; taking more than that is.
st.up.ushasti_famine.whole_arc_note: Tell both halves: he takes what he must to live and refuses what he does not need. Shankara uses this to show that the relaxation is for danger to life, and stops there.

st.up.mahidasa_illness.title: Mahidasa speaks to his illness
st.up.mahidasa_illness.teaching: A life seen as an offering has work still to complete, and that gives strength in illness.
st.up.mahidasa_illness.whole_arc_note: This is a meditation (purusha-yajna vidya) joined to prayer in each stage of life. It is not a promise that attitude cures disease and must never replace treatment.

st.up.satyakama_truth_about_birth.title: Satyakama tells the teacher he does not know who his father is
st.up.satyakama_truth_about_birth.teaching: What qualifies a person is truthfulness, shown when a lie would be easier.
st.up.satyakama_truth_about_birth.whole_arc_note: Follow Shankara: the mother was occupied serving guests in her husband's house and never asked, and he died early. Do not sensationalise her words. The story honours her honesty as much as his.

st.up.satyakama_four_hundred_cows.title: Sent away with four hundred lean cows, Satyakama learns from a bull, a fire, a swan and a waterbird
st.up.satyakama_four_hundred_cows.teaching: Unglamorous work done faithfully becomes the teaching; and what you learn alone is completed by asking.
st.up.satyakama_four_hundred_cows.whole_arc_note: Keep the ending. He learned from life and still asked his teacher. The story does not say you need no teacher; it says patient work makes you able to hear one.

st.up.upakosala_passed_over.title: Upakosala is passed over while every other student graduates
st.up.upakosala_passed_over.teaching: Service that seemed unnoticed was noticed; what you tended will itself speak for you.
st.up.upakosala_passed_over.whole_arc_note: The wife had already told the teacher, 'This student is worn out, teach him before the fires blame you.' The text takes his hurt seriously; no one tells him he is wrong to feel it. He refuses food from grief, which the story does not recommend.

st.up.shvetaketu_comes_home_proud.title: Shvetaketu comes home after twelve years, sure he knows everything
st.up.shvetaketu_comes_home_proud.teaching: Knowing many things is different from knowing that by which everything is known.
st.up.shvetaketu_comes_home_proud.whole_arc_note: The father does not humiliate him; he calls him 'somya', dear one, throughout. The pride is punctured by a question, and the son's willingness to ask is what the story honours.

st.up.shvetaketu_fifteen_day_fast.title: Fifteen days without food and Shvetaketu cannot recall a single verse
st.up.shvetaketu_fifteen_day_fast.teaching: The mind depends on the body; care of the body is care of the mind.
st.up.shvetaketu_fifteen_day_fast.whole_arc_note: A teaching experiment set by a father for a healthy student, to show mind depends on food. It is not a recommendation to fast.

st.up.tat_tvam_asi_seed_and_salt.title: A fig seed, a lump of salt, and 'that thou art'
st.up.tat_tvam_asi_seed_and_salt.teaching: What is real in you cannot be seen with the eye, and is the same reality that holds up everything.
st.up.tat_tvam_asi_seed_and_salt.whole_arc_note: The father repeats the teaching nine times without impatience, and the son asks again nine times without shame. Keep both. In Shankara's reading 'that thou art' asserts identity of the self with the real, and must not be thinned into 'you are connected to everything'.

st.up.man_from_gandhara.title: The blindfolded man left far from home
st.up.man_from_gandhara.teaching: Lost is not the same as hopeless; one true direction plus your own steps gets you home.
st.up.man_from_gandhara.whole_arc_note: Both parts matter: someone removes the blindfold, and he still has to walk, ask and use his own sense. Shankara reads the kind stranger as the teacher and the walk as one's own reflection.

st.up.narada_knows_everything_still_grie.title: Narada knows every subject and is still in sorrow
st.up.narada_knows_everything_still_grie.teaching: Yo vai bhuma tat sukham: the infinite alone is happiness; there is no happiness in the finite.
st.up.narada_knows_everything_still_grie.whole_arc_note: Learning is not mocked. Sanatkumara starts from what Narada knows and builds upward from it. And Narada's honesty about his sadness is what opens the teaching.

st.up.indra_virochana.title: Two students hear the same first answer; one goes home, one keeps coming back
st.up.indra_virochana.teaching: The first answer that satisfies you may be the place you stop growing; honesty about what still does not add up is the path.
st.up.indra_virochana.whole_arc_note: Prajapati does not lie; he gives each stage and waits to see who will question it. Do not use Virochana to sneer at caring for the body. His error is stopping, and stopping at a view that makes the body all there is.

st.up.senses_quarrel.title: The senses argue over who matters most, and each walks out for a year
st.up.senses_quarrel.teaching: The quiet thing that keeps everything running is known only when it starts to leave.
st.up.senses_quarrel.whole_arc_note: Breath does not gloat and no sense is declared useless. The body got by, poorly, without each. The point is what silently supports the rest.

st.up.shvetaketu_jaivali_five_questions.title: Shvetaketu fails five questions in public, and his father admits he does not know either
st.up.shvetaketu_jaivali_five_questions.teaching: There is no age or rank at which 'I do not know, teach me' stops being the right sentence.
st.up.shvetaketu_jaivali_five_questions.whole_arc_note: The son's anger is shown without rebuke, and the father's humility is the centre. Shvetaketu, by the Brihadaranyaka's telling, would not go back himself; the father went alone.

st.up.five_householders_ashvapati.title: A respected teacher says 'I cannot answer all of this' and takes everyone to someone better
st.up.five_householders_ashvapati.teaching: Knowing where your knowledge ends, and saying so, is itself learning.
st.up.five_householders_ashvapati.whole_arc_note: The king also first offers them wealth, and they decline: 'A man should speak of the thing he came for.'

st.up.first_being_afraid_alone.title: The first being looks around, sees no one, and is afraid
st.up.first_being_afraid_alone.teaching: Fear needs an 'other'; where you see no other, fear has nothing to stand on.
st.up.first_being_afraid_alone.whole_arc_note: Keep both lines. Fear is dissolved by seeing clearly; loneliness is treated as natural and is answered by relationship. Do not use the first line to tell a lonely person they should not want company.

st.up.balaki_ajatashatru.title: The proud teacher who runs out of answers and becomes the student
st.up.balaki_ajatashatru.teaching: Running out of answers is where learning starts, if you can say so.
st.up.balaki_ajatashatru.whole_arc_note: The king never mocks him and pays for the attempt. He does not make Balaki bow as a pupil; he takes his hand and walks with him.

st.up.maitreyi_what_would_i_do_with_weal.title: Maitreyi asks what she would do with wealth that cannot make her immortal
st.up.maitreyi_what_would_i_do_with_weal.teaching: Everything is loved for the sake of the Self; know that, and all is known.
st.up.maitreyi_what_would_i_do_with_weal.whole_arc_note: This is a woman choosing knowledge and being taught as an equal, and the tradition honours her as a brahmavadini. Katyayani's choice of the household is not belittled. Yajnavalkya's leaving belongs to his stage of life and is no licence to walk out on a family.

st.up.maitreyi_you_have_confused_me.title: Maitreyi tells her teacher, 'Right here you have confused me'
st.up.maitreyi_you_have_confused_me.teaching: The knower cannot be made an object of knowing; saying 'I do not understand' is how that became clear.
st.up.maitreyi_you_have_confused_me.whole_arc_note: Her objection improves the teaching; the text keeps it in both tellings. The line about 'no consciousness' must travel with his correction, or it sounds like annihilation, which Shankara explicitly denies.

st.up.janaka_contest_yajnavalkya_cows.title: Yajnavalkya has the thousand cows driven home before the debate begins
st.up.janaka_contest_yajnavalkya_cows.teaching: Confidence is the willingness to be examined on what you claim.
st.up.janaka_contest_yajnavalkya_cows.whole_arc_note: He backs the claim with a full day of answers. Without that, this is only swagger. The story also ends with Shakalya's death after pressing too far, so do not present the debate as harmless sport.

st.up.gargi_two_arrows.title: Gargi stands up twice before the greatest teacher of the age
st.up.gargi_two_arrows.teaching: The Imperishable is that on which even space is woven; it sees and is not seen.
st.up.gargi_two_arrows.whole_arc_note: Shankara reads the warning as about method (this deity is known through scripture, not by stacking inferences), not as silencing a woman. She returns, asks better, and judges the contest. Tell the whole of it.

st.up.janaka_steps_down_from_throne.title: King Janaka steps down from his seat and asks what will light his way
st.up.janaka_steps_down_from_throne.teaching: When every outer light has gone out, the Self is the light by which one sits, moves and works.
st.up.janaka_steps_down_from_throne.whole_arc_note: Janaka stays a king. His admission 'I do not know where I am going' comes from a man the world calls successful, and nothing in the story asks him to abandon his duties.

st.up.da_da_da.title: One syllable from the thunder, heard three ways
st.up.da_da_da.teaching: Damyata, datta, dayadhvam: restrain, give, be compassionate.
st.up.da_da_da.whole_arc_note: Shankara notes that gods and asuras here are kinds of people: those inclined to indulgence, to greed, to cruelty. So all three apply to humans.

st.up.bhrigu_sent_back.title: Bhrigu is sent back to look again, five times
st.up.bhrigu_sent_back.teaching: Tapas, steady inquiry, is itself Brahman; understanding deepens layer by layer: body, breath, mind, understanding, joy.
st.up.bhrigu_sent_back.whole_arc_note: The father never says 'wrong'. Each answer was true at its level and each was outgrown. Do not present the earlier answers as failures.

st.up.convocation_parting_words.title: The teacher's last words to a student going home
st.up.convocation_parting_words.teaching: Satyam vada, dharmam chara: speak truth, live rightly, and where unsure, do as the wise and gentle do.
st.up.convocation_parting_words.whole_arc_note: A teacher admits his own faults in his farewell and gives the student a method for cases the rules do not cover. Do not reduce it to a list of obedience rules.

st.up.kena_gods_and_yaksha.title: The gods take credit for a victory, and cannot burn a blade of grass
st.up.kena_gods_and_yaksha.teaching: The power by which you succeed is not of your own making.
st.up.kena_gods_and_yaksha.whole_arc_note: The gods' powers are real and remain theirs; the correction is to the claim of sole ownership. They are honoured afterwards, not shamed. Text not in the corpus (no Kena file): story from memory, no Sanskrit quoted.

st.up.prashna_wait_a_year.title: Six seekers arrive with their questions and are told to wait a year
st.up.prashna_wait_a_year.teaching: Some answers can only be heard by a mind that has been made ready.
st.up.prashna_wait_a_year.whole_arc_note: The wait is preparation, and it is shared by a teacher who is honest about his own limits. It is not a brush-off.

st.up.sukesha_refuses_to_bluff.title: Sukesha tells a prince, 'I do not know,' and the prince drives away in silence
st.up.sukesha_refuses_to_bluff.teaching: A person who speaks what is false withers from the root.
st.up.sukesha_refuses_to_bluff.whole_arc_note: He lost the patron and kept the question. The story does not pretend honesty was costless.

st.up.shaunaka_householder_asks.title: A great householder asks what one thing, once known, makes everything known
st.up.shaunaka_householder_asks.teaching: What is uncreated cannot be gained by more doing; it is known.
st.up.shaunaka_householder_asks.whole_arc_note: The lower knowledge and the rites are not thrown away; Shankara says they purify and prepare. The weariness (nirveda) is the mature result of having done them well. Do not present it as licence to drop one's duties.

st.up.two_birds.title: Two birds on one tree: one eats, one watches
st.up.two_birds.teaching: Beside the one in you who tastes pleasure and pain sits one who only witnesses; seeing that one ends grief.
st.up.two_birds.whole_arc_note: The tree and the fruits are real experience; the text does not say the eating bird imagines its pain. In Shankara's reading the two are the individual self and the Lord, and the release is in seeing, never in flying off somewhere else.

st.up.chariot.title: The chariot: who is holding the reins
st.up.chariot.teaching: The senses are good horses under a driver who is awake.
st.up.chariot.whole_arc_note: The horses are not to be killed or starved; they are what gets you there. The fault is in the unattended reins.

st.up.father_and_son_back_to_school.title: Shvetaketu says 'I do not know,' his father says 'neither do I,' and they go together
st.up.father_and_son_back_to_school.teaching: Not being proud is itself the qualification for knowledge.
st.up.father_and_son_back_to_school.whole_arc_note: The praise is for 'not going into pride'. The son's honest 'I do not know' made the father's possible.

st.up.pratardana_you_choose.title: Pratardana is offered any boon and says, 'You choose what is best for me'
st.up.pratardana_you_choose.teaching: The best thing a person can ask for is to know the self.
st.up.pratardana_you_choose.whole_arc_note: Indra's 'know me' is read by the tradition (Brahma Sutra 1.1.28-31, Shankara) as pointing to the inner self, Brahman, and not to the god's person.

st.up.fathers_last_handing_over.title: A father, about to die, hands himself over to his son
st.up.fathers_last_handing_over.teaching: What a parent was can be consciously received and carried on.
st.up.fathers_last_handing_over.whole_arc_note: This is a rite, mutual and formal. The son is given a way to carry the father forward, and the father a way to let go. It does not tell a grieving child to stop grieving.

st.up.brihadratha_frog_in_dry_well.title: King Brihadratha gives up his kingdom and still finds no peace
st.up.brihadratha_frog_in_dry_well.teaching: Even renouncing everything does not bring peace without knowledge; when stuck, ask for help plainly.
st.up.brihadratha_frog_in_dry_well.whole_arc_note: His catalogue of disgust with the body is the voice of a man in despair and is where the text starts. The teaching that follows moves him to the self; do not serve the lament alone as doctrine. Not for someone at risk: it voices 'what is the use of enjoying anything'.

st.up.shuka_at_janakas_gate.title: Shuka is kept waiting at the palace gate for seven days, then tempted for seven more
st.up.shuka_at_janakas_gate.teaching: Knowing something and resting in it are different; the second often needs a confirming voice.
st.up.shuka_at_janakas_gate.whole_arc_note: He was right all along and still needed to hear it from someone who lived it. That need is treated as legitimate. The test is of evenness under insult and under indulgence alike.

st.up.nidagha_after_the_pilgrimage.title: Nidagha returns from every holy place and feels nothing but weariness
st.up.nidagha_after_the_pilgrimage.teaching: Honest weariness with the passing is the beginning of inquiry; hold on to even one of the four gatekeepers.
st.up.nidagha_after_the_pilgrimage.whole_arc_note: The lament is close to depression in its words. The text answers it with a teacher's recognition and a path, never with 'yes, nothing matters'. Serve with the response. Mirrors Rama's lament in the Yoga Vasishtha.

st.gitas.janaka_asks_ashtavakra.title: A king asks a boy how to be free
st.gitas.janaka_asks_ashtavakra.source_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 1.1-4; the court scene and the bent body are from tradition (Mahabharata Vana Parva tells his birth and his debate with Bandi)
st.gitas.janaka_asks_ashtavakra.teaching: You are the witness of the body, not the body; rest there and be free now.
st.gitas.janaka_asks_ashtavakra.whole_arc_note: Only the dialogue is in the Gita. The laughter in court and the 'skin' retort are popular tradition and must be labelled so. The Mahabharata gives his bent body as his father's curse and his debate victory over Bandi; verify there before quoting details.

st.gitas.janaka_how_long_i_was_fooled.title: Janaka's astonishment: 'All this time I was fooled'
st.gitas.janaka_how_long_i_was_fooled.teaching: The self was never bound; bondage was a long mistake, and seeing it is delight.
st.gitas.janaka_how_long_i_was_fooled.whole_arc_note: This comes after a king's lifetime of duty and a teacher's direct instruction. It is the fruit and cannot be handed to a beginner as a technique. Janaka keeps ruling afterwards.

st.gitas.ashtavakra_tests_janaka.title: The teacher tests the king: 'You know the self. Why still chase wealth?'
st.gitas.ashtavakra_tests_janaka.teaching: Freedom is shown in non-attachment while acting, and it can stand being questioned.
st.gitas.ashtavakra_tests_janaka.whole_arc_note: This is a test between a teacher and a ripe student. The teacher's rebuke is safe only inside this scene. Janaka's reply is not permission for indulgence: the next chapters describe a person with no craving at all.

st.gitas.janaka_tired_of_doing.title: Janaka: first I tired of doing, then of talking, then of thinking
st.gitas.janaka_tired_of_doing.teaching: Peace comes when the compulsion to do, to say and to think has run itself out.
st.gitas.janaka_tired_of_doing.whole_arc_note: Spoken by a realised king who goes on governing. It describes ease after understanding. It must not be offered as approval of withdrawal to someone who is depressed or burnt out and cannot act.

st.gitas.avadhuta_why_do_you_weep.title: Dattatreya asks his own mind, 'Why do you weep, friend?'
st.gitas.avadhuta_why_do_you_weep.teaching: The self you are has no birth, age or death; the weeping belongs to a mistaken identity.
st.gitas.avadhuta_why_do_you_weep.whole_arc_note: This is a liberated sage's self-talk about fear of ageing and death. It is not said to another person in mourning and must never be used to tell a griever their tears are baseless.

st.gitas.swan_on_insults.title: The golden swan: 'When I am abused I say nothing'
st.gitas.swan_on_insults.teaching: Words are arrows; the one who does not shoot back keeps his peace and his merit.
st.gitas.swan_on_insults.whole_arc_note: The swan describes his own chosen practice from a position of freedom. It is not an instruction to someone being abused to stay and take it; Bhishma's own teaching elsewhere upholds resisting wrong. Serve to people working on their own reactivity, never to the wronged as a first word.

st.gitas.lakshmana_private_question.title: Lakshmana waits until they are alone, then asks Rama how to cross
st.gitas.lakshmana_private_question.source_ref: Ram Gita (Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 5), verses 1-8
st.gitas.lakshmana_private_question.teaching: Do your duty as an offering until the mind is pure; then know the self.
st.gitas.lakshmana_private_question.whole_arc_note: Rama's answer keeps action and knowledge in sequence (duty first, then inquiry). The rope-snake section is a non-dual teaching for a prepared devotee; do not offer it against real danger.

st.gitas.learned_seers_no_peace.title: Seers who mastered the scriptures admit, 'Still there is no peace in us'
st.gitas.learned_seers_no_peace.teaching: Mastery of texts does not by itself still the mind; knowing one's own nature does.
st.gitas.learned_seers_no_peace.whole_arc_note: A later sectarian gita; the frame echoes Narada before Sanatkumara. Use as a supporting story, not a lead.

st.yv.rama_stops_eating_after_pilgrimage.title: Young Rama comes home from his travels and loses interest in everything
st.yv.rama_stops_eating_after_pilgrimage.teaching: A season when nothing satisfies can be the mind asking a serious question, and deserves a serious hearing.
st.yv.rama_stops_eating_after_pilgrimage.whole_arc_note: The elders neither scold him nor medicate the mood away; they ask and listen, and what follows is a long teaching that ends with Rama taking up his duties. The text reads this as awakening, but a modern reader with these signs may also be depressed and should be pointed to real help as well.

st.yv.rama_speaks_what_is_the_point.title: Rama tells the court: 'People are born to die and die to be born. What is this happiness?'
st.yv.rama_speaks_what_is_the_point.teaching: The honest question 'what is the point?' is the first qualification for wisdom.
st.yv.rama_speaks_what_is_the_point.whole_arc_note: His speech must travel with its ending: he asks to be taught how to live, and the whole work ends with him acting in the world. His threat to stop eating is the low point of a mind in pain, which the text answers. Mark for risk screening.

st.yv.dasharatha_cannot_let_rama_go.title: Dasharatha: 'He is not yet sixteen. Take me instead'
st.yv.dasharatha_cannot_let_rama_go.teaching: Love wants to keep the child from every risk; dharma and trust sometimes ask it to let him go.
st.yv.dasharatha_cannot_let_rama_go.whole_arc_note: The father's fear is given full voice and is not mocked. He lets go on the strength of trusted counsel, not of being shamed.

st.yv.arishtanemi_asks_about_heaven.title: Offered heaven, King Arishtanemi asks what is wrong with it
st.yv.arishtanemi_asks_about_heaven.teaching: A prize that sets you comparing and then runs out is worth asking about before you accept it.
st.yv.arishtanemi_asks_about_heaven.whole_arc_note: He does not despise the offer; he does due diligence on it. The frame also holds that knowledge and action together are the way, like a bird's two wings.

st.yv.karunya_stops_acting.title: Karunya finishes his studies and cannot see why he should do anything
st.yv.karunya_stops_acting.teaching: Knowledge and action are two wings; neither alone carries you.
st.yv.karunya_stops_acting.whole_arc_note: His paralysis comes from a real intellectual conflict and is treated as such. The resolution is 'both', never 'stop thinking and get on with it'.

st.yv.vasishtha_effort_over_fate.title: Vasishtha's first lesson to a despairing prince: fate is your own past effort
st.yv.vasishtha_effort_over_fate.teaching: There is no fate apart from the fruit of your own action; present effort can overcome the past.
st.yv.vasishtha_effort_over_fate.whole_arc_note: This is said to a capable prince sunk in fatalism. It defines right effort as guided by scripture, teacher and good conduct. It must not be turned into blaming people for illness, poverty or what others did to them.

st.yv.lila_fears_losing_her_husband.title: Queen Lila asks how to keep her husband from dying
st.yv.lila_fears_losing_her_husband.source_ref: Yoga Vasishtha, Utpatti Prakarana, sargas 15-19 (story runs to sarga 59)
st.yv.lila_fears_losing_her_husband.teaching: No practice buys exemption from death; fear of loss ends by knowing what one is.
st.yv.lila_fears_losing_her_husband.whole_arc_note: The learned men's honest 'no' is part of the story and should be kept. The long middle is a non-dual teaching through visions. World-as-mind teaching: for reflection in calm times only. Never serve to someone facing a real threat, a fresh loss or abuse; there it reads as 'your pain is not real'.

st.yv.karkati_needle.title: Karkati gets exactly the boon she asked for and it makes her smaller
st.yv.karkati_needle.teaching: A wish born of hunger shrinks the one who gets it; satisfaction comes when the hunger itself is seen through.
st.yv.karkati_needle.whole_arc_note: The arc is desire, getting it, regret, and a second effort without appetite. The later compromise about what she may eat is the text's own; do not embroider it.

st.yv.man_who_beats_himself.title: The man in the great forest who beats himself and runs
st.yv.man_who_beats_himself.teaching: The mind strikes itself with its own imaginings and then flees the pain; inquiry, a steady look, ends it.
st.yv.man_who_beats_himself.whole_arc_note: The explanation is the text's own allegory of mind. Keep the fact that not everyone he stopped was helped.

st.yv.three_princes_who_never_were.title: The nurse's tale of three princes, two unborn and one never conceived
st.yv.three_princes_who_never_were.teaching: Much of what the mind treats as solid is a story told on a story.
st.yv.three_princes_who_never_were.whole_arc_note: A deliberately absurd nursery tale to loosen the grip of taking every thought-built scenario as fact. World-as-mind teaching: for reflection in calm times only. Never serve to someone facing a real threat, a fresh loss or abuse; there it reads as 'your pain is not real'.

st.yv.lavana_lifetime_in_an_hour.title: King Lavana lives a whole life of poverty and loss in a few moments on his throne
st.yv.lavana_lifetime_in_an_hour.teaching: The mind can make a lifetime in a moment, and a moment of a lifetime.
st.yv.lavana_lifetime_in_an_hour.whole_arc_note: The original frames the forest family as chandala, an outcaste life presented as a fall. Do not retell that framing as degradation; tell it as a life of poverty, love and loss. Caste-sensitive: review before any public use. World-as-mind teaching: for reflection in calm times only. Never serve to someone facing a real threat, a fresh loss or abuse; there it reads as 'your pain is not real'.

st.yv.shukra_follows_a_daydream.title: Shukra sits beside his meditating father and follows one glance for lifetimes
st.yv.shukra_follows_a_daydream.teaching: Mana eva manushyanam: the mind is the person; you go where your attention lives.
st.yv.shukra_follows_a_daydream.whole_arc_note: The father's rage at Death is shown and corrected without shaming him. The teaching is about where attention goes, not a condemnation of desire as such. World-as-mind teaching: for reflection in calm times only. Never serve to someone facing a real threat, a fresh loss or abuse; there it reads as 'your pain is not real'.

st.yv.dama_vyala_kata.title: Three warriors who could not lose, until they learned to say 'I'
st.yv.dama_vyala_kata.teaching: Fear enters with 'I' and 'mine'; action free of self-concern is unshaken.
st.yv.dama_vyala_kata.whole_arc_note: Vasishtha's instruction is explicit: do not be like Dama, Vyala and Kata; be like Bhima, Bhasa and Dridha. The story is about self-concern breeding fear, and does not praise mindlessness.

st.up.raikva_janashruti.title: A generous king overhears two swans say a man under a cart outshines him
st.up.raikva_janashruti.teaching: Whatever good people do flows to the one who knows what he knows, as lesser throws of the dice are won by the highest throw.
st.up.raikva_janashruti.whole_arc_note: Raikva twice calls the king 'shudra'. Shankara reads the word as one who was 'pierced by grief' (shuch) on hearing the swans, and not as a statement of caste. The second offer includes the king's daughter as a bride; this is in the text and is flagged gender_sensitive. Retellings should not hide it and should not dwell on it as a transaction. The point of the story is a giver learning that reputation and wisdom are different things, and returning humbly after being refused.

st.up.artabhaga_take_my_hand.title: 'Take my hand. This is not a question for a crowd'
st.up.artabhaga_take_my_hand.teaching: When the body returns to the elements, what a person did goes on; one becomes good through good action.
st.up.artabhaga_take_my_hand.whole_arc_note: Keep both parts: the tenderness of taking him aside, and the content, that what carries on is karma. Shankara reads the private talk as being about karma as the cause of further births, not a final word on the self. Do not turn it into 'nothing remains'; the Upanishad goes on to teach the self that does not die.

st.up.family_around_the_dying.title: 'Do you know me? Do you know me?' The family around a dying man
st.up.family_around_the_dying.protagonist: the relatives of the dying man
st.up.family_around_the_dying.teaching: When a dying person no longer knows us, he is returning into the one being that is also our own self.
st.up.family_around_the_dying.whole_arc_note: This is the tenth of Uddalaka's nine-fold refrain 'tat tvam asi'. Shankara reads the merging as a return into sat, the real. It is a consolation about what the dying man is, offered to the living. Do not use it to tell a caregiver that their loved one's confusion does not matter, and do not serve it in the first raw days of a loss without a gentler plan around it.

st.up.accused_holds_the_hot_axe.title: A man is dragged in, accused of theft, and handed a red-hot axe
st.up.accused_holds_the_hot_axe.teaching: The one who is joined to the truth is not burned; the one who hides in a lie is.
st.up.accused_holds_the_hot_axe.whole_arc_note: The ordeal is an ancient legal practice and is told as an image; it must never be read as advice to submit to any test or to accept punishment to prove innocence. Shankara reads it as the difference between one who identifies with the real (sat) and one who identifies with the unreal: the first is not bound. For a person who is wrongly accused, the use is the inner footing, being covered by truth, alongside every practical step to clear one's name.

st.up.dogs_chant_for_food.title: The dogs who chanted 'Om, let us eat'
st.up.dogs_chant_for_food.teaching: Chanting the highest words with only the stomach in mind turns worship into a request for food.
st.up.dogs_chant_for_food.whole_arc_note: Read by many as a satire on priests who chant only for fees and food; Shankara instead takes the dogs as deities or sages in disguise who were pleased with the student's study and came to teach him. Both readings are in the tradition; commentary confidence for either is medium. Do not use it to mock anyone's simple prayers for their needs; the Upanishad itself treats food as sacred.

st.up.shvetashvatara_who_governs_us.title: A circle of seekers asks: who runs our lives, in joy and in pain?
st.up.shvetashvatara_who_governs_us.teaching: Time, nature, chance and fate each explain a little; the seers found by meditation the one power that governs them all.
st.up.shvetashvatara_who_governs_us.whole_arc_note: The arc is inquiry first, then meditation, then devotion. Do not skip the honest testing of every explanation; it is what makes the turn to refuge earned. The text says the individual is not master of his pleasure and pain, which is not a call to stop acting.

st.gitas.gods_grow_comfortable.title: The gods grow comfortable, lose ground piece by piece, and are afraid
st.gitas.gods_grow_comfortable.teaching: Comfort that wears away discipline makes one both careless and afraid; putting fear aside and returning to effort turns it.
st.gitas.gods_grow_comfortable.whole_arc_note: The text is clear that the loss came from their own slackening through indulgence, and the recovery from their own renewed effort, before grace appears. Do not tell it as luck or as rescue alone.

st.gitas.ashtavakra_laughed_at_in_court.title: A boy bent in eight places walks into the king's court, and the court laughs
st.gitas.ashtavakra_laughed_at_in_court.source_ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva 132-134 (the court debate); the court's laughter and Ashtavakra's reply are popular retelling
st.gitas.ashtavakra_laughed_at_in_court.teaching: A person is to be measured by what they know and are, not by age or body.
st.gitas.ashtavakra_laughed_at_in_court.whole_arc_note: Mark clearly: the debate and the gatekeeper are in the Mahabharata (Vana Parva, Tirtha-yatra section, from memory, not in our corpus). The laughter scene and the 'judge by skin' line are a widely told retelling, not epic text. Do not present them as scripture. The bent body came from his father's curse while he was in the womb, for correcting his father's recitation; if that is told, tell it whole.

st.yv.punya_consoles_pavana.title: Two brothers lose their parents; one does the rites, the other cannot stop weeping
st.yv.punya_consoles_pavana.teaching: Grief clings to roles; seeing the self beyond 'mother', 'father' and 'son' brings peace.
st.yv.punya_consoles_pavana.whole_arc_note: Two things must stay together: Punya first does the rites and then goes to find his brother; the teaching comes from someone who shares the loss. Punya's lines ('neither is she your mother nor he your father') are Advaitic and can wound a fresh griever if quoted alone. Uses the Yoga Vasishtha's teaching that relations and the world are appearances in consciousness. Not for someone facing a real threat or a fresh loss, where 'it is not real' wounds; serve only to a person who has asked the deeper question. Default not_for includes griever even though grief is its subject: release it to a griever only in a week-3 (self) plan after the person has asked where the dead have gone, and only after human review.

st.yv.bali_same_days.title: King Bali has everything and is sick of doing the same things every day
st.yv.bali_same_days.teaching: The repetition that wearies us lives in the mind; mastering the mind is the one act that does not need repeating.
st.yv.bali_same_days.whole_arc_note: Bali does not abdicate. His weariness becomes inquiry, and the inquiry becomes inner freedom inside his life. Do not use this to tell a bored person to quit their life; the turn is from repetition to the mind that experiences it.

st.yv.prahlada_refuge_in_victor.title: Prahlada, defeated and alone, takes refuge in the god who defeated his family
st.yv.prahlada_refuge_in_victor.teaching: When there is no way out, wholehearted refuge in the highest is itself the way.
st.yv.prahlada_refuge_in_victor.whole_arc_note: This is the Yoga Vasishtha's version, which differs from the Bhagavata's (where Prahlada is devoted from childhood). Here the devotion begins in defeat and grief. Do not make it a story of giving in to an oppressor: Vishnu in the tradition is the just order, and the turn is towards truth, not towards whoever has power over you.

st.yv.prahlada_woken_to_rule.title: Prahlada disappears into meditation for ages, and his kingdom falls into chaos
st.yv.prahlada_woken_to_rule.teaching: Inner freedom is meant to return to its duty; a liberated person can carry responsibility without being bound by it.
st.yv.prahlada_woken_to_rule.whole_arc_note: The arc ends on the throne, not in the cave. The text counts the anarchy as the cost of his absence. It is a corrective to any reading of the Yoga Vasishtha as a call to withdraw.

st.yv.uddalaka_restless_meditation.title: Young Uddalaka sits down to meditate and his mind will not stay
st.yv.uddalaka_restless_meditation.teaching: A restless mind is not overcome by force but by patient return and clear inquiry into what one is.
st.yv.uddalaka_restless_meditation.whole_arc_note: The text spends a long time on the failures before the success. Keep the repetition and the change of approach (from willing the mind still to inquiring into it); do not compress it into 'he meditated and found peace'.

st.yv.vitahavya_argues_with_his_mind.title: Vitahavya closes his eyes in a cave and finds his mind still talking
st.yv.vitahavya_argues_with_his_mind.teaching: The mind runs because it borrows life from awareness; seeing that, one stops obeying it.
st.yv.vitahavya_argues_with_his_mind.whole_arc_note: The long burial of his body in mud during samadhi is part of the later story and is not a practice to imitate. The usable core is the self-talk: a calm, reasoning dialogue with one's own mind.

st.yv.suraghu_punish_or_pardon.title: King Suraghu cannot bear to punish, and cannot afford not to
st.yv.suraghu_punish_or_pardon.teaching: A ruler who must cause pain can act justly without being torn, by seeing that pain and pleasure arise in the mind and resting in the self.
st.yv.suraghu_punish_or_pardon.whole_arc_note: He keeps his duty, including punishment. The teaching is about the inner state of the one who must decide, not a licence for harshness or a call to resign. Keep both halves of the dilemma he states.

st.yv.bhasa_vilasa_old_friends.title: Two childhood friends meet in old age and admit they never found peace
st.yv.bhasa_vilasa_old_friends.teaching: Years of effort without discernment wear out the body without bringing peace; only knowing the self brings rest.
st.yv.bhasa_vilasa_old_friends.whole_arc_note: This is a tender story of friendship as well as of wasted effort. Keep the warmth of their meeting; the regret is shared, not one judging the other.

st.yv.janaka_overhears_the_siddhas.title: King Janaka overhears a song in his garden, climbs to his roof alone, and questions everything
st.yv.janaka_overhears_the_siddhas.teaching: A single honest moment of inquiry can free a person, who then returns to his duties without being bound by them.
st.yv.janaka_overhears_the_siddhas.whole_arc_note: He goes back to his duties the same day. The story is the classic case for knowledge inside action. Do not stop the telling at the roof.

st.yv.bhagiratha_begs_in_his_old_city.title: Bhagiratha gives away everything and goes begging in the city he once ruled
st.yv.bhagiratha_begs_in_his_old_city.teaching: Freedom is tested by standing without shame where one once stood in honour; the free person can rule or beg with the same mind.
st.yv.bhagiratha_begs_in_his_old_city.whole_arc_note: The arc ends with him ruling again and doing the greatest work of his life. Giving everything away is his teacher's specific prescription for him and is not offered as a general rule. Do not use this to tell anyone to quit a job or give away their savings.

st.yv.chudala_laughed_at_by_husband.title: Queen Chudala finds peace, and her husband laughs at her
st.yv.chudala_laughed_at_by_husband.teaching: The truth one has found does not depend on being believed; it can wait, and keep loving.
st.yv.chudala_laughed_at_by_husband.whole_arc_note: The text sides with Chudala; his laughter is shown as his blindness. Flag gender_sensitive because the dismissal is gendered and must be told as the husband's error, never as a joke. The story continues in st.yv.shikhidhvaja_burns_everything; this first part should not end on her silence as if silence were the lesson.

st.yv.shikhidhvaja_burns_everything.title: King Shikhidhvaja leaves his kingdom, burns his last possessions, and is still not free
st.yv.shikhidhvaja_burns_everything.teaching: Renouncing things, places or even the body is not renunciation; letting go of the mind that claims them is.
st.yv.shikhidhvaja_burns_everything.whole_arc_note: SELF-HARM THEME: he moves to end his life and is stopped with the words that the body is innocent and its destruction is no renunciation. Never serve this story to a reading with any risk signal. The arc ends with return to ordinary life and rule; it is a refutation of escape, not an endorsement of it. Kumbha's test with Madanika is a later episode and can be omitted from short tellings without changing the meaning.

st.yv.kacha_eight_years_no_peace.title: Kacha leaves home on his father's word, and after eight years asks why he is still not at peace
st.yv.kacha_eight_years_no_peace.teaching: The 'everything' that must be renounced is the mind itself, which holds all things.
st.yv.kacha_eight_years_no_peace.whole_arc_note: This mirrors Shikhidhvaja's story and should not be told as a recommendation to leave home. The father's grief at his son's leaving is in the text and should stay in. The literal reading (strip yourself of possessions) is shown to fail twice before the real meaning lands.

st.yv.bhushunda_the_old_crow.title: Vasishtha asks the oldest crow in the world how he has outlived every age
st.yv.bhushunda_the_old_crow.teaching: Death and fear find little hold on the one who watches the breath and is not burned by worries about past and future.
st.yv.bhushunda_the_old_crow.whole_arc_note: The breath practice described is detailed and meant to be learned from a teacher; use the story for the attitude (present attention, freedom from brooding) rather than as a breathing instruction. The longevity is the story's image, not a promise.

st.bh.fruit_passed_hand_to_hand.title: The fruit of immortality that came back to the king
st.bh.fruit_passed_hand_to_hand.source_ref: Legend, not text: frame-story of the Vikrama-charita (Simhasana-dvatrimshika, unit II; Edgerton 1926); the verse the king speaks is Niti Shataka 2 (popular numbering)
st.bh.fruit_passed_hand_to_hand.teaching: Attachment runs in a chain where each chases someone who chases another; seeing the chain, including oneself in it, frees.
st.bh.fruit_passed_hand_to_hand.whole_arc_note: LEGEND, NOT TEXT. Mark it as tradition every time. The source framing contains generalisations against women; leave them all out (rule: content that demeans women stays out) and never single out the queen as the villain or describe any punishment of her (a variant has her executed; do not use). Keep the focus on the king's attachment and his own 'and on me'. Scholars doubt that the poet was a king (Wortham, Kosambi).

st.bh.forced_laughter_before_fools.title: 'I swallowed my tears and laughed with an empty heart'
st.bh.forced_laughter_before_fools.teaching: It is our own hope of gain that makes us flatter and smile on cue; seeing that is the start of dignity.
st.bh.forced_laughter_before_fools.whole_arc_note: The verse is a confession, not advice to quit a job. Its force is in naming who held the strings. Pair with a verse on self-respect (Niti 31) or contentment, never with a verse that blames the reader.

st.bh.wrinkles_but_craving_young.title: Grey hair, wrinkled face, weak limbs, and craving alone stays young
st.bh.wrinkles_but_craving_young.teaching: We think we consume pleasures, but they consume us; time does not pass, we do, and craving never ages.
st.bh.wrinkles_but_craving_young.whole_arc_note: Never use this to mock ageing or the body. Its point is the mismatch between an ageing life and an unaged wanting. Light enough for a reel, deep enough for week 2.

st.bh.proud_man_asks_for_his_children.title: A proud man stammers a request, only because his children are hungry
st.bh.proud_man_asks_for_his_children.teaching: A self-respecting person will not beg for himself, but will swallow his pride for those who depend on him.
st.bh.proud_man_asks_for_his_children.whole_arc_note: Bhartrihari's section condemns begging for one's own wants, and this verse marks the exception: asking for those who depend on you. Do not use it to shame anyone who asks for help; the verse honours the man who asks.

st.bh.three_kinds_of_people.title: Those who never start, those who quit at the first wall, and those who keep going
st.bh.three_kinds_of_people.teaching: The lowly do not start for fear of obstacles; the middling stop when obstacles come; the best never give up what they have begun.
st.bh.three_kinds_of_people.whole_arc_note: Wortham reads it of the pursuit of wisdom; it is usually applied to any worthy undertaking. Do not use it to shame someone who stopped for good reason (illness, harm); it is about stopping out of fear.

st.bh.ascetic_and_king.title: An ascetic in bark faces a king in silk: who is the poor one?
st.bh.ascetic_and_king.teaching: The poor one is whoever has vast craving; where the mind is content, rich and poor are the same.
st.bh.ascetic_and_king.whole_arc_note: Some verses in this section praise living on alms and are monastic in tone; the usable centre is verse 53 on contentment. Do not use it to tell a person in real poverty that their need is only in the mind.

st.bh.house_of_many_then_one.title: The house where there were many, and now there is one
st.bh.house_of_many_then_one.teaching: Time empties houses one by one; those who bore us and those we grew with become memories, and we are next.
st.bh.house_of_many_then_one.whole_arc_note: These are elegy verses. They name loss and do not prescribe; never follow them in a plan with a verse that tells a griever to stop grieving. Good as a see_name day for empty nest, ageing parents, or a family home sold.

st.bh.dog_and_elephant.title: The dog rolls over for the hand that feeds it; the elephant waits to be coaxed
st.bh.dog_and_elephant.teaching: The small-minded grovel for scraps; the great receive with steadiness and self-respect.
st.bh.dog_and_elephant.whole_arc_note: The library notes some verses in this section lean towards intolerance of insult (a warrior-king ideal). Use these two for self-respect, not for pride or for contempt of people who must ask for work or help.

st.viv.monkeys_of_varanasi.title: Chased by monkeys in Varanasi, he hears a stranger shout 'Face the brutes'
st.viv.monkeys_of_varanasi.source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'What Is Religion?', Complete Works vol. 1 (his own account)
st.viv.monkeys_of_varanasi.teaching: The troubles we flee from chase us; when we turn and face them, they fall back.
st.viv.monkeys_of_varanasi.whole_arc_note: Documented in his own words in a lecture. The common retelling names the stranger as an old sannyasi; the CW text says only 'a stranger'. Do not use it for a situation of real physical danger or abuse, where safety comes first and 'face it' could harm; it speaks to fears and troubles one has been running from.

st.viv.frog_in_the_well.title: The frog in the well meets a frog from the sea
st.viv.frog_in_the_well.source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'Why We Disagree', Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 15 September 1893, Complete Works vol. 1
st.viv.frog_in_the_well.teaching: Each of us sits in a small well and calls it the whole world; the wider truth seems a lie from inside the well.
st.viv.frog_in_the_well.whole_arc_note: He told it to explain why religions quarrel, and included the Hindu in the well too. Use it against narrowness of any kind, never to mock a particular faith or person.

st.viv.lion_among_sheep.title: A lion cub raised by sheep, who bleats and runs
st.viv.lion_among_sheep.source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'The Real Nature of Man', Complete Works vol. 2 (also vols 1, 3, 7)
st.viv.lion_among_sheep.teaching: We are not weak or sinful by nature; we have forgotten what we are, and one clear look can show it.
st.viv.lion_among_sheep.whole_arc_note: He uses it for the Vedantic claim that weakness is a mistaken identity, not a sin. Use it for self-worth and the self level; do not use it to tell a struggling person they are simply choosing to be weak.

st.viv.have_you_seen_god.title: A young man asks every preacher in Calcutta, 'Have you seen God?'
st.viv.have_you_seen_god.source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'The Vedanta in All Its Phases' (Calcutta, 1897), Complete Works vol. 3 (his own account)
st.viv.have_you_seen_god.teaching: Religion is realisation; ask for the one who has seen, and keep asking until you find them.
st.viv.have_you_seen_god.whole_arc_note: Documented in his own words. Popular retellings add Ramakrishna's further words ('as I see you, only more intensely'); those are from the Gospel and biographies, not this lecture, and should be marked if used. His honest doubt was the qualification, not an obstacle.

st.viv.family_starving_or_the_mission.title: His father dies, the family is starving, and he is torn between them and his calling
st.viv.family_starving_or_the_mission.source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'My Life and Mission' (Pasadena, 1900), Complete Works vol. 8 (his own account)
st.viv.family_starving_or_the_mission.teaching: Great work is rarely done without a terrible inner struggle between love for one's own and the call one believes in.
st.viv.family_starving_or_the_mission.whole_arc_note: Told in his own words, with its harshest line ('What if a mother or two brothers die? It is a sacrifice'). Do not quote that line as advice; it is a man describing his own agony. NOT for anyone being pushed to abandon dependents, a caregiver, or a parent of young children. Use it to honour how hard a calling against family duty is, not to settle such a choice for anyone.

st.viv.letter_to_mary_on_grief.title: 'I was not good enough to that person': a letter to a grieving friend
st.viv.letter_to_mary_on_grief.source_ref: Letter to Mary Hale, Pasadena, 20 February 1900, Complete Works vol. 8
st.viv.letter_to_mary_on_grief.teaching: The feeling that we were not good enough to the one we lost is itself a form of sorrow, not a verdict.
st.viv.letter_to_mary_on_grief.whole_arc_note: Documented letter. Its gift is that a great teacher admits his own regret about his father. Safe for griever plans; does not tell anyone to stop grieving.

st.viv.ascetic_housewife_butcher.title: A proud young ascetic is taught by a housewife and a butcher
st.viv.ascetic_housewife_butcher.source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'What Is Duty?' (Karma-Yoga ch. 4), Complete Works vol. 1; retelling of the Vyadha Gita, Mahabharata, Vana Parva
st.viv.ascetic_housewife_butcher.teaching: Doing the duty in front of you, wholeheartedly and without attachment, leads higher than any special power.
st.viv.ascetic_housewife_butcher.whole_arc_note: The source has a translator's footnote describing the Vyadha's caste in demeaning terms; leave it out. The point of the story is that the hierarchy of station is overturned. The woman is the first teacher and is illumined; do not reduce her to a model of wifely service. Flag gender_sensitive for that reason.

st.viv.ghost_that_must_be_kept_busy.title: A man gets a ghost that must be kept busy, or it will eat him
st.viv.ghost_that_must_be_kept_busy.source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'We Help Ourselves, Not the World' (Karma-Yoga ch. 5), Complete Works vol. 1
st.viv.ghost_that_must_be_kept_busy.teaching: The world, like a curly tail, will not be made straight for good; work for it anyway, and do not let the restless mind devour you.
st.viv.ghost_that_must_be_kept_busy.whole_arc_note: Told with humour. Its point, in context, is that we help ourselves by doing good, the world will not be finally fixed, and a restless mind that must always be fed is a danger. Do not use it to say that effort to improve things is pointless; the chapter urges work, without fanaticism.

st.viv.chicago_no_speech_prepared.title: Seven thousand people, every speaker prepared, and he has nothing written
st.viv.chicago_no_speech_prepared.source_ref: Letter to Alasinga Perumal, Chicago, 2 November 1893, Complete Works vol. 5 (his own account)
st.viv.chicago_no_speech_prepared.teaching: One can be unprepared and terrified and still step up, after a moment of surrender.
st.viv.chicago_no_speech_prepared.whole_arc_note: Documented in his own letter, which is honest about nerves and about having been 'out of pocket' just before. Keep the fear in; the story is about walking up while afraid, not about being naturally fearless.

st.viv.sage_who_would_not_teach.title: A sage who would not answer questions, and then said: 'Let the end and the means be joined'
st.viv.sage_who_would_not_teach.source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'What Is Duty?' (Karma-Yoga ch. 4), Complete Works vol. 1; the sage is identified in the tradition as Pavhari Baba (from memory, not stated here)
st.viv.sage_who_would_not_teach.teaching: When the means and the end become one, work done wholly in the present becomes worship and frees us from worry over results.
st.viv.sage_who_would_not_teach.whole_arc_note: The identification with Pavhari Baba comes from Vivekananda's other writings and biographies, not this passage; mark it. Do not present the waiting as a technique to extract answers; it is respect for a teacher's way.

st.viv.slandered_by_an_old_friend.title: An old friend from home tells America he is a fraud
st.viv.slandered_by_an_old_friend.source_ref: Letters to Alasinga Perumal (1894) and to Professor J. H. Wright (1894), Complete Works vols 5 and 7 (his own words)
st.viv.slandered_by_an_old_friend.teaching: When someone you trusted slanders you out of jealousy, you can name the hurt, refuse to hate, and let the work answer.
st.viv.slandered_by_an_old_friend.whole_arc_note: Keep the hurt in: he calls it a terrible shock and is not serene at first. His refusal to defend himself is tied to his monastic vow; do not present it as what every wronged person should do. A wronged user may need to defend their name; this story shows how to keep the heart free of hatred while the facts are handled.

st.viv.boy_gopala_and_his_mother.title: A poor widow's small son is afraid to walk home through the woods
st.viv.boy_gopala_and_his_mother.source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'The Story of the Boy Gopala', Complete Works vol. 6 (a devotional tale he retold)
st.viv.boy_gopala_and_his_mother.teaching: A parent's faith, passed to a child, makes the child unafraid; love and faith, more than learning, bring the Lord near.
st.viv.boy_gopala_and_his_mother.whole_arc_note: This is a devotional tale Vivekananda retold, not history; say so. The text describes the widow as waiting for death to rejoin her husband; that line should not be presented as an ideal for widows. The miracle answers the faith of mother and child; do not use it to promise that a frightened parent's child will be magically protected. Use it for a parent's loneliness and the trust she passes on.

st.vr.valmiki_grief_becomes_verse.title: A bird is shot, and Valmiki's grief finds a form
st.vr.valmiki_grief_becomes_verse.teaching: Grief that is given a form can be carried, and can carry others.
st.vr.valmiki_grief_becomes_verse.whole_arc_note: Keep both halves. He does not rise above the grief, and he does not only vent it. The curse on the hunter is part of the text; the poem grows from the compassion under the anger, and a writer should not present the curse itself as the model.

st.vr.valmiki_asks_is_there_such_a_perso.title: Valmiki asks: is there anyone like this alive today?
st.vr.valmiki_asks_is_there_such_a_perso.teaching: It is a sound instinct to look for a life to learn from, and to ask someone who has seen more than you.
st.vr.valmiki_asks_is_there_such_a_perso.whole_arc_note: The list is about character under pressure (truthful, grateful, master of anger, free of envy), and Narada admits such a person is hard to find. Do not turn it into a claim that goodness is common or easy.

st.vr.dasharatha_lets_ram_go_with_vishva.title: A father is asked to send his teenage son into danger
st.vr.dasharatha_lets_ram_go_with_vishva.source_ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, sargas 19 to 22
st.vr.dasharatha_lets_ram_go_with_vishva.teaching: Holding a child back out of love can cost the child the very thing that would make him strong.
st.vr.dasharatha_lets_ram_go_with_vishva.whole_arc_note: The fear is honoured, not mocked: the text gives the father's pleading in full. He is not told that love is weakness. He is given a reason to trust the hands he is placing his son in. Do not clip it to 'let your children go'.

st.vr.vishvamitra_envies_the_sage_cow.title: A king meets a strength his power cannot buy
st.vr.vishvamitra_envies_the_sage_cow.source_ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, sargas 52 to 56
st.vr.vishvamitra_envies_the_sage_cow.teaching: When what you have cannot get you what another person has, the honest step is to see what they actually built and begin building it.
st.vr.vishvamitra_envies_the_sage_cow.whole_arc_note: He begins from envy and humiliation, not from noble motives, and the text does not hide that he destroyed a hermitage on the way. The change takes thousands of years and several failures (Menaka, Rambha). Do not present the turn as instant or the envy as harmless.

st.vr.vishvamitra_menaka_ten_years.title: Ten years gone like a day: Vishvamitra after Menaka
st.vr.vishvamitra_menaka_ten_years.teaching: A long lapse does not cancel the aim; you count the loss honestly, blame no one, and start again.
st.vr.vishvamitra_menaka_ten_years.whole_arc_note: Two things must stay: the regret is real and painful, and he sends Menaka away with kind words. The lapse is his and he owns it. A telling that makes her the villain, or that treats the ten years as worthless sin, clips the text.

st.vr.vishvamitra_anger_begins_again.title: He beat desire and lost to anger, and began once more
st.vr.vishvamitra_anger_begins_again.source_ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, sargas 64 and 65
st.vr.vishvamitra_anger_begins_again.teaching: Mastery over one weakness does not cover the next; each one has to be met, and each fall can be the start of the next attempt.
st.vr.vishvamitra_anger_begins_again.whole_arc_note: Rambha is wronged here: she came under orders and in fear, and the curse on her stands. The text treats the curse as his failure, not his right. Also keep the ending: the rival's acknowledgement and friendship close a quarrel that began with envy.

st.vr.bhagiratha_finishes_what_three_gen.title: Bhagiratha finishes what three generations could not
st.vr.bhagiratha_finishes_what_three_gen.source_ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, sargas 42 to 44
st.vr.bhagiratha_finishes_what_three_gen.teaching: Long work is finished by the one who treats each new obstacle as the next step of the same work.
st.vr.bhagiratha_finishes_what_three_gen.whole_arc_note: Do not flatten it into 'never give up'. The text shows a task that is real, inherited, and for others; and it shows solved problems opening onto new ones. Three good men failed before him without blame.

st.vr.shunahshepa_the_middle_son.title: Shunahshepa, the son neither parent chose to keep
st.vr.shunahshepa_the_middle_son.source_ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, sargas 61 and 62
st.vr.shunahshepa_the_middle_son.teaching: When those who should protect you do not, you may seek refuge elsewhere and ask plainly for what you need.
st.vr.shunahshepa_the_middle_son.whole_arc_note: The parents' favouritism is stated as a fact and is not excused. Vishvamitra's own sons refuse to help and he curses them in anger, which the text records. Keep the boy's clear-eyed speech; do not turn this into praise of sacrifice or obedience.

st.vr.trishanku_refused_by_everyone.title: Trishanku is refused, cast out, and taken in by one man
st.vr.trishanku_refused_by_everyone.source_ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, sargas 57 to 60
st.vr.trishanku_refused_by_everyone.teaching: A person who has been turned away by all and comes for refuge is to be received first and judged later.
st.vr.trishanku_refused_by_everyone.whole_arc_note: The tradition does not treat Trishanku's wish as wise; his teacher's refusal was sound, and the result is partial. The usable thread is how a person shamed by every gatekeeper is received by one man with compassion. Do not sell this as 'you can have anything if you find the right backer'.

st.vr.ahalya_unseen_years_and_return.title: Ahalya: years unseen, then received with honour
st.vr.ahalya_unseen_years_and_return.source_ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, sargas 48 and 49
st.vr.ahalya_unseen_years_and_return.teaching: A person is larger than their worst act, and the honour they are shown can be the last step of their return.
st.vr.ahalya_unseen_years_and_return.whole_arc_note: Stay with Valmiki: she is not turned to stone here, and she is not blameless or tricked. Indra is punished as well. The point the tradition draws is that a wrong, honestly lived through, does not fix a person's worth for ever, and that the first act toward her is a bow. Never use this to police women, and do not suggest years of isolation as a prescription.

st.vr.parashurama_challenges_ram.title: An angry elder challenges Ram on the road home
st.vr.parashurama_challenges_ram.source_ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, sargas 74 to 76
st.vr.parashurama_challenges_ram.teaching: Meet a challenge to your worth with what you can do, and leave the challenger his dignity.
st.vr.parashurama_challenges_ram.whole_arc_note: Both men carry the teaching. The younger is firm without contempt. The elder, once shown, lets go of his standing without bitterness. Do not cut the elder's grace to make this a story of a young man putting an old one in his place.

st.vr.ram_sita_love_grows.title: How Ram and Sita's love grew in the quiet years
st.vr.ram_sita_love_grows.teaching: Love deepens where two people see each other's qualities and let their hearts speak plainly.
st.vr.ram_sita_love_grows.whole_arc_note: Keep it small. The passage is about affection that grows from qualities and from inner openness over time, in a marriage arranged by elders. Do not inflate it into a romance, and do not use it to say every arranged match will turn out so.

st.vr.ram_remembers_one_kindness.title: What Ram was like before any trouble came
st.vr.ram_remembers_one_kindness.teaching: What you choose to keep in memory shapes who you become: keep the kindness.
